AC system piping contamination caused by droplet entrainment from S/P water during containment venting at Fukushima Daiichi NPS Unit 1
abstract: The high-level contamination in the atmospheric control (AC) system piping in Fukushima Daiichi NPS Unit 1 (1F1) was believed to be related to primary containment vessel (PCV) venting; however, the mechanisms remain unclear. The Nuclear Regulation Authority’s study group examined potential causes, such as leakage from vacuum isolation valves or a decrease in the decontamination factor due to boiling under reduced pressure; however, these factors could not explain the contamination. Therefore, based on the similarity between JAEA’s ALPHA test of aerosol entrainment from a flashing pool and the 1F1 accident, we investigated whether the contamination of the AC system piping could be attributed to the deposition of droplets entrained from the pressure suppression pool. Our study showed that the radioactive entrained droplets passing through the AC system piping were nearly identical to the environmental release predicted by WSPEEDI reverse calculations during PCV venting. Furthermore, in Unit 3 (1F3), which underwent PCV venting similarly to that in 1F1, no significant contamination was observed in the AC system piping. The differences between 1F1 and 1F3 clarify why contamination increased only during PCV venting in 1F1. Therefore, from the perspective of insights gained and source term reduction, recommendations are provided regarding the factors to consider when implementing PCV venting.

Experimental Evaluation of Cesium Removal from Contaminated Concrete by Preheating and Attrition Treatment
abstract: Laboratory-scale preheating and attrition experiments were conducted using simulated CsCl-contaminated concrete containing 0.063 mmol Cs/g to evaluate Cs distribution fractions among recycled aggregates and powder fractions under controlled laboratory conditions. Preheating and attrition treatment is a mortar-removal technique for concrete based on mechanical milling. SEM/EDS observations revealed that Cs was predominantly distributed in the mortar phase, whereas its concentration in aggregates was negligible. After 2 h of preheating and attrition treatment at 300 o C, the Cs concentration in recycled aggregates decreased to 0.002–0.027 mmol Cs/g, corresponding to a maximum reduction of 96.2% relative to the original contaminated concrete. Mass-based Cs distribution analysis indicated that more than 80% of the total Cs was transferred to fine powder fractions during treatment. Although preheating at 500 o C accelerated mortar removal, excessive thermal damage caused fragmentation of aggregates and hindered effective recovery of recycled aggregates. These results demonstrate that moderate-temperature heating combined with mechanical attrition enables selective separation of low-Cs-contaminated concrete composite (aggregates) from high-Cs-contaminated concrete composite (mortar) and provides quantitative insight into the achievable Cs removal extent during the preheating and attrition process.

Experimental evaluation of a modular phase-change material-based thermal energy storage system
abstract: Latent heat thermal energy storage (LHTES) offers a compact and energy-dense solution for residential heat storage; however, its practical deployment remains limited by challenges such as low thermal conductivity, uncertainty in heat release from supercooled states, and a lack of experimentally validated system-level performance at the household scale. This study presents the innovative solution in the developed control system and the precise experimental evaluation of a modular phase change material (PCM)-based thermal storage system designed for domestic applications with controllable on-demand heat release. The developed heat thermal energy storage system is based on sodium acetate trihydrate (SAT) and is evaluated under realistic charging and discharging conditions using a controlled hydronic loop. A key methodological contribution is the integration of loop calorimetry with a dense three-dimensional network of 105 in-situ temperature sensors that enabled detailed system-level analysis. In addition, a transparent tank design provides direct optical process behavior and state access, allowing for improved interpretation of thermal processes and front propagation. The novelty of the work lies in combining controllable supercooling with a modular household-scale demonstrator and a multi-modal experimental approach for system-level validation. The experimental results show stable repeated charging and discharging without phase separation. Thermal mapping reveals that the heat-transfer front originates at the finned aluminum heat exchanger and propagates toward the peripheral regions of the PCM. The focus of the study is on a long-duration experiment, including an intentional idle period, system measurement data, and energy efficiency computation. These results demonstrate the feasibility of controllable, on-demand heat release in PCM-based storage and provide quantitative insights for system optimization in real residential applications.

Numerical Study on the Influence of Upstream Groove Morphological Parameters on Flow and Heat Transfer Characteristics of Tandem Cylinders at Low Reynolds Numbers
abstract: The thermal performance is crucial in heat exchange and cooling systems, and surface structure optimization to enhance performance has become a key topic in fluid dynamics research. This study uses numerical simulations to investigate the effect of different surface patterns on the thermal behavior of a tandem cylinder system. The system consists of cylinders with identical diameters (D) and a spacing of 4D, where the upstream cylinder has grooves and the downstream cylinder is smooth. The study is conducted under laminar flow conditions (Re ≤ 200), analyzing three groove structures (square, triangle, and dimple) and exploring the impact of different groove frequencies (N = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10) on thermal performance. The results indicate that, at Re = 100 and N = 10, square grooves promote stable secondary vortices, thereby suppressing the continuous renewal of near-wall vorticity. In contrast, triangular and dimpled grooves enhance shear-layer oscillations and reattachment processes, resulting in a more uniform and strongly unsteady near-wall vorticity distribution. Moreover, the heat transfer efficiency increases with Re. Specifically, at Re = 200, dimpled and triangular grooves show a 2% and 2.4% improvement in heat transfer compared to square grooves. In general, higher groove frequencies reduce heat transfer efficiency, but at Re = 200 and N = 10, the heat exchange performance of dimpled and triangular grooves outperforms square grooves. The study also establishes a correlation between time-averaged Nusselt number to groove area, Re, and N.

title: Mathematical modeling of sorption immobilization and dehydration of saline liquid radioactive waste using expanded perlite M100
abstract: Saline liquid radioactive waste (LRW) can be generated during the operation and decommissioning of nuclear facilities, requiring safe treatment and long-term isolation. Conventional treatment methods require high energy consumption and complex infrastructure. For facilities with large accumulated inventories of LRW, such as the BN-350 reactor plant, low-energy approaches enabling conversion of waste into a non-flowable state are highly relevant. Sorption immobilization using porous mineral sorbents represents a promising option; however, its practical implementation requires a quantitative description of kinetically limited sorption and subsequent moisture removal processes. In this work, two complementary computational modules were sequentially developed. At the first stage, a mathematical description of water sorption from an LRW solution by expanded perlite M100 was formulated based on a hybrid model that accounts for temperature dependence and salt precipitation during solution concentration. At the second stage, a two-dimensional model of diffusion-controlled dehydration of the “perlite-salt precipitate” system was implemented using numerical simulation and validated against the results of two independent laboratory experiments. The obtained results confirm the applicability of sorption immobilization as a low-energy and technologically simple approach for the treatment of large volumes of LRW, while the developed model can be used to estimate processing timeframes and support process scale-up for industrial implementation.

Numerical Simulation of the Behavior of Radionuclide Polonium under a Typical Accident in Lead-Bismuth-Cooled Reactors
abstract: The safety concerns associated with polonium ( 210 Po) are critical for the development of lead-bismuth reactors. To investigate the release and migration of polonium following a lead-bismuth eutectic (LBE) coolant leakage accident, this study combines accident sequence analysis with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. The research systematically summarizes the solidification process of molten LBE and the post-solidification polonium release rate curve, while quantitatively analyzing the migration behavior of 210 Po after LBE leakage into the reactor pit. The results showed that in the solidification process of liquid LBE, the radioactive concentration of 210 Po at the bottom of the reactor pit increased sharply, and the concentration on the exhaust vent was higher due to ventilation. After the LBE solidified, the total activity of 210 Po in the reactor pit decreased significantly, but the space with concentration exceeding the limit value continued to increase and tended to be stable after a period of time. There were differences in the concentration peak value and the time to reach the safety limit value at each monitoring point in the reactor pit, but the trend of concentration changes was similar. The change in the concentration of radioactive effluents at the exhaust vent clarified the key time nodes for accident emergency treatment. In addition, the research has found that the surface enrichment behavior of polonium enhances the migration of polonium over long-time scales. The research results provide support for the design and radiation protection of lead-bismuth-cooled reactor.

Intrusion Analysis for Physical Protection Systems Based on Multilevel Flow Modeling
abstract: : Physical protection systems (PPS) constitute the primary barrier against the risks of theft and sabotage at nuclear facilities. Prevailing PPS assessment approaches emphasize path-vulnerability analysis and multi-criteria decision-making, yet they have not provided a comprehensive representation and causal reasoning from the perspective of system-level functional consistency. From a PPS functional-consistency standpoint, we introduce Multilevel Flow Modeling (MFM) into PPS modeling and analysis, develop an MFM/PPS functional modeling approach, and, using the physical protection system of a representative small modular reactor as a case study, construct cross-hierarchical functional models and validate causal inference. Within a means-end hierarchical framework, MFM/PPS links detection, delay, and response functions to the top-level PPS objective and uses qualitative causal reasoning to identify vulnerable links in the defense chain and propagation pathways of component failures. Results indicate that MFM/PPS effectively reveals latent goal-support vulnerabilities and cross-path critical-barrier risks in PPS design, enables assessment of redundancy adequacy, and enhances system integrity and interpretability.

Reliability-based probabilistic finite element analysis of nonlinear thermal conduction in IFMIF-DONES HFTM specimen capsules
abstract: Nuclear fusion is a promising candidate to meet long-term energy demands, but its deployment requires structural materials capable of withstanding the extreme thermo–mechanical conditions of future power plants. In the International Fusion Materials Irradiation Facility - DEMO Oriented Neutron Source (IFMIF-DONES), the thermal performance of specimen capsules in the High Flux Test Module (HFTM) is governed by strongly temperature-dependent properties and heterogeneous nuclear heating, which render the problem inherently nonlinear. This work develops a probabilistic Finite Element (FE) framework for the reliability-based thermal design of HFTM specimen capsules. A three-dimensional nonlinear model is formulated with temperature-dependent thermophysical properties and nuclear heating prescribed at Gauss points from neutronic transport calculations. Convective boundary conditions at helium-cooled surfaces are represented by effective heat transfer coefficients, initially estimated from the Gnielinski correlation and subsequently refined by constrained optimisation. The FE solver is coupled with Monte Carlo sampling to evaluate failure probabilities with respect to temperature range and uniformity. Three complementary performance metrics are introduced to interpret the IFMIF-DONES thermal requirements in terms of local and global reliability. Sensitivity analysis based on standardised (rank) regression coefficients identifies heater efficiency, helium-gap conductivity and Eurofer97 thermal conductivity as key drivers of thermal reliability, highlighting the need for accurate characterisation of these parameters in future HFTM designs.

abstract: Low-load operation of marine hydrogen–diesel dual-fuel engines may deteriorate engine performance and hydrogen combustion efficiency. To address this issue, this study proposes a strategy that combines an increased compression ratio with split diesel injection to restore engine performance and reduce NOx emissions. A CFD model of a 10.5 MW-rated marine engine was developed and validated against experimental data for both diesel and hydrogen-diesel dual-fuel operation. The effects of compression ratio, diesel injection timing, and diesel split injection control were examined both individually and in combination at 20% load. The results show that the combination of elevated compression ratio and advanced diesel injection timing enables performance comparable to the diesel baseline at 60% hydrogen substitution ratio (HSR), but with a NOx penalty, whereas the individual strategies are insufficient to recover baseline performance. The most effective strategy is the combination of high compression ratio (CR = 19) and diesel split injection. At the recommended control point of 60% HSR, this strategy achieves a hydrogen combustion efficiency of 96.5% and an indicated thermal efficiency of 53.9%, corresponding to a 3.0% improvement over the diesel baseline, while reducing NOx emissions by 1.59 g/kWh. This study demonstrates the performance potential of low-load operation and offers insights into the stable and efficient operation of hydrogen-fueled marine engine under varying loads.

Calculation of kinetic parameters in lead-cooled fast reactors
abstract: In Lead Fast Reactors (LFRs), some accurate calculations of the kinetic parameters β eff and Λ eff are necessary because of their fast kinetics. The response frequency to a reactivity change exhibits a weak sensitivity to the mean neutron generation time, implying that relatively larger uncertainties in Λ eff can be tolerated during low-reactivity transients. Monte Carlo methods represent the current best-estimate approach for the evaluation of kinetic parameters, thanks to their capability to model complex geometries and detailed neutron physics without homogenization assumptions. Among these, the Iterated Fission Probability (IFP) method enables the direct calculation of β eff and Λ eff within Monte Carlo frameworks. However, the recent implementation of the IFP method in the OpenMC code has not yet been systematically validated for fast reactor systems, which are essential for the reliable deployment of LFR technology. To address this gap, a set of MOX-fuelled experimental benchmarks representative of fast-spectrum systems is selected from the ICSBEP and IRPhEP databases and modelled using OpenMC and Serpent. The objective is not merely to reproduce reference values, but to assess the capability of Monte Carlo IFP implementations to reproduce experimental kinetic parameters within uncertainty bounds. The computed kinetic parameters are compared against reference values from experimental measurements and high-fidelity calculations when measurements are unavailable. Different calculation methods and nuclear data libraries are considered to evaluate associated uncertainties. Additional analyses are performed to assess the impact of temperature, neutron leakage, and fuel inventory evolution under irradiation. Sensitivity and representativity analyses are carried out to quantify nuclear data uncertainties and to support the transposition of validation results from fast-spectrum benchmarks to LFR systems, in accordance with ASN Guide 28. The results show that both OpenMC and Serpent are able to reproduce experimental kinetic parameters within acceptable uncertainty margins. This work provides a targeted validation of the IFP methodology for fast reactor systems and supports its application to the estimation of kinetic parameters in LFR designs under development.

Pool Boiling Heat Transfer of Horizontally Oriented Double-Sided Enhanced Tubes
abstract: This study experimentally investigates the pool boiling heat transfer characteristics of R134a on the outer surfaces of three double-sided enhanced tubes with different surface structures at a saturation temperature of 6 °C (corresponding to a saturation pressure of 361.98 kPa) and heat fluxes ranging from 25 to 60 kW/m2. The internal helical grooves enhance boundary-layer disturbance and turbulent mixing, while the external fin arrays increase the available surface for bubble nucleation and the density of active nucleation sites, thereby promoting bubble generation and departure. The experimental results show that the refrigerant-side heat transfer coefficients of the E1, E2, and E3 tubes are 5.78–6.79, 5.33–6.71, and 4.31–6.02 times higher than those of the smooth tube, respectively. When the heat flux exceeds 35 kW/m2, the E1 tube facilitates bubble growth and timely detachment, reduces thermal resistance, and exhibits superior heat transfer performance. Four existing correlations were evaluated, and a new correlation was developed based on the present experimental data. The proposed correlation predicts 93% of the measured data within ±15% error.

title: Effect of Rectangular Winglet Pairs in Fin-Tube Heat Exchanger: An Irreversibility Analysis
abstract: The present study investigates the entropy-generation and irreversibility characteristics of air flow across a fin-and-tube heat exchanger fitted with rectangular winglet pairs (RWPs). A three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics analysis was carried out for Reynolds numbers between 2000 and 4000 and angles of attack of 15°–60°, considering RWP locations at upstream, adjacent, and downstream positions relative to the tube centerline. The total, thermal, and viscous entropy-generation rates were evaluated using second-law formulations, and exergy-based parameters such as the entropy-generation ratio (EGR), irreversibility distribution ratio, Bejan number, and thermal efficiency index were employed to assess overall performance. Results show that an upstream RWP at 30° angle of attack and Reynolds number of 3000 provides the best thermodynamic performance, reducing the total entropy-generation rate by approximately 17% (EGR = 0.83) and increasing the heat-transfer improvement number by about 18%. The Bejan number remains above 0.95 for all cases, confirming that heat-transfer-related irreversibility dominates over viscous effects. Exergy analysis further indicates that the total irreversibility decreases while the thermal improvement factor increases with optimized RWP placement. The findings offer practical guidance for the design of energy-efficient fin-tube heat exchangers using vortex generators.

title: Experimental Investigation of Integrated Heat Pipe—Liquid Cooling for a Battery Pack
abstract: This study investigates a hybrid tab-cooled heat sink combining sintered-wick copper heat pipes embedded in a high-conductivity aluminum block with computer numerical control machined serpentine liquid cooling channels for a 15-cell lithium-ion battery pack (capacity: 2.5 Ah per cell, parallel connection). Performance was evaluated under constant-current discharge rates (1, 3, and 4 C, where C denotes nominal capacity rating) and automotive drive cycles (Urban Dynamometer Driving Schedule (UDDS), Short Dynamometer Driving Schedule (SDDS), and Worldwide Harmonized Light Vehicles Test Procedure) at coolant flow rates from 0 to 0.5 liters per minute. At 3 C discharge, peak temperature decreased from 81.6 °C to 62.9 °C with active cooling, extending safe operation from 50 to 93% depth-of-discharge before reaching the 60 °C threshold. Temperature variation among cells was reduced by 40%. Dynamic drive cycles showed peak temperature reductions of 19 °C (UDDS) and 22 °C (SDDS). Thermal resistance analysis revealed maximum reductions of 66% (1 C) and 39% (3 C) versus baseline. At low discharge rates, the system is convection-limited, making liquid cooling highly effective. However, at high rates (3–4 C), heat pipe operational limits become the primary constraint, indicating applications requiring sustained operation above 3 C would benefit more from enhanced heat pipe capacity than from increased liquid cooling flow rates.

Effects of multiple simultaneous soft faults in variable-speed rooftop units: Experimental analysis and criticisms in detection and diagnosis
abstract: Soft faults in cooling systems, such as heat exchanger fouling or improper refrigerant charge, commonly arise from inadequate maintenance practices. To mitigate energy performance degradation, effective fault detection and diagnosis techniques must be implemented. However, diagnosing multiple simultaneous faults remains particularly challenging, especially in variable-speed systems, where control-induced interactions can significantly distort conventional fault signatures originally established for constant-speed operation. Based on the outcomes of previous experimental investigations on single faults, this study experimentally investigates the combined effects of evaporator fouling, condenser fouling, and refrigerant undercharge in a 17.5 kW c variable-speed rooftop unit. The analysis examines how individual fault signatures interact, dominate, compensate for one another, or deviate from linear superposition. The results indicate that sensible cooling capacity degradation is primarily driven by evaporator fouling, with reductions of 14.1% and 18.4% observed under evaporator fouling alone and under combined evaporator and condenser fouling conditions, respectively. An additional 3–4% decrease in capacity is observed when refrigerant undercharge is further introduced. In terms of thermodynamic variables capable of detecting the anomalies, the discharge pressure and the subcooling remain condenser fouling-dominated in the fouled unit with correct refrigerant charge; conversely, the undercharge induces nonlinear and competing effects, such as a mitigation of the discharge pressure increase (with residuals up to 2.4 bar). A symptom matrix is proposed to classify linear dominance, nonlinear contributions, and competing interactions under multiple-fault conditions, revealing that diagnostic rules derived under single-fault or fixed-speed assumptions cannot be directly extended to variable-speed systems operating under concurrent disturbances, where control-induced compensation reshapes fault observability.

Autonomous multi-object tracking coupled with infrared thermography for two-phase flow analysis in pulsating heat pipes under variable gravity
abstract: A Multi-Object Tracking (MOT) algorithm is introduced for analysing two-phase slug–plug flows through the simultaneous measurement of bubble velocity and infrared-based liquid temperature. Vapour bubbles are detected through the infrared intensity contrast arising from the distinct emissivity and transmissivity of the liquid and vapour phases, enabling robust dichotomic phase segmentation. The tracking procedure builds on a nearest-neighbour approach, augmented with a custom weighted function designed to ensure reliable bubble pairing across consecutive frames. The approach is demonstrated on a flexible polymeric flat Pulsating Heat Pipe (PHP) filled with FC-72 and tested under microgravity and hypergravity conditions during the 77th ESA Parabolic Flight Campaign. More than 5800 tracking events were processed, providing detailed velocity profile and liquid temperature trends in the adiabatic section, with a minimum detectable velocity of 4 mm/s within a range of ±200 mm/s. The method offers a quantitative characterization of slug–plug flow dynamics together with a combined velocity–temperature analysis under variable gravity, establishing a robust pathway for automated diagnostics of two-phase flow in thermographic experiments.

title: From air to water: science, technology, and future of atmospheric water harvesting (AWH)
abstract: Water scarcity is one of the most serious challenges facing the world today, especially in regions with limited access to clean and reliable water sources. Atmospheric Water Harvesting (AWH) is an emerging technology that offers a sustainable and decentralized way to collect fresh water directly from the air. This review focuses on recent developments in AWH systems, especially those introduced after 2020, and explains how these systems are improving in terms of efficiency, energy consumption, and suitability for different climates. This review compares the performance, limitations, and deployment readiness of four major AWH classes: condensation-based systems that cool air to condense water vapor, sorption-based systems that use desiccant materials to absorb and release water, radiative cooling systems that use heat loss to the night sky to form dew, and hybrid systems that combine multiple approaches to improve performance. New materials such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), hygroscopic polymers, and phase-change materials have increased the ability of Atmospheric Water Generator (AWG) devices to extract water even in low-humidity environments, while also reducing energy needs. Solar power and other renewable energy sources are being used to make AWH systems more environmentally friendly and completely off-grid. Distinguishing itself from existing literature primarily focused on laboratory-scale material science, this paper presents a holistic, post-2020 synthesis of Atmospheric Water Harvesting (AWH) that prioritizes system-level operationality. This study integrates technical performance, environmental adaptability, and empirical benchmarking of Atmospheric Water Generators (AWGs) tested under real climatic conditions. Furthermore, it validates the transition from lab to field by including microbial safety benchmarks and evaluating decentralized, sustainable water security. This paper also highlighted case study of a solar-powered TEC-AWG system that demonstrated promising energy to water conversion and met basic microbial safety benchmarks. The water collected met drinking standards based on bacterial testing. Although AWH technologies are improving, challenges such as high costs, the need for thermal regeneration, and integration with other systems still exist. The review emphasizes AWH’s relevance for off-grid, arid, and disaster-prone regions, and discusses pathways for commercial scaling. Moreover, this review concludes by highlighting future research areas such as advanced control using machine learning, use of waste heat, and development of durable and low-cost materials.

title: Coupled effects of substrate temperature, inclination, and CNT/PS hybrid nanoparticles on evaporation and deposit morphology of sessile droplets
abstract: Evaporation and deposition of particle-laden droplets on substrates are central to coating, printing and thermal management. The coupled roles of substrate inclination, temperature and particle composition remain insufficiently quantified. In this study, sessile droplets containing mixed CNT/PS nanoparticles are placed on substrates at different temperatures and inclination angles, and the transient droplet shape, liquid–vapour interfacial temperature, and final sedimentary patterns are systematically analysed. At low temperatures, droplets exhibit pronounced sliding on inclined surfaces, reflected by temporary increases in the normalised contact diameter. A cooling-degree metric, I cold, is proposed together with deviation and stability indicators, which reveal that higher inclination angles stabilise interfacial cooling and shift the interfacial cooling centre toward the downhill side. In contrast, higher substrate temperatures enhance thermal disturbance due to improved internal heat conduction. Meanwhile, this study proposes parameters to explore the synergistic effects of gravity, substrate temperature, and loaded particle type on sedimentary patterns. The study notes that the coffee-ring pattern on inclined substrates is strongly asymmetric: the lower half of the ring is systematically thicker, and this asymmetry is amplified by increased PS loading and higher substrate temperatures. Gravity primarily controls the macroscopic thickness asymmetry, whereas substrate temperature and particle composition govern microscopic roughness, as evidenced by the fluctuation coefficient R σ , the effective correlation length ξ eff , and the spectral energy ratio between high- and low-frequency height modes R E . These results provide a quantitative framework for tuning droplet evaporation and particle deposition on inclined surfaces through combined control of inclination, heating and nanoparticle formulation.

Specific Absorbed Fractions and S Values for Alimentary Tract of Korean and Asian Populations
abstract: To support nuclear medicine dosimetry for Korean and Asian populations, this study established comprehensive datasets of specific absorbed fractions (SAFs) and radionuclide S values in the alimentary tract using the mesh-type reference Korean phantoms (MRKPs). SAFs were computed for photons and electrons (0.001–10 MeV) and alpha particles (1–12 MeV). By coupling these SAFs with ICRP-107 nuclear decay, S values were derived for 1,252 radionuclides, including 333 radionuclides of relevance to nuclear medicine. All calculations were performed using Geant4 Monte Carlo code. Selected results were then compared with corresponding values obtained using the ICRP-145 mesh-type reference computational phantoms (MRCPs), which are representative of Caucasian populations, to assess inter-population differences. While small differences within 20% were generally observed, non-negligible differences were observed in specific cases. For example, in the female stomach with contents as source region and stem cells as target region, electron SAFs differed by up to 61%, and S values differed by up to 31% for selected therapeutic radionuclides. Because the datasets developed in this study explicitly reflect anatomical and anthropometric characteristics of Korean and Asian populations, they are expected to provide a more reliable, population-specific foundation than currently available datasets for nuclear medicine dosimetry in these populations.

Nuclear Structure Evolution and Collective Dynamics in Even–Even 98−108Ru Isotopes via IBM-1 and IBM-2
abstract: This theoretical study investigated the low-lying collective excitations of the 98-108 Ru isotopes within the frameworks of IBM-1 and IBM-2. The evolution of nuclear structure is reflected in the increasing R4/2 ratios from 2.14 in 98 Ru to 2.745 in 108 Ru, indicating a gradual transition from vibrational U(5) toward O(6) and more rotational-like behavior. The calculated energy spectra, quadrupole properties, and collective observables including the g-factors showed good overall agreement with the experimental data. These results are the best from previous studies. Nevertheless, certain discrepancies persist, particularly in weak interband B(E2) transitions and sensitive B(M1) transition strengths, reflecting the intrinsic model limitations. The root-mean-square errors in the energy-levels are up to 91.1and 126.6 keV and R 2 values reaching up to 0.9984 compared and 0.9914 for IBM-2 and IBM-1, respectively. For B(E2) values, IBM-2 also achieves better agreement with experimental data where the RMSE decreases from 0.073 to 0.00071 e 2 b 2 and R 2 value is equal to 1. Furthermore, the analysis of the potential energy surfaces confirms a gradual structural evolution with increasing neutron number, highlighting the interplay between the vibrational and rotational modes. Overall, the present results provide a coherent description of shape evolution and collective dynamics in the 98-108 Ru isotopic chain within the Interacting Boson Model framework.

Modeling a generic TRISO-fueled heat pipe microreactor using SCALE: Depletion, transportation criticality, and shielding
abstract: This paper demonstrates the applicability of the SCALE code system to tristructural-isotropic (TRISO)-fueled heat pipe microreactors through depletion, transportation criticality, and shielding analyses of a generic reference design. The study conducted supports US Nuclear Regulatory Commission code readiness efforts for advanced non–light-water reactor technologies and is intended as a code capability demonstration rather than as an optimization of a specific microreactor design. The modeled reactor employs high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) uranium oxycarbide (UCO) TRISO fuel and beryllium oxide (BeO) reflectors and operates at 7.5 MWth with a nominal lifetime of about 3 effective full power years. Representative cases for fresh and irradiated cores were selected to exercise SCALE methods relevant to reactor operation and post-irradiation transport. The discharged-core decay heat is approximately 6% of operating power immediately after shutdown. Transportation criticality calculations show that internal water ingress is the dominant reactivity effect, with fully flooded fresh core and irradiated core configurations remain above the subcriticality criterion, even with the available control mechanisms. Shielding calculations for a simplified transportation package indicate that normal-condition dose rates are governed mainly by shielding thickness and cooling time, whereas the breached hypothetical accident case is governed primarily by cooling time. Overall, the study shows that SCALE supports depletion, transportation criticality, and shielding evaluations efficiently for TRISO-fueled heat pipe microreactors within a single code system.

title: Spatio-temporal analysis of sprays by using Phase Doppler Anemometry data
abstract: Spray characterization commonly relies on statistical quantities assuming quasi-steady behavior, although stochastic and instability-driven mechanisms govern atomization. Despite widespread application of Phase Doppler Anemometry (PDA), the temporal characteristics of sprays and their implications for modeling are unexplored. Deviations from Poisson arrival statistics indicate droplet clustering, i.e., time-dependent behavior. The present study investigates the spatio-temporal characteristics of an airblast atomizer using PDA datasets, including droplet size, velocity, and arrival time. Interparticle arrival time distributions are evaluated against theoretical Poisson statistics using chi-squared testing and effect size analysis. Multimodality is observed in specific spray regions, indicating pronounced clustering and temporal intermittency. K -means clustering combined with gap statistics quantifies droplet clusters across 10,800 datasets covering various atomizing pressures, temperatures, liquids, and spatial positions. Approximately 30% of datasets exhibit clustering, affecting up to 40% of droplets. Cluster occurrence depends on atomizing pressure and spatial position, while no clear dependence on preheating temperature was observed within the investigated range of conditions. After removing secondary clusters, the spray approaches quasi-steady behavior, indicating that clustering dominates unsteadiness in the core region, while mixing governs peripheral fluctuations. Despite the identified clustering in arrival times, the distributions of droplet size and velocity remain statistically similar across clusters, indicating that clustering reflects temporal intermittency rather than dynamic sorting of droplet populations. This supports a kinematic packing interpretation consistent with intermittency imposed by the carrier flow. The results demonstrate that neglecting clustering may bias spray statistics and modeling, emphasizing the need to incorporate temporal structures into advanced spray models.

Large-scale vision-based interfacial characterization for heat transfer prediction in horizontal mini-channel flow boiling
abstract: Flow boiling is a promising solution for high heat flux thermal management, but existing models struggle to capture the strong coupling between local phase distribution, flow regime, and heat transfer coefficient (HTC). In this work, we combine high-speed visualization, advanced computer vision, and machine learning to build a regime-aware framework for horizontal mini-channel flow boiling under terrestrial conditions. A large dataset of 107 cases over broad ranges of inlet mass flux, wall heat flux, and inlet subcooling is acquired in a single mini-channel, and more than 3 . 8 × 1 0 5 images are processed with benchmarked instance-segmentation models, from which a refined YOLOv8-based pipeline is selected. The vision model yields spatially resolved, time-averaged interfacial features, including streamwise void-fraction and dry-fraction distributions, which reveal systematic trends with operating conditions and multiple flow regimes. These image-derived void-fraction profiles are then used to evaluate several standard void-fraction correlations, highlighting regime- and condition-dependent strengths and limitations. Finally, hybrid neural networks combining scalar operating parameters with one-dimensional axially varying interfacial distributions are developed: a quality-informed baseline using streamwise quality, and a region-resolved model using vision-based void- and dry-fraction distributions. The region-resolved model predicts local HTC with mean absolute percentage errors of about 14%–15%, while offering enhanced physical interpretability, demonstrating that vision-based interfacial distributions can effectively replace explicit quality profiles in HTC prediction and support more reliable, data-driven flow-boiling design.

title: Transfer learning of digital shadows for fouling monitoring in heat exchangers
abstract: Fouling is a prevalent challenge that requires precise monitoring and identification to maintain optimal heat exchanger performance. Typically, monitoring methods focus on controlled variables such as pressure, temperature, and the flow rates of hot and cold fluids. However, while some heat exchangers benefit from extensive historical data and comprehensive operational knowledge, others face limitations due to incomplete or insufficient information. This paper proposes a methodology that combines data-driven modeling with transfer learning techniques, specifically Joint Distribution Adaptation (JDA), to diagnose the state of the heat exchanger. Using temperature data from a well-documented source heat exchanger, we identify a reference auto-regressive (AR) model under clean conditions to serve as a digital shadow of the physical system (heat exchanger). As the operating conditions of the heat exchanger change, deviations (errors) between the observed and predicted behavior evolve, providing a basis for monitoring. These changes are analyzed by extracting features from the error signals. To track the impact of fouling on system performance, a support vector machine (SVM) classifier is used to monitor the evolution of the global heat transfer coefficient. The knowledge and expertise gained from the source heat exchanger are then transferred to a target heat exchanger using a JDA algorithm, which may differ in geometry or operating conditions but requires more data to identify a new model or train a classifier from scratch. The results demonstrate the specific contexts and scenarios in which the trained and classified model from the source heat exchanger can be effectively applied to the target exchanger, highlighting the potential of this approach to extend operational insights to data-limited systems.

title: Design optimization and sensitivity analysis of a nocturnal radiative cooling enclosure for a cylindrical body
abstract: This study presents an experimental and numerical investigation of an enclosure-type passive radiative cooling system. A cooled object, represented by a cylinder, was placed inside the box. A steady-state radiative–convective–conductive model based on a geometry-resolved radiosity formulation and view-factor matrices is developed to describe radiative exchange between the cooled object (cylinder), enclosure surfaces, and the sky. Experimental validation performed under four meteorological conditions shows good agreement with calculations, with a coefficient of determination R 2 = 0.994. The cylinder exhibits sub-ambient cooling, with temperature differences between the top and lateral surfaces remaining around 1–1.5 °C. A sensitivity analysis is performed to evaluate the influence of meteorological conditions, material emissivities, and geometric parameters on both the temperature drop and the cooling efficiency of the proposed radiative cooler (RC). The results showed that relative humidity and ambient temperature are the most influential atmospheric parameters, through their impact on the effective sky temperature. Among material properties, the emissivity of the cylinder is found as the dominant parameter which can improve cooling efficiency from 0.21 to 0.48. Inner-wall emissivity mainly affects the lateral surface and outer-wall emissivity has negligible influence. Geometric parameters, particularly cylinder elevation, significantly affect the performance of the RC. These results provide practical design guidelines for enclosure-based radiative cooling systems incorporating a cooled object.

abstract: This study presents the design and simulation of an energy degrader system for the Thailand Institute of Nuclear Technology (TINT) cyclotron facility, developed to reduce 15–30 MeV proton beams to 2–5 MeV for PIXE and PIGE applications. SRIM and Geant4 simulations were utilized to optimize foil thickness and characterize beam dynamics. Varying the foil thickness (0.1 -1.4 mm) achieved degraded energies between 2 and 15 MeV. However, multiple Coulomb scattering increased the energy spread (1–29%) and RMS transverse emittance 80–395 mm·mrad). Four representative cases yielded energies of 11.8, 9.1, 6.3, and 2.8 MeV, with energy spread peaking at 16.9% for the lowest energy. To mitigate beam quality degradation, a two-stage collimator system was implemented. This reduced the transverse emittance by approximately 5 mm·mrad compared to a single-collimator setup, achieving proton transmission rates of 0.3–2% (0.6–4 µA from a 200 µA initial beam). Radiation safety was evaluated by mapping the neutron ambient dose equivalent, H*(10), using Geant4. Peak neutron dose exceeding 1.5 × 10−12 µSv per primary proton near the degrader assembly, confirming that local shielding with borated polyethylene is essential. These results provide benchmark beam parameters for future PIXE and PIGE applications and support the design of downstream beam transport systems, including a dipole magnet spectrometer for energy selection and analysis.

title: Detection methods and measurement techniques for neutron beam characterization in boron neutron capture therapy: a review
abstract: Boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT) is a binary therapeutic modality whose efficacy depends not only on the targeting ability of boron drugs but also on the quality of the neutron beams, where the latter is determined by its characteristics – specifically its radiation components and their associated key beam properties. While simulations can provide valuable assessments of these characteristics, measurements offer more direct and reliable characterization, rendering them indispensable for neutron beam quality assessment. BNCT neutron beams comprise thermal neutrons, epithermal neutrons, fast neutrons, and gamma rays, and mastering the detection methods for these components is fundamental to quality evaluation. Building on these methods, a set of dedicated techniques targeting the diverse properties of BNCT beams has been developed and implemented throughout system commissioning, acceptance testing, and routine quality assurance procedures. To better align with clinical demands, further development and optimization of these detection methods and measurement techniques are needed. This review systematically summarizes the detection methods for the four radiation components and analyzes techniques for key beam properties, such as real-time beam intensity, neutron spectrum, neutron spatial distribution, out-of-field leakage, and in-phantom dose. By comprehensively synthesizing their principles, research status, and practical applications, this review provides critical insights into the potential and challenges of their clinical implementation, clarifies directions for future basic research and translation, and aims to accelerate BNCT technological innovation and clinical application.

Selective Precipitation of Strontium and Barium from Molten MgCl2 Following Chlorination Using Carbonate and Sulfate Reagents
abstract: Growing interest has focused on separation technologies that selectively dissolve high heat–generating fission products (FPs), such as strontium (Sr), in molten salts via direct chemical reactions with used nuclear fuel (UNF) without electrochemical processes, thereby reducing disposal volume. Separated FPs can be precipitated using suitable reagents and converted into stable waste forms for final disposal. Previous studies have shown that SrO in simulated nuclear fuel can be separated through chlorination with molten MgCl 2 , producing SrCl 2 that dissolves into the salt phase. This study investigates the precipitation behavior of Sr and Ba dissolved in MgCl 2 using two precipitants, K 2 CO 3 and MgSO 4 , following chlorination reactions between MgCl 2 and SrO or BaO. K 2 CO 3 preferentially reacted with MgCl 2 to form MgCO 3 , which decomposed into MgO and CO 2 (g), rendering it unsuitable for this system. In contrast, MgSO 4 reacted with Sr- and Ba-containing MgCl 2 melts to form SrSO 4 and BaSO 4 without generating additional Mg-containing by-products through reaction with the MgCl 2 solvent salt, although MgO originating from the preceding chlorination step may remain in the recovered solid products. When MgSO 4 was added to MgCl 2 containing both Sr and Ba, a mixed sulfate phase (Ba 0 . 75 Sr 0 . 25 SO 4 ) formed. These results demonstrate that sulfate-based precipitants are suited for the separation of Sr and Ba from molten MgCl 2 salts and offer a viable strategy for managing high heat–generating FPs.

title: Thermal characteristics of developing flow in an annular pipe
abstract: The paper investigates the behaviour of turbulent flow through a domain exhibiting an abrupt transition in cross-sectional geometry from a circular to an annular pipe using Large Eddy Simulation (LES). Three Reynolds numbers, based on the hydraulic diameter of the annular section, were selected, namely 8 900, 16 200 and 40 500, with an inner-to-outer diameter ratio of D inner / D outer = 0.5 and a Prandtl number of 4.327 (liquid water). Equal heat fluxes were applied to both the inner and outer surfaces of the annular section, ensuring a flux ratio q * = q ″ inner / q ″ outer = 1 . The results reveal significant flow laminarisation along the outer wall at the entrance of the annular section, driven by strong flow acceleration from the vena contracta, followed by its deceleration. In the locally retarded flow region near the outer wall, laminar and turbulent fluxes are both relevant. Farther downstream, as the flow redevelops a fully turbulent regime, turbulent heat fluxes become the primary driver. By contrast, the separated flow region adjacent to the inner wall displays turbulent shear stresses nearly an order of magnitude higher than those in fully developed annular flows. Consequently, turbulent fluxes are most significant at the inner wall. The heat transfer results obtained in this work allow assessment of Nusselt number correlations in developing annular flow, showing that the Gnielinski (2015, Heat Transfer Engineering , 36 (9), pp. 787–789 ) and Taler and Taler (2017, E3S Web of Conferences , 13, p. 02008), when combined with the Hausen distance correction, yield a good level of accuracy at the inner wall (10–30% relative difference).

Knudsen pump for atmospheric and over-atmospheric pressure applications: System design, fabrication procedure and performance evaluation
abstract: Knudsen pumps are promising candidates for vibration-free gas pumping in a variety of scientific and industrial applications, particularly where miniaturization is required. Based on thermal transpiration flows induced by temperature gradients along microchannels, they operate without moving parts and therefore offer high reliability. However, current fabrication techniques limit the realization of submicron channels needed for high performance operation at atmospheric and over-atmospheric pressures. To address this challenge, the present study investigates the feasibility of using Bessel beam technology for channel fabrication, enabling the creation of dense arrays of nanochannels with diameters of only a few nanometers at writing speeds of up to 1 kHz. Numerical simulations of gas flow and heat transfer were performed to design and optimize a single-stage, parallel-channel architecture while accounting for microfabrication constraints. The proposed design consists of 294,294 parallel nanochannels arranged within a 1 × 1 cm 2 glass substrate, each with a diameter of 600 nm and a length of 500 μ m . Under simulated atmospheric operating conditions with moderate heating up to 100 °C, an average temperature difference of approximately 46.8° C across the channels is predicted, resulting in a thermomolecular pressure difference of 1575 Pa and a maximum mass flow rate of 3.43 × 10 − 10 kg s − 1 . When normalized by the total channel area, the predicted mass flow rate is much higher than previously reported Knudsen pumps, while maintaining a pressure difference among the highest values reported in the literature. The results demonstrate the potential of Bessel beam microfabrication for future high-performance Knudsen pumps operating at over-atmospheric pressures.

title: A Real-Time Digital Twin Simulation Platform for the AHPR1000 Safety System Test Facility
abstract: To address the high risk of high-temperature and high-pressure physical testing, the long testing cycle, and the low efficiency of control logic integration in integrated safety system tests for advanced pressurized water reactors, this study proposes a real-time digital twin simulation platform for the AHPR1000 integrated safety system test facility based on closed-loop coupling between a mechanistic model and a virtual distributed control system (DCS). According to the requirements of steady-state operation, accident transient simulation, control logic verification, and operating condition reproduction, a full-scope thermal-hydraulic model covering 14 subsystems, including the reactor coolant system, pressurizer system, main steam system, feedwater system, safety injection system, and residual heat removal system, was established. A large-scale tag mapping, data interaction, and operating state management mechanism was further developed between the model side and the virtual DCS side. The platform supports real-time monitoring and control of more than 3000 tags and provides functions such as freeze/unfreeze, reset, snapshot saving, online parameter tuning, and multi-scenario switching. The steady-state validation results show that the platform reproduces key thermal-hydraulic parameters with good accuracy and can operate continuously and stably for more than 100 h. The transient validation results, taking a 2-inch cold-leg small-break loss-of-coolant accident as an example, demonstrate that the platform can reasonably reproduce key processes including primary loop depressurization, safety system actuation, tank level variation, and accident mitigation. The results indicate that the proposed method can effectively balance system-level physical fidelity, real-time performance, and closed-loop control integration requirements, and can provide technical support for safety system testing, control strategy verification, operator training, and digital twin applications in advanced nuclear power systems.

Feasibility of an Inconel mesh for the input absorber of an open cavity receiver at a solar tower
abstract: This study evaluates the feasibility of Inconel 600 wire mesh as an inlet absorber in open-cavity solar receivers under high-flux conditions. A combined semi-analytical and CFD-based approach is employed to quantify the coupled influence of mass flow rate and incident flux on the thermal response of the mesh and on the air recirculation ratio (ARR) of the receiver. The analysis showed that the ratio between mass flow rate and incident flux density governs the onset of thermal instabilities, with low values leading to pronounced local hot spots and temperatures exceeding 1000 °C under peak-flux conditions. Full-scale exposure tests of a VoCoRec module under high-flux artificial sunlight confirmed the predicted hot-spot locations and reveal severe degradation of the first mesh layer, including hole formation and oxide-scale spallation. Post-test characterization by optical microscopy, SEM and XRD indicated that material failure is driven by stress-assisted oxidation at wire intersections and bending regions, despite the nominal oxidation resistance of Inconel 600. The combined numerical and experimental evidence demonstrated that conventional woven Inconel mesh is rather unsuitable for operation near the upper temperature limits of Inconel 600 in tower receivers and highlighted straight-wire or alternative porous geometries as more robust design options for future inlet absorbers.

Nusselt number correlation for shell-side heat transfer in single-row spiral-wound heat exchanger under cryogenic conditions
abstract: Accurate Nusselt number correlations for shell-side heat transfer in single-row spiral-wound heat exchangers (SWHEs) are essential for the design of liquefied natural gas (LNG) plants and other cryogenic processes. No experimentally validated correlation for the transitional flow regime with a binary ethane–nitrogen working fluid at deep-cryogenic temperatures (T ≈ −100 °C) has previously been reported. The present paper addresses this gap with 22 steady-state measurements on a single-layer laboratory SWHE ( D shell = 75 mm, d out = 12 mm, A = 0.258 m 2 ) using a binary ethane–nitrogen mixture. Systematic variation of the molar ethane fraction yielded shell-side Reynolds numbers Re shell = 1539–2984 (transitional flow regime) and Prandtl numbers Pr = 0.724–0.800. The shell-side heat transfer coefficient h shell spanned 16.37–42.11 W·m −2 ·K −1 and the Nusselt number Nu shell = 8.7–24.9. A new correlation was derived by two-step ordinary least squares (OLS) regression on 13 training points ( R 2 = 0.709). The Prandtl exponent was fixed at 1/3 per Pohlhausen boundary-layer theory and the Chilton–Colburn analogy, preventing overfitting from the strong collinearity between Re and Pr in the dataset. Independent validation on a 9-point hold-out set yielded a mean absolute error MAE = 10.71%, with no systematic bias. Measurement uncertainties (Kline–McClintock propagation) gave Nu shell uncertainties of 3–8%. Comparison with fourteen published correlations (six variants of Messa et al. Messa et al. (1969) [29] plus eight further sources) confirmed that none predicts Nu shell within ±7% for the complete cryogenic dataset.

Dominant nuclide identification and progeny contribution to dose with a focus on controlled release scenarios
abstract: To establish emergency planning zones, it is necessary to understand how dose to residents changes with distance, represented as a dose–distance(D–D) curve, under different accident scenarios. Previous studies have shown that the nuclide contribution to dose—specifically, whether aerosol or gaseous nuclides are dominant—has a strong influence on the shape of D–D curves. The objective of this study is to identify the dominant nuclides for each accident scenario, focusing on progeny nuclides, to clarify the distinction between aerosol- and gas-dominated scenarios, and to quantitatively understand the characteristics of the D–D curves for each accident scenario under selected range of meteorological conditions. To this end, we developed a Python tool called “Dose Evaluation framework for Consequence-Informed and Scenario-Oriented Navigation: DECISION.” Modeling of progeny nuclides was found to have a substantial effect on controlled releases based on comparisons with monitoring post observations during the Fukushima–Daiichi accident. Dominant nuclides were identified, and the distinction between aerosol- or gas-dominated scenarios was clarified. The dominant nuclides for high decontamination factor (DF) scenarios are Kr-88 and Xe-135 (progeny nuclide of I-135) in 6- and 24-h release timing, respectively, regardless of precipitation. Meanwhile, the dominant nuclide among low DF scenarios is I-131, but the influence of Te-132 becomes evident under precipitation, regardless of release timing. Further, the characteristics of D–D curves for each accident scenario were identified, and it was suggested that the D–D curves were highly dependent on nuclides under precipitation, regardless of the stability class.

title: Development of integrated system-level analysis capabilities in SAM for molten salt reactors
Practical considerations for shielding-mass constraints on mobile heat-pipe microreactors
abstract: Mobile nuclear microreactors are frequently proposed for remote power generation, resilient energy systems, and defense-related applications. Although many designs emphasize compactness and autonomy, radiation shielding requirements impose fundamental constraints on reactor mobility. Mobile microreactors are intended to be moved repeatedly during their operational lifetime, often immediately following shutdown with limited cooling. Transportable reactors may be relocated after extended cooling periods, whereas relocatable systems are typically deployed once and moved only at end of life. These distinctions have significant implications for reactor design. This study evaluates shielding mass and pre-shipment cooling times as a function of reactor power as a first order consideration to determine whether a truly mobile microreactor is viable for a representative heat pipe microreactor concept. A highly enriched uranium (HEU) tri-structural isotropic (TRISO)–fueled heat pipe concept was scaled to fit within a typical conveyance, and then operation was modeled at three power levels to generate a representative source term for shielding thickness calculations. Results show that, for the HEU TRISO heat-pipe cases considered here, shielding mass strongly constrains the feasible mobile power envelope and becomes particularly restrictive near the 5 MW thermal (MWth) scale. The 5 MWth case approaches routine mobility feasibility assuming an idealized reactor-adjacent shielding configuration. Notably, the analyses neglect thermal constraints and the mass of other necessary reactor features and is therefore only useful as a cursory example of the practical restrictions that must be addressed to achieve routine microreactor mobility. However, it demonstrates the feasibility of a truly mobile microreactor at a useful power level. Because the modeled microreactor used HEU, the applicability for civilian deployment is limited. The findings further suggest that compact high-assay low-enriched uranium metallic fuel forms may offer significant advantages for future mobile reactor concepts.

Gamma-ray Compton scattering: a tool for activity localization in metallic waste arising from decommissioning
abstract: The Compton scattering phenomenon was investigated with the aim of characterizing metallic waste from decommissioning. The distinction and quantification of activity located on the surface or within the volume of steel samples and their concurrent determination can be achieved by using the photo-peak and the Compton-edge counts from experimental and Monte Carlo N-Particle (MCNP) simulated spectra. Two gamma-ray detectors were evaluated: a High-Purity Germanium (HPGe) and a Cerium Bromide (CeBr 3 ) scintillator detector. Simulated and experimental spectra of radioactive sources in steel were analysed. The Compton-to-photo-peak ratio (C/P) was determined for varying steel shielding thicknesses between the source and detector. Activity quantification and discrimination between surface and volume activity were demonstrated using the C/P versus the absolute photo-peak efficiency plot. The activity at the surface and within the volume in 1-mm-thick carbon steel slab arrays, with 137 Cs filter paper sources placed between the slabs and on the arrays, were validated through gamma-spectrometry measurements and simulations. Two methodologies based on photo-peak and Compton-edge analysis were employed. This study demonstrates that the localization and the concurrent quantification of both activities in metallic waste is feasible, enabling a more accurate evaluation of scaling factors and thereby an improved selection of decontamination and clearance procedures.

title: Investigation of pressure wave propagation under In-box LOCA scenario in the test blanket module for the CFETR COOL blanket
abstract: The supercritical CO 2 cOoled Lithium-lead (COOL) blanket is considered as one of the advanced blanket candidates for the Chinese Fusion Engineering Test Reactor (CFETR). The COOL Test Blanket Module (TBM) is designed based for the CFETR COOL blanket. The tritium breeding technology of the COOL blanket will be tested using the COOL TBM in the Chinese fusion test facility BEST. The COOL TBM employs the same material and similar structure with the CFETR COOL blanket to maintain relevance. In-box Loss-of-Coolant Accident (LOCA) is one of the most serious accidents of the TBM. Under the LOCA scenario in the COOL TBM, the leakage of 8 MPa S-CO 2 into the lithium-lead breeding zone generates intense localized pressure spikes, posing a severe threat to the structural integrity of the TBM. In this paper, the in-box LOCA is simulated using CFD methods to examine pressure-wave propagation inside the TBM and to investigate the influence of rupture size, rupture location, and lithium-lead initial pressure on the post-LOCA pressure distribution. The computational results indicate that the peak pressure can reach 12.5 MPa after the LOCA, which presents a significant challenge to the structural integrity of the blanket.

title: Study on the neutronics characteristics of a mixed-spectrum lead-bismuth fast reactor design based on BeO component box
abstract: Mixed-spectrum reactors offer improved neutron economy and safety, but fine spectral control via internal materials in lead-bismuth fast reactors remains unexplored. Beryllium oxide provides high thermal conductivity and excellent moderation, yet its systematic use as fuel assembly cladding for spectral softening lacks evaluation. This study investigates a mixed-spectrum lead-bismuth fast reactor core with beryllium oxide component boxes using OpenMC version 15.0 and the ENDF/B-VII.0 nuclear data library. By varying beryllium oxide thickness and fuel enrichment, a three-stage non-monotonic k eff evolution is revealed: first a decrease due to thermal neutron absorption, then an increase from 9 Be (n,2n) reactions, and finally a re-decrease caused by excessive moderation. The optimal thickness for neutron multiplication is 3.5 to 4 centimeters. At 16% enrichment, proper spectral softening raises the initial k eff to 127% of the zero-thickness case. Burnup analysis shows a window effect: an overly thin beryllium oxide box of 1.2 centimeters shortens core lifetime, while an appropriate thickness of 4 centimeters extends it. Power flattening requires strong boundary reflection; only with sufficiently strong reflection does a thickness of 2.4 centimeters achieve the most uniform power distribution. These findings provide quantitative guidance for mixed-spectrum lead-bismuth fast reactor design toward miniaturization, long lifetime, and proliferation resistance.

Energy micropiles for integrated bridge deck thermal regulation and abutment retrofitting
abstract: Transportation infrastructure, including bridges and viaducts, is increasingly affected by premature deterioration due to environmental exposure and mechanical fatigue. Conventional winter maintenance strategies based on salt-based deicers are inefficient at low temperatures and contribute to corrosion and environmental degradation, while rising summer temperatures intensify pavement fatigue and permanent deformations. In this context, this study investigates the integration of Energy Micropiles (EMPs) into structural retrofitting interventions, which are often required to enhance the load-bearing capacity of piers and abutments through foundation reinforcement. These systems combine structural strengthening with ground heat exchange, enabling the transfer of thermal energy to hydronic heated pavement systems embedded within the bridge deck. A two-dimensional finite element model is developed to simulate the coupled thermo-mechanical behaviour of an EMP-retrofitted abutment foundation under Mediterranean climatic conditions. The analysis quantifies both thermal performance and structural response under snow-melting (heat extraction) and cooling-down (heat injection) operation, Results show that the system can sustain continuous operation for approximately 2–3 days before thermal interference significantly reduces efficiency. In this period, the central micropile reaches peak heat fluxes of 92 W/m in winter and 132 W/m in summer, while edge micropiles maintain higher and more stable thermal exchange due to reduced thermal interference. Soil thermal conductivity is the dominant controlling parameter, increasing peak heat fluxes by up to +263%, whereas volumetric heat capacity contributes to longer-lasting but less pronounced thermal smoothing effects. From a mechanical perspective, thermally induced stresses remain limited, with maximum tensile stresses of approximately 250 kPa and compressive stresses up to 750 kPa, confirming that the structures are not compromised under operational conditions. However, prolonged operation leads to progressive thermal saturation of the surrounding soil, reducing efficiency and highlighting the need for intermittent operation strategies or auxiliary heat pump integration in high-demand periods. Overall, EMPs demonstrate a reliable dual functionality as both structural reinforcement elements and renewable energy exchangers. The findings provide direct engineering guidance for design, indicating that system layout, soil-dependent thermal performance, and operational scheduling must be explicitly considered to ensure safe, efficient, and durable implementation in bridge and viaduct retrofitting projects.

Flow boiling critical heat flux in MICRO-scale heat sinks and comparison with correlations
abstract: The growing demand for high-performance miniature electronics is forcing the heat dissipation requirements to increasingly higher levels. Flow boiling in micro-scale heat exchangers is a good choice for cooling these high heat flux devices. In such systems, the prediction of critical heat flux (CHF) is a crucial aspect in thermal-fluid system design, as it defines the maximum limits of thermal management systems. Different CHF mechanisms were identified and studied in the literature, leading to the development of numerous correlations. However, significant discrepancies still exist among these studies. The present study investigated experimentally the critical heat flux of HFE-7100 in single and multi-channels heat sinks. Saturated flow boiling experiments were conducted at inlet pressure of 1, 1.5 and 2 bar, inlet subcooling of 5 K and 10 K and mass flux of 100–750 kg/m 2 s. The wall heat flux was increased gradually until the CHF was reached at 435 kW/m 2 and 308.6 kW/m 2 for the single channel and the multi-channels, respectively. Events leading to the CHF occurrence were identified in the present study using a high-speed, high-resolution camera and thermocouple readings. The present results were also used to evaluate eight flow boiling CHF correlations, with some found to agree with the current experimental data. In the present study, both mass flux and inlet pressure had a noticeable effect on the CHF phenomenon. However, the effect of inlet pressure remains to be properly evaluated and included in these correlations.

Sampling Based Methods for Estimating Functional Failure Probability of Passive Safety Systems
abstract: Passive Safety Systems (PSSs) in nuclear power plants, although characterized by lower driving forces than active safety systems, can achieve high reliability due to their operation mechanisms being based on natural phenomena, which are inherently less prone to failure. However, because the operation of PSSs relies on complex Thermal–Hydraulic (TH) phenomena, they may fail to satisfy the required performance under various conditions, leading to functional failures caused by the combined effects of TH behavior and operating conditions even in the absence of mechanical component failures. Therefore, the reliability quantification of PSSs should consider both mechanical failure probability and functional failure probability. The latter typically requires repeated TH analyses and entails a significant computational cost. To address this challenge, the present study improves computational efficiency by simplifying input–output calculations based on the independence of variables and the principle of superposition. Although these definitions may cause discrepancies between actual system behavior and the approximated results during the sampling process, a conservative approach was adopted to compensate for potential errors. In particular, noting that recently designed Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) predominantly employ PSSs as their primary safety features, this study analyzes a model based on an SMR design incorporating such PSSs.

Simulation and modelling of a vibrating rod bundle: Finite elements model results and CFD-based prediction of added coefficients
abstract: Simulations of the ALAIN experiment, a reduced-scale model of a pressurized water reactor fuel assembly, were conducted to investigate the behaviour of a vibrating fuel assembly immersed in an axial flow. Analysis of the dry vibration of the assembly revealed that the mode shapes of the vibrating assembly closely match those predicted theoretically for an Euler–Bernoulli beam. However, predicting the vibration frequencies proved more challenging due to the presence of the grid-spring-dimple systems, which tend to reduce the natural frequencies. RANS simulations of the flow around the vibrating rod bundle indicate that the vibration has a negligible effect on the mean properties of the turbulent flow, but it significantly amplifies the magnitude of the forces acting on the assembly, particularly when the assembly is immersed in axial flow. This effect is captured by the fluid-added modal coefficients and a methodology allowing their computation from numerical simulations is presented.

Human Reliability Dependency Assessment in Beyond Design-Basis Accidents: Extending the EMBRACE Dependency Equation
abstract: A dependency assessment is used to explicitly model causal relationships between two or more human events within an accident scenario and to estimate the conditional occurrence probability of subsequent human failures under the existence of antecedent human failures. This paper extends an existing dependency assessment method [empirical data-based crew reliability assessment and cognitive error analysis (EMBRACE)] for use in the human reliability analysis (HRA) of beyond design-basis accident (BDBA) scenarios requiring diverse and flexible coping strategies (FLEX).This work first identifies the key dependency mechanisms that are insufficiently represented in conventional internal event HRAs, including equipment inoperability and inaccessibility under extreme hazards; insufficiency of temporal, spatial, and manpower resources; changes in decision-making organizations; and additional performance shaping factor degradations. A generalized dependency equation is then proposed that augments the original EMBRACE formulation with new variables for equipment inoperability and inaccessibility, resource insufficiency, and decision-maker sameness, while preserving the existing terms for procedure transition similarity, cue recognition dependency, recovery factor, and additional contextual effect.Two case studies, namely, a storm-induced station blackout with direct current load shedding and FLEX power restoration, and a multi-unit earthquake scenario with portable generators, demonstrate how the extended equation quantitatively captures BDBA-specific dependencies and yields conditional human error probabilities that reflect resource sharing, cognitive coupling, and environmental constraints. The results indicate that the proposed framework improves traceability and realism in dependency quantification for FLEX-related human failure events and can support risk-informed decision making for severe external hazard scenarios. This work also highlights the need for further empirical data on BDBA-related human performance and organizational behaviors.

title: Production of High-Purity 123 I Radioisotope from Natural and Enriched Tellurium Dioxide Using 122 Te(d,xn) 123 I Reaction: Simulations, Targetry, Purification, and Quality Analysis
abstract: Iodine-123 is a clinically important radionuclide used in single photon emission computed tomography for diagnostic imaging. This study presents the optimized production of high-purity 123I via the 122Te(d,n)123I nuclear reaction using natural and 99.6% enriched tellurium dioxide (TeO2) targets. Reaction cross sections were analyzed using the TALYS-based Evaluated Nuclear Data Library (TENDL-2023) and compared with available experimental data to identify an optimal deuteron energy range. Monte Carlo simulations performed with Stopping and Range of Ions in Matter (SRIM)/Transport of Ions in Matter (TRIM) determined the deuteron penetration depth and target thickness to achieve efficient energy deposition and maximum yield. Experimental irradiations were conducted on the U-120 cyclotron at Tomsk Polytechnic University, and the separation of 123I from irradiated TeO2 targets was performed through an automated dry distillation process. The optimal energy window of 8 to 14 MeV resulted in a 123I production yield of 62.65 MBq/μA·h when using 99.6% enriched TeO2 targets, whereas the maximum yield from natTe was 9.5 MBq/μA·h. The dry distillation at 700°C yielded 91% ± 4% recovery efficiency and more than 99.5% purity with minimal target loss. The results confirm that the 123Te(d,n)123I reaction is a technically viable and efficient route for producing clinical-grade 123I in small-to-medium cyclotron facilities, offering a reliable alternative to high-energy xenon-based production methods.

A simple formulation of heat flux factor for transient heat loads
abstract: The heat flux factor is used to characterize pulsed heat loads in high heat flux experiments on plasma-facing materials. a material-dependent quantity called the critical heat flux factor FHFC is introduced. It is the heat flux factor required for the surface temperature to reach a critical temperature. Based on the analytical solution of transient heat conduction in a semi-infinite solid, an analytical expression between FHFC, thermophysical properties, and temperature difference is derived. The formulation is intended as a simplified screening metric for the preliminary comparison of candidate plasma-facing materials, rather than as a substitute for detailed nonlinear thermal analysis. The results show material comparisons across the periodic table and temperature – heat-flux-factor maps illustrating characteristic material limits under transient heat loads.

title: Uncertainty propagation calculation from model parameters in thermal scattering of H-1 bound in H 2 O to neutronics parameters with deterministic sampling method and sandwich formula
abstract: In order to reduce the nuclear data-induced uncertainties in neutronics parameters of nuclear reactors, the data assimilation using integral data is promising. Generally, integral data used in the data assimilation are obtained at room temperature whereas concerned neutronics parameters are at high temperature, and thus this inconsistency in temperature can bring an issue. In the present paper, this is addressed by focusing on the thermal scattering cross sections of H-1 bound in H2O. Uncertainties of neutronics parameters due to the model parameter uncertainties in the TSL data evaluation is quantified with the deterministic sampling method and the sandwich formula using covariance matrices and sensitivity coefficients. It is demonstrated that the deterministic sampling method is effective and that uses of covariance matrices and sensitivities not for scattering cross sections but for scattering matrices are mandatory in the sandwich formula. Standard deviations of k∞ at high temperature of the LWR fuel pincells and correlations between them and keff of the critical experiments at room temperature are calculated. Results of the uncertainty propagation calculations are significantly dependent on the assumed uncertainties in the model parameters of thermal scattering.
