Detector-Targeted Weight Window Generation via Absorbing Markov Chain Reachability in Monte Carlo Transport
abstract: This work presents a detector-targeted, data-driven weight window (WW) generation procedure based on an absorbing Markov chain surrogate of neutron transport. A collision-indexed transition model is estimated from track-based tallies on a discretized state space, after which a sparse reachability solve yields the probability that a history starting from each state will eventually reach a user-specified detector region before termination. This reachability probability is used as an importance proxy to construct WW bounds for production simulations. The method is demonstrated on two-dimensional labyrinth streaming configurations derived from the Protvino benchmark, including a modified geometry with an additional bend. The resulting WW estimators remain statistically consistent with analog sampling while improving efficiency by approximately 10× in figure of merit (FOM) for the reference case and near 400× for the modified case. These results indicate that reachability-based, detector-specific importances can provide an inexpensive and effective pathway to automated WW generation for labyrinth streaming problems.

title: Expert Insights into Challenges in the Probabilistic Risk Assessment for Advanced Nuclear Power Technologies
abstract: The nuclear industry is advancing the design and deployment of new reactor technologies that incorporate safety-enhancing features. Meanwhile, weather-driven natural hazards can disrupt the operation of nuclear power plants (NPPs). Studies have indicated that the intensity, persistence, and frequency of these hazards are likely to increase over time. Given the limited operational experience with advanced nuclear technologies, it is essential to develop strategies to evaluate their safety and potential vulnerabilities under natural hazard conditions.To address these issues, we conducted a literature review and distributed a questionnaire to practitioners to gather insights into the effects of weather-related hazards on NPPs and the challenges of performing probabilistic risk assessments (PRAs) for advanced reactors. The collected responses were analyzed and synthesized to provide a consolidated perspective from the PRA community.Based on the respondents’ judgments, natural hazards capable of inundating NPP systems (e.g. flooding, severe storms, and hurricanes) are generally considered most significant for the safety of NPPs. These findings suggest respondents view the primary difficulties in developing a PRA for advanced reactors stemming from evolving designs and emerging technologies, rather than from limitations in the current PRA tools, techniques, standards, or guidance. Ultimately, these expert insights can inform research and development efforts aimed at enhancing PRA methods for advanced reactors.

title: MARVEL Microreactor System Thermal-Hydraulic Design and Analysis
Dynamic probabilistic risk assessment of seismically induced internal flooding considering aftershock effects using physics-based flood propagation and fragility models
abstract: This study develops a dynamic probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) method for combined earthquake and internal flooding events in nuclear power plants. The method explicitly integrates seismic fragility analysis with a flood propagation model, enabling evaluation of how earthquake-induced structural damage influences subsequent water intrusion, and vice versa, in a combined, interdependent manner. Seismic effects are evaluated using fragility functions across different ground-motion levels. These are implemented in a fault tree to estimate the failure probability of safety-related equipment. Internal flooding is evaluated by calculating the water level in each room and converting it into equipment failure probability using a water-level-dependent flood fragility model. The system behavior is treated as time-dependent. A state-transition-based dynamic PRA framework is used to update the probability of loss of function at each time step, consistent with a Markov-type state-transition formulation. Uncertainty in the leak rate and barrier damage is accounted for using a Monte Carlo simulation. By combining these models, the method can describe the progression of accident scenarios involving seismic damage and flooding. The results indicate that different scenarios can be governed by distinct mechanisms under different conditions. In some cases, seismic fragility is dominant, while in others, flooding becomes dominant. Mixed behavior is also observed. Therefore, this approach can be useful for evaluating complex scenarios that are difficult to treat with conventional PRA methods.

A plastic scintillator-based cosmic ray test platform
abstract: Cosmic-ray test platforms play a crucial role in the prototyping, calibration, and characterization of particle detectors, providing a cost-effective and flexible complement to accelerator-based beam tests. In this work, we present the design and performance of a versatile cosmic-ray test platform based on triangular plastic scintillator bars. The core tracking system consists of four measurement planes, each comprising two orthogonal layers of scintillator arrays. To reduce readout complexity while preserving high spatial precision, a wavelength-shifting fiber encoding scheme is employed. At the device-under-test position, the system achieves a spatial resolution of approximately 0.5 mm through a charge-weighted center-of-gravity reconstruction method. Benchmarking with a fused silica module demonstrates the platform’s accuracy in quantifying position-dependent photon yields and detection efficiencies. Our work shows that the hardware design, integrated with high-precision tracking reconstruction, provides a robust platform for cosmic-ray reconstruction. Furthermore, this system is adaptable for tracking applications in future particle and nuclear experiments

abstract: Metals with low melting points are used as thermal fluids in thermodynamic applications, like cooling circuits of advanced nuclear power plants or high temperature heat pipes. For alkali metals such as sodium and potassium, there is a risk of spontaneous, highly exothermic reactions with oxygen or formation of an explosive hydrogen atmosphere when in contact with water. In the event of a leak or a complete rupture of e.g., a heat pipe, liquid alkali metals will be released into the environment. These highly exothermic or potentially explosive reactions pose a hazard potential, which is currently difficult to assess. An experimental setup was developed, in which potassium is heated up and then released suddenly into air in a controlled manner. As a basis for further experimental work, reactions of potassium released at high temperatures into air are qualitatively evaluated at different temperatures and potassium quantities. The experiments allow to draw conclusions on the hazard potential and to ensure safety of staff and surroundings during mechanical testing of specimens filled with liquid potassium. The experimental methodology is transferable to other highly heated reactive coolants.

Large-eddy simulation of heat-generating molten salt flows in wall-bounded geometries: Application to molten salt reactors
abstract: Turbulent wall-bounded molten salt flows are encountered in Molten Salt Reactors (MSRs), where heat is generated volumetrically within the fluid due to nuclear reactions. This work aims to quantify the influence of volumetric heat generation on both Kolmogorov scales and large scales across different layers of turbulent molten salt flows characterized by low kinematic viscosity and high Prandtl numbers. For this purpose, turbulent channel flow of molten salt with variable thermophysical properties is modeled using Large-Eddy Simulation (LES). To verify the LES framework, a grid resolution study is first performed and the performance of five subgrid-scale (SGS) models (Smagorinsky, Turbulent Kinetic Energy (TKE), buoyancy-modified TKE, dynamic TKE, and WALE), together with an SGS-free approach are assessed through comparison with DNS data. The results demonstrate that the presence of a volumetric heat generation enhances SGS kinetic energy in the buffer layer (y+ < 40) while decreasing it in the outer layer. As a result, the Reynolds stress components increase in the near-wall region while decreasing at the channel center. Moreover, the mean Kolmogorov velocity scale ( u η ) decreases, while the mean Kolmogorov length scale ( η ) increases. Additionally, the results indicate that constant coefficient models, such as Smagorinsky and TKE fail to predict the solution accurately. Compared with the reference correlations, these models underpredict the friction factor by 39% and the Nusselt number by 82%, owing to their high dissipation rates and consequent inability to resolve small eddies. However, incorporating the buoyancy term into the TKE equation improves velocity predictions in the outer layers ( y + > 50 ).

title: Design Characteristics and Preliminary Performance Analysis on Passive Safety Systems of i-SMR
abstract: ABSTRACT An innovative small modular reactor (i-SMR) is being developed in the Republic of Korea with a fully passive safety concept comprising the passive auxiliary feedwater system (PAFS), passive containment cooling system (PCCS), and passive emergency core cooling system (PECCS). These systems are thermally and hydraulically coupled through the compact steel containment vessel (CV) and the emergency cooling tank (ECT), forming an integrated passive safety architecture. This study presents the design characteristics of the i-SMR passive safety systems and their preliminary thermal-hydraulic performance evaluated using MARS-KS. To investigate the integrated passive response, an inadvertent opening of one emergency depressurization valve (IOEDV), exhibiting thermal-hydraulic behavior similar to that of a loss-of-coolant accident, was analyzed. The results show rapid depressurization of the reactor coolant system, effective containment cooling, and subsequent gravity-driven recirculation from the CV to the reactor vessel through the PECCS. The CV pressure was reduced to less than one-half of its peak value within 24 h, and the primary system reached the safe shutdown condition within 36 h. Sustained natural circulation in the PAFS and PCCS and sufficient ECT inventory were maintained for 30 days without operator action, providing a system-level basis for future design verification and safety validation.

title: Thermodynamic origin of root-like architectures in topology-optimized porous electrodes
abstract: Recent studies have shown that topology optimization can generate high-performing porous architectures, often exhibiting graded, branched, or root-like morphologies. However, the physical origin of these recurring structures remains unclear. In this work, we develop a theoretical framework linking reaction–diffusion transport, topology optimization, and nonequilibrium thermodynamics to explain the emergence of root-like porous electrodes. Starting from a simplified first-order reaction–diffusion model with porosity-dependent effective properties, classical relationships for effectiveness factor and characteristic penetration depth are revisited and extended to graded media. Scaling arguments are then proposed for branch spacing, root thickness, and root length by balancing axial reactant delivery with lateral consumption in the surrounding reactive matrix. A thermodynamic interpretation is further introduced in which the penetration depth represents a crossover distance beyond which transport-related irreversibility becomes increasingly dominant. Density-based topology optimization is then employed to maximize overall reaction rate under finite porosity constraints. The optimized structures evolve from uniform to hierarchical root-like networks, showing substantially improved utilization compared with conventional uniform porous layers. The predicted geometric trends are consistent with the optimized morphologies. These results suggest that root-like porous architectures are not arbitrary numerical artifacts, but physically meaningful responses to coupled transport, reaction, and thermodynamic constraints. The present framework provides mechanistic design principles for reaction-diffusion-limited porous electrodes.

CHF enhancement on a large heating surface in saturated pool boiling using combined porous structures
abstract: This study explores the enhancement of critical heat flux (CHF) on a large heating surface (30 mm in diameter) during saturated pool boiling at atmospheric pressure. Although many CHF enhancement techniques have been developed, their performance tends to decline with larger heater sizes, leaving reliable methods for large heating surfaces limited. To address this challenge, we propose a two-layer structured boiling surface composed of a copper electrodeposited porous plate (EPP, lower layer) and a stainless-steel honeycomb porous plate (SUS-HPP, upper layer). This design synergizes capillary-driven liquid supply with improved vapor removal. The proposed structure allows for sustained nucleate boiling up to 5.5 MW/m 2 without reaching CHF, suggesting that the actual CHF exceeds this threshold. This represents a CHF enhancement of at least 4.5 times that of a plain copper surface and outperforms each layer when used independently. Our findings indicate that the combined effects of liquid retention and vapor removal in the upper layer, alongside robust capillary-driven liquid supply in the lower layer, significantly reduce CHF degradation on large heating surfaces. The proposed structure demonstrates higher CHF enhancement than previously reported values for 30-mm-diameter heaters (approximately 3.2 to 4.5 times higher), highlighting its potential as a scalable solution for high heat flux cooling applications involving large-area heaters.

Human reliability analysis in the nuclear industry of Korea: History, current status, and path forward
abstract: In socio-technical systems such as nuclear power plants (NPPs), human performance degradation is one of the primary factors in safety-significant events. Human reliability analysis (HRA) has therefore become indispensable in probabilistic safety assessment (PSA) to enhance system safety by quantifying the likelihood of human errors pertaining to safety-critical tasks. Accordingly, the quality of PSA results heavily depends on the robustness of HRA, particularly regarding context-based task analysis and accurate quantification methods. While HRA research in the Rep. of Korea has historically focused on large-scale commercial plants, the industry is currently shifting toward advanced reactors, including small modular reactors (SMRs), which necessitates a corresponding shift in HRA focus. In this paper, the landscape of HRA research activities in Korea is described by introducing past achievements and current methodologies based on a general HRA process. Furthermore, this paper suggests future research directions to address the necessities for developing and validating SMR-specific HRA methodologies.

abstract: Owing to their remarkable compactness and outstanding thermal efficiency, printed circuit heat exchangers (PCHEs) represent a highly viable candidate for systems coupling molten salt with supercritical carbon dioxide S-CO 2 . Investigating the geometric configuration and thermal-hydraulic behavior of such PCHEs is essential to further optimize their operating efficiency and structural density. This study proposes a new hybrid PCHE architecture that integrates zigzag continuous passages on the molten salt side with discontinuous airfoil-fin channels on the S-CO 2 side. A numerical framework, thoroughly verified against standard benchmark cases, was deployed to investigate the thermal and fluid dynamic characteristics of this new design. Across a range of operating scenarios, the variant featuring zigzag channels achieved a 2.89% to 13.9% enhancement in heat transfer effectiveness ( ε ) over the conventional straight-channel counterpart, albeit at the cost of a 36.5% to 40.5% rise in frictional pressure drops. Moreover, optimization of zigzag geometry in terms of pitch length, characteristic angle, and channel radius identified thermally optimal structures based on PEC, ε , and other indicators. Furthermore, flow–thermal coupling analysis revealed oscillatory temperature variations with phase-shifted peaks caused by structural disturbances and property contrasts. Meanwhile, slight inlet temperature increases on both molten salt and S-CO 2 sides improved overall performance. Finally, an empirical Nusselt number correlation for molten salt was proposed, with a deviation within ±1.2%.

Roadmap to Right-Size Emergency Planning Zones for Microreactors
abstract: Microreactors, as a class of advanced nuclear technologies, offer reduced power output, compact footprints, passive safety systems, and inherent modularity, features that fundamentally alter the basis for emergency planning zone (EPZ) sizing. Traditional EPZ frameworks, developed for large light water reactors, may be overly conservative when applied to microreactors. A risk-informed, performance-based approach is required, one that reflects the significantly lower source term, simplified accident progression, and limited off-site radiological impact of these designs. NUREG-0396, Planning Basis for the Development of State and Local Government Radiological Emergency Response Plans in Support of Light Water Nuclear Power Plants (1978), established a two-zone EPZ model: a 10-mile plume exposure zone and a 50-mile ingestion pathway zone. Importantly, it allows for scaling based on a “realistic appraisal of accident consequences” (Sec. IV), thus supporting a graded, risk-informed methodology particularly relevant for microreactors. This approach has precedent. NuScale Power demonstrated through detailed deterministic and probabilistic safety analyses that its design warranted a reduced-size EPZ. NuScale’s use of mechanistic source term modeling and level 3 probabilistic risk assessment showed minimal off-site consequences, supporting the approval of a site-boundary EPZ by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Similarly, X-Energy’s Xe-100 high-temperature gas-cooled reactor incorporates robust tristructural isotropic fuel and passive decay heat removal systems, justifying a reduced EPZ through source term and dose consequence modeling consistent with Protective Action Guide (PAG) thresholds. The current paper presents a structured framework for EPZ sizing tailored to microreactors, grounded in NUREG-0396 and supported by regulatory guidance (e.g. RG 1.183, NUREG-0800) and recent licensing precedent. It aims to facilitate scalable, risk-aligned emergency planning for microreactors deployed in remote, off-grid, or specialized defense environments.

A Robust and Energy-Efficient Wireless Sensor Network for Radiometry Monitoring
abstract: Wireless sensor networks used for radiometry monitoring must ensure long-term operation, reliable data delivery, and efficient utilization of limited energy resources in harsh and remote environments. Conventional clustering protocols often suffer from rapid energy depletion, unreliable communication, and limited spectral efficiency, especially when battery replacement is impractical. This paper proposes a robust and energy-efficient wireless sensor network framework that integrates vice-cluster-head–based routing, radio-frequency energy harvesting–aware power control with large-scale fading decoding, and turbo trellis coded modulation to enhance reliability and transmission performance. The proposed design improves network robustness through backup-assisted clustering, efficient use of harvested energy via fairness-based power allocation, and reliable data transmission without bandwidth expansion. Simulation results demonstrate substantial performance gains over conventional protocols. The proposed system achieves a network lifetime of 1300 ± 137 h, representing improvements of 20.3% over vice-cluster-head low-energy adaptive clustering hierarchy routing and 57.8% over the low-energy adaptive clustering hierarchy protocol, while energy efficiency increases to 89%. Latency is reduced to 3.8 ± 0.2 ms, and spectral efficiency reaches 5.34 bps/Hz, exceeding the max–min fairness benchmark by up to 151% under wireless power transfer constraints. Parameter analysis further shows that a downlink energy harvesting duration of 25 channel uses provides an effective balance between lifetime and throughput, while shared pilot allocation with moderate pilot length ensures reliable channel estimation. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a practical and high-performance solution for radiometry-monitoring applications requiring continuous operation, efficient energy usage, and reliable data transmission.

title: GPU Acceleration of the CUPID Two-Fluid Thermal–Hydraulic Code: Design, Algorithmic Challenges, and Performance Evaluation
abstract: The three-dimensional thermal–hydraulic analysis code CUPID was extended with a GPU-accelerated implementation to support high-fidelity simulations for advanced small modular reactor (SMR) analysis. Key components of the two-fluid, three-field solver were ported to GPUs using CUDA Fortran, with optimizations targeting memory access and kernel parallelism while preserving the original numerical algorithms. The GPU-enabled version, CUPID-G, was verified using representative single- and two-phase benchmark problems, demonstrating numerical consistency with the CPU code. A 10-million-cell i-SMR prototype quarter-core transient simulation was successfully executed on a single GPU within a practical turnaround time. Performance evaluations show up to O(10×) speedup over single-core CPU execution and comparable acceleration compared with a 40-core CPU. The CUPID-G provides a scalable foundation for next-generation SMR analysis and establishes a pathway toward fully GPU-centric multi-physics coupling in virtual reactor development environments.

Jet impingement heat transfer in metallic foams: single vs multiple jets
abstract: Improving heat transfer between the solar receiver and the working fluid is critical for enhancing the efficiency of concentrating solar power (CSP) systems. This study presents an experimental investigation of convective heat transfer using air jet impingement over open-cell aluminum foams, aiming to develop more efficient solar receiver configurations. Five metallic foams with porosities ranging from 78.7 % to 91.5 % and pore densities ranging from 10 to 50 PPI were tested under Reynolds numbers from 1,422 to 12,612 . Foam morphology and chemical composition were characterized using SEM–EDS, while heat flux and pressure drop were directly measured. The results show that both the heat transfer coefficient and the Nusselt number increase with Re and foam permeability. Multiple-jet impingement consistently outperformed single-jet configurations, particularly for highly permeable foams under the investigated conditions. Among the tested samples, the foam with P = 91.52 % and 10 PPI exhibited the best overall thermo-hydraulic performance under multiple-jet impingement, while the foam with P = 81.72 % and 50 PPI achieved a heat flux enhancement of up to approximately 641 % relative to natural convection under single-jet conditions. These findings demonstrate the combined influence of permeability, Reynolds number, and jet configuration on thermo-hydraulic performance and highlight the potential of metallic foams for the development of high-efficiency CSP receivers.

abstract: Circulating fluidized bed (CFB) gasification is widely used in industry to convert coal particles to syngas. Optimizing the design of industrial circulating fluidized bed gasifier is of great importance to the sustainability and efficiency of gasification processes. However, experimental study of design parameters is usually extremely expensive, time-consuming, and labor-intensive. Building upon our previous publication, besides operational conditions, a thorough analysis of two crucial structural parameters, bottom straight height (BSH) and cone angle (CA), have been further conducted for the optimization of the high-temperature preheating preheating 15Mwth KEDA® CFB gasifier. Optimal gasification performances are achieved with a BSH of around 1 m, as evidenced by the higher heating value (HHV) of 6.05 MJ/Nm 3 , cold gas efficiency (CGE) of 68.5%, and carbon conversion efficiency (CCE) of 80.3%. It has been discovered that decreasing the CA from 24° to 9° improves temperature distributions and increases the upward movement of mass and heat, improving gasification performance. Compared with BSH, CA has smaller impacts on gasification performances. Collectively, this work provides valuable insights into the design and optimization of CFB gasifiers, and can be used to guide the development of more efficient and sustainable gasification systems.

Encoder-only transformer with simulation-to-experiment transfer for radionuclide identification in NaI(Tl) spectroscopy
abstract: Radionuclide identification is central to nuclear safety, security, and environmental monitoring, yet NaI(Tl) detectors remain limited by low resolution, peak overlap, background variability, and simulation-experiment discrepancies. Existing neural-network models typically achieve high accuracy on simulated spectra but generalize poorly to experimental measurements due to domain shift. This study proposes an encoder-only transformer for radionuclide identification using NaI(Tl) spectra. The model is trained and fine-tuned on experimentally measured data. By leveraging self-attention, it captures global spectral dependencies and consistently outperforms conventional neural networks, such as Convolutional Neural Network, Residual Network, and Multilayer Perceptron in realistic measurement scenarios. This approach offers a generalizable framework for reliable and efficient radionuclide identification, supporting broader applications in nuclear safety, security, and environmental monitoring. A calibrated Geant4 model provides simulated spectra for seven radionuclides ( 241 Am, 226 Ra, 57 Co, 60 Co, 137 Cs, 152 Eu, 133 Ba), augmented by synthetic mixture generation. Experimental spectra were acquired of four radionuclides ( 60 Co, 137 Cs, 152 Eu, 133 Ba) including all 15 source combinations from single- to four-nuclide mixtures. The model is pretrained on simulated spectra and fine-tuned with a limited amount of experimental data, while all remaining spectra are reserved for testing. It consistently outperforms traditional peak analysis method and neural networks (Convolutional Neural Network, Residual Network, and Multilayer Perceptron) and achieves about 95% average accuracy on simulated spectra and 93% on experimental spectra, surpassing the strongest baseline by over 3 percentage points. Fine-tuning yields consistent improvements, especially for complex triple-nuclide mixtures, confirming the robustness and data efficiency of the model under realistic NaI(Tl) measurement conditions. Ablation results confirm that both the encoder-only architecture and the simulation-to-experiment training strategy contribute critically to performance gains, while efficiency analysis shows that the model achieves millisecond-level inference suitable for practical deployment.

title: Constraints on Nuclear-Driven Photon Generation and Radiation Transport in Extreme-Energy Systems
abstract: Nuclear-driven photon generation occupies a narrow and technically demanding intersection of nuclear physics, radiative transfer, thermal management, shielding, and high-energy photonics. This article develops a system-agnostic constraints framework for platforms in which a nuclear source is coupled, either directly or indirectly, to an external photon-emitting stage. Rather than describing an implementable device, the analysis asks under what conditions source specific energy can survive the compounded penalties of interface recovery, thermal-to-electric conversion, optical conversion, transport attenuation, threshold behavior, heat rejection, and shielding burden? A compact hierarchy of governing equations is derived for source power density, internal photon production, optical-depth losses, steady-state waste-heat rejection, and first-order shielding mass. These relations are then reduced to closed-form inequalities which are understood with realistic screening ranges for η h , η te , and η p g ; optical-depth sensitivity under shielding and window geometries; radiator-area scaling under high source power; first-order shielding-mass interpretation; an explicit benchmark pathway and uncertainty propagation. Historical nuclear-pumped-laser studies and modern radioisotope power literature are synthesized with current neutron-photon transport methods, attenuation studies, thermoelectric materials literature, and nuclear-photonics applications to delimit the feasible regime. The resulting analysis shows that source energy density alone is insufficient: viability depends on simultaneous closure across energy conversion, radiative transport, heat rejection, mass-limited shielding, and experimentally testable benchmark assumptions. The article is offered as a theoretical constraints study rather than a design disclosure.

Defect-controlled transport properties of non-stoichiometric and ion-irradiated Ceria
abstract: The transport properties of cerium dioxide (CeO₂), a surrogate for UO₂ nuclear fuel, were investigated as a function of defect structure induced by controlled reduction and ion irradiation. Non-stoichiometric ceria (CeO₂₋ₓ, x up to 0.22) was synthesized via reducing annealing, and its thermal and electrical properties were measured over a wide temperature range. Thermal conductivity decreases with increasing oxygen vacancy concentration due to enhanced phonon scattering, consistent with a modified Callaway model. In contrast, electrical conductivity increases by several orders of magnitude, governed by small-polaron hopping between Ce3 + /Ce4 + sites. Ion irradiation (600 keV Kr) further modifies electron transport behavior, producing a highly conductive near-surface region. Radiation-induced electrical degradation (RIED) is observed, with conductivity increasing with fluence and irradiation temperature. A model linking oxygen depletion to bandgap narrowing is proposed to describe the irradiation-induced conductivity evolution. These results demonstrate that defect engineering via reduction and irradiation provides a powerful route to tune transport properties in fluorite oxides and offers insight into defect-controlled behavior in nuclear fuel materials.

title: Ambient dose equivalent assessment from a pulsed electron beam using GEANT4-based Monte Carlo simulation
abstract: Radiation protection is a critical aspect of particle accelerator facilities, where dose equivalents due to radiation generated during beam operation must remain within regulatory safety limits for both workers and the public. This study presents a methodology for evaluating the ambient dose equivalent produced by pulsed electron beams using GEANT4-based Monte Carlo simulations. The fluence-to-ambient dose equivalent conversion coefficient for photons was calculated for energies ranging from 0.01 to 30 MeV and benchmarked against reference data from ICRP Publication 74 and FLUKA simulations. The results show good agreement with established datasets, with minor deviations observed in the 20–30 MeV range, likely due to the improved energy resolution used in the present calculations. The developed approach was applied to simulate radiation transport and create radiation maps for the electron linear accelerator hall at Chiang Mai University. By incorporating the time structure of the pulsed electron beam, the ambient dose equivalent distributions for both photon and neutron radiation were determined. These radiation maps provide vital data for identifying potential leakage points and optimizing local shielding to ensure compliance with radiation safety standards. Ultimately, by improving radiation safety assessment methodologies for pulsed accelerator facilities, this research enhances protection for workers and public, contributing directly to global goals for sustainable and resilient infrastructure.

Arbitrary Order Statistical Moments of Neutron Energy and Lethargy Across Multiple Collisions During Neutron Moderation Without Absorption
abstract: We revisit the classical problem of neutron moderation in an infinite medium without absorption. We consider the multiscattered collision densities F1E,F2E,… denoting the collision densities for neutrons that have undergone 1, 2, ... collisions, and develop a recursive formula that allows for expectation values taken over the density FNE to be alternatively expressed in terms of the preceding density FN−1E. We apply the formula to recursively and efficiently derive the statistical moments for neutron energy and lethargy, up to arbitrary order, across multiple collisions. We also investigate some implications of the derived statistical moments on the problem of estimating the number of collisions required to slow down a neutron.

title: Initial Study on Machine Learning Predictive Models for Lattice-Level Neutronic Analysis in High-Temperature Gas-Cooled Reactors
abstract: High-temperature gas-cooled reactors (HTGRs) are being developed not only for electricity generation but also to produce hydrogen, leveraging the high outlet coolant temperature up to 950°C from the reactor core. To achieve this condition safely, the power density distribution within the core should be optimized through effective in-core fuel management. Depending on the reactor’s intended application and core design, the neutronic parameters should be calculated for each core configuration. In this present study, high-fidelity simulations based on the Monte Carlo (MC) method were performed to predict the key neutronic parameter of multiplication factors kinf. Although it produces highly accurate results, the MC method is time-consuming and computationally intensive, particularly for large-scale parametric studies. This initial study proposes using surrogate models developed through machine learning techniques to predict important neutronic parameters more efficiently. The current stage focuses on developing a predictive model at the lattice level of HTGRs. The widely used ensemble method Random Forest regression was adopted. A dataset consisting of approximately 640 samples was prepared and used for model training and validation. The model’s performance was evaluated using the coefficient of determination R2 and the root-mean-square error, yielding values of 0.998 and 0.011, respectively. Furthermore, when applied to predict the kinf values, the model demonstrated good agreement with MC simulation, with prediction errors ranging from 0.9% to 5.5%, depending on the uranium enrichment and the fuel packing fraction.

title: Comprehensive Characterization of Nano-Eu 2 O 3 Reinforced Borotellurite Glasses: Synthesis, Physical, Structural, and Gamma and Neutron Attenuation Properties
abstract: This study presents a systematic investigation of lithium borotellurite glasses reinforced with nano-Eu2O3, with the aim to enhance the structural stability and radiation shielding performance. Glasses were synthesized with Eu2O3 concentrations from 0 to 10 mol % and characterized through density, X-ray diffraction, and transmission electron microscopy. The results showed that the density increased steadily from 4.030 to 4.734 g/cm3 with the Eu addition, while the molar volume also expanded, indicating that the incorporation of larger Eu3+ ions induced network expansion alongside densification.The X-ray diffraction patterns showed amorphous structures for all the compositions except Eu(n)2, which exhibited local crystallinity, later suppressed at higher Eu levels. The transmission electron microscopy pictures and energy dispersive spectroscopy mapping showed homogeneous nanoparticle distribution without clustering. Gamma-ray attenuation studies demonstrated clear improvements with Eu doping: the linear attenuation coefficient increased from 8.33 cm−1 (Eu(n)0) to 12.42 cm−1 (Eu(n)10) at 81 keV, while the half-value layer values decreased, confirming superior low-energy absorption. Experimental neutron studies revealed ΣR values comparable to standard neutron moderators, with Eu(n)10 showing a favorable balance of gamma and neutron shielding.Limitations include the restricted photon energy window and single neutron source. Future work should extend testing to higher energies, thermal/epithermal neutron ranges, and mechanical and durability assessments. Overall, nano-Eu2O3 reinforcement provides a promising pathway toward multifunctional transparent shielding glasses.

title: Acceleration of the Convergence of a Core Thermal-Hydraulic Code Using Initialization from a Neural Network
abstract: For safety studies of nuclear reactor cores, a finite-volume thermal-hydraulic code with a porous medium approach named THYC-coeur has been developed by EDF to simulate steady-state flows of a two-phase mixture within the core of a nuclear reactor. The steady-state solution is obtained through a fictitious transient. Despite a relatively low individual computational time, many state points are considered in the safety studies, which can represent significant CPU time. To speed up the computation, one possible objective is to reduce the number of iterations (i.e. the number of time steps) required to reach convergence. In the present work, the idea is to train a neural network (NN) to predict steady-state solutions and use this prediction to initialize the transient computation. This method allows combinating the advantages of NN prediction, in terms of rapidity, with that of the THYC-coeur model, in terms of the physical validation of the solution. To evaluate the potential of this method, a simplified one-dimensional code was designed. This code simulates a two-phase water vapor flow in a heated channel. A NN was trained to predict the solution fields from imposed boundary conditions. In this paper, we present the methodology, the database selection process, the structure of the NN, and the optimization of the network’s hyperparameters. This paper examines two different physical models: the 3-equation model and the 4-equation model. Initially, a simple loss function is used to predict the fields of these two models. The observed accelerations are approximately 70% for the 3-equation model and 48% for the 4-equation model. A detailed study of the correlation between prediction accuracy and the resulting acceleration has shown that the low-frequency components in the entropy field prediction error significantly slow down the search for the steady state. The highlight of this work is that by introducing spatial frequencies in the error for the optimization of the NN, the number of iterations is reduced between 61% (4-equation model) and 83% (3-equation model) from baseline simulations.

title: Quantitative visualization of a radioactive plume using gamma-ray imaging spectrometry: estimation of initial release condition by machine learning and feasibility of real-time analysis in emergency monitoring applications
abstract: A novel monitoring method for the quantitative visualization of 3D distribution of a radioactive plume accidentally released from a nuclear facility was proposed, and the feasibility of its analysis method was demonstrated in our previous study by means of a preliminary test using hypothetical data. The method combines gamma-ray imaging spectroscopy with an Electron Tracking Compton Camera (ETCC) and real-time high-resolution atmospheric dispersion simulation driven by wind observations. The 3D plume distribution is reconstructed inversely from the direct gamma-ray images by several ETCCs deployed around the target area. This reconstruction employs a regularized optimization in which the air‑concentration field predicted by the dispersion simulation serves as prior information. We also prototyped a method to identify a release point, which is required as input conditions for the atmospheric dispersion calculation, solely from gamma-ray images of the ETCC immediately after the release. A method based on machine learning was employed in test analyses targeting the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station. The results show good performance in identifying the release point when using theoretical gamma-ray image data. In practical aspect, the scope of application and accuracy of the method was evaluated using hypothetical gamma-ray image data under realistic assumptions. Moreover, the feasibility of real-time analysis was confirmed by implementing an analysis workflow designed based on the 10-minute interval data acquisition.

title: Analysis of signal characteristics and influencing factors of self-powered gamma detector for reactor
abstract: Self-powered gamma detector (SPGD) can be used for monitoring the gamma flux in the reactor core. This study establishes a Monte Carlo simulation model of SPGD with a focus on the space charge effect in the insulator and the current contribution from the collector. To evaluate candidate emitter materials, simulations are performed under the Very High Temperature Reactor (VHTR) spectrum. The results show that SPGDs using lead (Pb) and bismuth (Bi) as emitters achieve a gamma signal proportion exceeding 99%. Additionally, the effects of emitter diameter, insulator thickness, and collector thickness on gamma sensitivity are analyzed. Experimental validation is conducted using a cobalt-60 source on a zirconium-type SPGD and a rhodium-type self-powered neutron detector (SPND), yielding relative deviations between the simulated and experimental gamma sensitivities of -4.55% and -9.45%. Thus, the proposed model can be used for the sensitivity prediction of SPGD and the analysis of gamma background current in SPND.

title: Evaluation of neutron-induced independent fission yields for 37 fissioning systems
abstract: A new independent fission yield (IFY) library is evaluated and verified, which contains 37 fissioning systems dominating fission rates under typical irradiations. 20,951 experimental data items for chain yields and 5,017 for fractional independent yields are collected and analyzed to produce recommended experimental data. The systematics models (Katakura five-Gaussian model for chain yields, Zp model for fractional independent yields) and Hauser-Feshbach theory for isomeric yield ratios are used to predict the unmeasured data, after fitting parameters of systematics models to the recommended experimental data. The generalized least-square method is used to adjust the IFYs to conform to physical constraints, and simultaneously the covariances of IFYs are produced. The new IFY library is verified in various application scenarios, including calculations of fission pulse decay heats, delayed neutron yields, fission product inventories in spent nuclear fuel, and physics simulations of an operated pressurized water reactor. It is shown that results obtained with IFYs evaluated in this work have comparable accuracy to those based on the existing evaluated nuclear data libraries. Notably, the delayed neutron yields calculated based on IFYs of this work generally show better agreement with measured data; the inventories of fission products in spent nuclear fuel, such as 134,137Cs, 145-150Nd, and 150,152Sm, calculated with IFYs of this work are closest to the measured data.

Enhanced dental panoramic imaging from cone-beam computed tomography projection data using single-energy material decomposition
abstract: Background Conventional dental panoramic imaging is often limited by soft tissue overlap and shadow artefacts from the cervical vertebrae, reducing diagnostic visibility. Purpose This study presents a single-energy material decomposition (SEMD) framework that generates material-specific panoramic images directly from pre-acquired cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) projections without additional scans. Methods Single-energy projections were separated into soft- and hard-tissue components, and panoramic projections were extracted along the desired scan trajectory to reconstruct material-decomposed images with reduced tissue overlap and vertebral shadows. The SEMD approach was evaluated using numerical simulations and physical phantom experiments. Results Numerical simulations and phantom experiments demonstrated improved anatomical delineation and higher diagnostic contrast than conventional panoramic imaging. Quantitative evaluations showed increased lesion contrast-to-noise ratios, low normalized root-mean-square error and normalized mean absolute error relative to the ground-truth material maps, and improved perception-based image quality scores in the hard-tissue image. Conclusions The proposed framework enables material-specific panoramic imaging from a single CBCT acquisition, improving lesion visibility.

Research Progress of Spent Fuel Reprocessing Processes Based on Carbonate Medium
abstract: The reprocessing strategies for spent nuclear fuel (SNF) in carbonate solutions and molten carbonate media were reviewed, with emphasis placed on summarizing and comparing the principal concepts and process schemes developed by researchers in the United States, Russia, Japan, Korea, and China for SNF reprocessing using carbonate-based systems. The major technological advances, potential advantages, and prospective development pathways of carbonate-mediated SNF reprocessing are discussed, with particular attention to their future research directions and application prospects.

Proposal of a drag coefficient model for bubble chain rising in stagnant LBE pool based on volume of fluid method
abstract: In the event of a steam generator tube rupture (SGTR) accident in a liquid lead-bismuth eutectic (LBE)-cooled reactor (LFR), a small rupture in the tube wall may lead to the leakage of high-pressure, low-temperature liquid water into a low-pressure, high-temperature pool of liquid LBE. Consequently, the liquid water quickly vaporizes, and a chain of steam bubbles may be formed following the continuous leakage of liquid water. Existing drag models, primarily developed for isolated bubbles, show significant limitations when applied to bubble chains, in which interactions between bubbles are observed. This study investigates the effect of the spacing between adjacent bubbles on the terminal velocity in a chain in stagnant LBE and develops a novel drag coefficient model that incorporates this key parameter. Bubble dynamics obtained using neutron radiography, including terminal velocity in a chain and equivalent bubble diameter of a single bubble chain rising in stagnant LBE, were used to validate the volume-of-fluid (VOF) method. Subsequently, extensive numerical simulations covering a wider range of parameters were conducted to establish a comprehensive drag coefficient database. The numerical results demonstrated that the drag coefficient of the bubbles in the bubble chain decreases as the ratio of the bubble spacing to the equivalent bubble diameter decreases. A new drag model was proposed by introducing this ratio into the functional form of the correlation along with the bubble Reynolds number and Weber number. The proposed drag coefficient model shows excellent agreement with the numerical databases and significantly outperforms existing models.

title: The liquid utilisation bottleneck in interfacial thermal conductance at metal/water interfaces
abstract: The vibrational density of states (VDOS) Overlap is widely expected to correlate positively with the interfacial thermal conductance ( G ), yet it fails to do so at numerous systems, and at gold/water interfaces, it actually decreases with increasing G . Here, we use non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations of numerous metal/water interfaces for a range of solid/liquid interaction strengths ( ɛ ɛ SL ) to explain this contradiction. We show that the VDOS Overlap is a contingent metric: its trend with ɛ ɛ SL depends on the relative positioning of the interfacial solid and liquid VDOS distributions, which is set by the extent of the bulk solid spectrum. By comparing the spectrally decomposed heat flux (SDHF) to the VDOS within each medium, we find that the degree to which the interfacial liquid utilises its available vibrational modes ( η IL ) tracks the cross-metal hierarchy in G as closely as bulk-spectrum measures, while remaining invariant with ɛ ɛ SL within each metal. An additional finding is that the bottleneck to cross-metal energy transport lies on the interfacial liquid side, not in the spectral similarity between the two media: η IL matches the predictive power of the bulk-spectrum measures and additionally locates the limiting side of the interface, which a bulk-spectrum measure of the solid alone does not.

Technical and scientific perspectives on domestic gas ovens: A comprehensive review
abstract: Domestic gas ovens are a widely used residential cooking appliance in both developed and developing economies, yet the scientific literature addressing their performance, energy efficiency, and environmental impact remains fragmented and disproportionately small relative to their contribution to household energy consumption. This semi-systematic review consolidates the available evidence by combining peer-reviewed studies with grey literature from regulatory and standardisation bodies, and assesses each source against explicit methodological criteria. The appliance is first situated within its technical and regulatory context, comparing energy efficiency and emission frameworks across the European Union, the United States, and Brazil and examining the role of structural design, materials, and combustion-related pollutant formation. The experimental evidence is then examined, organised by the physical region of the appliance, from cavity-scale temperature distribution and convective flow to burner-scale combustion and ignition, and to pollutant emissions under both standardised and real-use operation. The numerical modelling literature is subsequently assessed with attention to the combustion, turbulence, and radiation strategies adopted for this appliance class, and to the validation practices and modelling assumptions that constrain their predictive credibility. Fuel-flexibility considerations associated with hydrogen blending in natural gas networks are addressed transversally, where the relevant physical mechanism is discussed. The integration of regulatory, experimental, and numerical perspectives within a single critical framework constitutes the first dedicated assessment of domestic gas ovens as a thermally coupled appliance class and delineates a coherent research agenda for the field.

Synergistic enhancement of mechanical and X-ray shielding properties in natural rubber latex gloves containing Bi2O3 nanoparticles through multilayer design
abstract: This study evaluated the effectiveness of multilayer design for simultaneous enhancement of the X-ray shielding and mechanical properties with heavy-metal fillers by incorporating nano-Bi 2 O 3 within a middle layer while having pristine NRL as the outer layers, with each layer having a thickness of 1 mm. To assess the benefits of this design, 3-mm-thick single-layer and multilayer NRL gloves containing equivalent nano-Bi 2 O 3 contents ranging from 0 to 200 phr were systematically investigated. The results showed that increasing nano-Bi 2 O 3 content progressively enhanced X-ray attenuation. Specifically, attenuation efficiencies reached approximately 37% for single-layer gloves and 70% for multilayer gloves at 60 kV, with similar trends for other X-ray energies. Mechanical testing also revealed that single-layer gloves exhibited increases in tensile modulus but notable reductions in tensile strength and elongation at break after adding fillers. In contrast, multilayer gloves, while having similar mechanical trends, maintained superior mechanical performance due to the presence of pristine NRL outer layers that improved the transfer of external forces. Furthermore, based on ASTM D7866 and ASTM D3578, the recommended equivalent nano-Bi 2 O 3 content for single-layer gloves was restricted to 80 – 100 phr, whereas a substantially wider range of 30 – 140 phr was achieved for the multilayer structure.

title: Comprehensive evaluation of phase change material-branched fin coupled configuration for shell-and-tube type thermal energy storage systems
abstract: In the sustainable energy transition, phase change material-based energy storage has gained significant attention for its effectiveness in harvesting renewable energy. Branched fins are actively explored to improve the charging performance of latent-heat thermal energy storage systems. Despite several efforts, optimal design configurations are still evolving. To this end, this study numerically investigates the role of branched fin structures in reducing the charging time by proposing two configurations. The numerical predictions show good agreement with experimental data, with an average error of 3.1% and 4.2% for the baseline (no fin) and finned models, respectively. New insights were drawn on the underlying mechanisms of the charging process in the baseline model. The molten phase-change material liquid fraction and velocity patterns indicate that convection currents influence the total charging (melting) time. Branched fins in symmetrical and asymmetrical layouts and fin geometric parameters were systematically investigated for both models in horizontal and vertical orientations of the system. An optimum branch length was determined by balancing heat-transfer enhancement against the associated reduction in energy-storage capacity, yielding a heat-transfer enhancement ratio of 1.175 relative to the baseline case. Introducing fins into the baseline model considerably reduces the charging time. Notably, in a horizontally oriented system, an asymmetrical arrangement of branched fins yielded an 83% reduction in the charging time of the baseline model. For a given fin surface area, the optimal number of branched fins was identified as 5 in a horizontal, asymmetrical arrangement, resulting in an 82% reduction in charging time compared to the baseline model. A further increase in fin number beyond this showed no notable enhancement in charging performance. The results demonstrated that the charging time can be significantly reduced by adding longer fins in an asymmetrical layout for a horizontally oriented system. The results reported will be a novel addition to the scientific database and promote the adoption of shell-and-tube-based systems.

title: Analysis of Entropy Generation and Multi-Parameter Optimization of Flying-Wing Fins in Condensers
abstract: This study investigates the application of flying-wing fins (FWF) in refrigerator condensers. Compared with conventional condensers, FWF structures eliminate contact thermal resistance and reduce refrigerator energy consumption by 6.06%. The heat transfer mechanism, entropy generation characteristics, and parameter optimization of FWF are comprehensively analyzed. Results show that the local convective heat transfer coefficient decreases along the flow direction, with the maximum value in the wave-crest region and the minimum in the wave-trough region. The Colburn j factor is positively correlated with fin pitch (Fp) and amplitude (A), but negatively correlated with fin length (H) and thickness (Ft). The fanning friction factor (f) increases with A and Ft, decreases with H, and first increases then decreases with Fp. Fin height (Fh) exerts minimal influence on j and f factors. Thermal entropy generation and flow entropy generation are negatively correlated with Fp and positively with other parameters. The Bejan number remains around 0.9, indicating that thermal entropy generation dominates total entropy generation. Finally, the contribution ratios of key parameters to j and f factors are quantified. These findings clarify the heat transfer behavior of FWF and provide a theoretical foundation for designing high-efficiency flying-wing condensers with reduced energy consumption.

title: Analytical Relationships Among Thermal Penetration Depth Definitions in Heat Conduction
abstract: Thermal penetration depth is a widely used concept in heat-transfer analysis for characterizing the spatial and temporal extent of thermal influence. Over time, multiple penetration-depth definitions have emerged throughout the heat-transfer literature in response to differing analytical objectives and application domains, complicating comparisons among reported results. This analysis examines the principal penetration-depth formulations reported in the literature, develops a unified taxonomy comprising diffusion-length, thermal-front, threshold-isotherm, attenuation-based, penetration-time, and resistance-corrected definition families, and derives analytical relationships among them. The results indicate that many commonly used formulations may be interpreted as criterion-dependent representations of a common diffusion-based transport scale. The analysis further suggests that apparent discrepancies among reported penetration depths arise primarily from differences in extraction criteria rather than differences in the underlying transport physics. By clarifying the relationships among definitions that have evolved across diverse heat-transfer applications, the resulting framework provides a unified perspective for interpreting, comparing, and communicating penetration-depth concepts throughout the heat-transfer literature.

Feasibility study on deep learning-based human organ dose estimation in monoenergetic point-source exposures
abstract: Rapid and accurate estimation of organ-absorbed doses is critical for effective radiological protection and emergency response. While Monte Carlo (MC) simulations provide high fidelity, their computational cost hinders real-time application. This study proposes a deep neural network (DNN)-based surrogate model to predict organ-absorbed doses and effective doses for an adult male using the ICRP Publication 145 mesh-type reference computational phantom. A dataset comprising approximately 54,000 cases was generated using Geant4 simulations for point sources emitting 1 MeV photons isotropically. Various data transformation strategies, including log and Box-Cox transformations, were evaluated to optimize model performance. The proposed DNN model reproduced MC-calculated doses with a mean absolute relative error (ARE) of less than 2.5%, which is comparable to the inherent statistical uncertainty of the training data. Notably, the model demonstrated a processing time of 0.76 s for 5000 cases, significantly outperforming conventional gamma-constant-based methods in both accuracy and real-time applicability. An error analysis suggested that prediction residuals were partially associated with the statistical noise of the simulation data and related to geometric complexities, such as anatomical shielding and steep dose gradients near the body surface. These findings validate the feasibility of the proposed AI-driven approach as a robust tool for real-time computational dosimetry.

title: Thermal-Hydraulic Performance and Transient Safety Evaluation of a Power-Uprated Natural Circulation SMR with a Truly Optimized PWR Core
abstract: In this study, a 330 MWt (100 MWe-class) base natural circulation small modular reactor (NC-SMR) was conceptually established, and the thermal-hydraulic performance and transient safety margin of a power-uprated NC-SMR adopting the Truly Optimized PWR (TOP) core design were evaluated. Using the MARS-KS code, both models were systematically assessed under steady-state conditions and a limiting anticipated operational occurrence induced by increased feedwater flow. The TOP core design achieved a 3.03% power uprate (340 MWt) while maintaining highly stable operation without enlarging the reactor pressure vessel or causing significant deviations in the core inlet and outlet temperatures. During the overcooling transient, both models demonstrated sufficient thermal safety margins and safely achieved stable reactor shutdown states. The TOP core slowed the primary cooldown rate, delaying the high-power reactor trip by approximately 15-19 seconds, which secured an extended response time for safety system actuation. Furthermore, despite the limiting conditions and uprated power, the minimum departure from nucleate boiling ratio was successfully maintained at 3.05, remaining well above the thermal safety limit. Ultimately, the overall findings demonstrate that adopting the TOP core design is a highly promising approach to securing larger reactor power per module for NC-SMRs.

Economic assessments on the transition from light water to fast reactor fleet for Pu management
abstract: The EU PUMMA project has been devoted to showing the flexibility of the fast reactor for Pu management, for which a European fuel cycle scenario consisting in the transition between a light water reactor fleet to a fast reactor fleet has been studied. This scenario has been analyzed to show that a single sodium-cooled fast reactor is able to manage the Pu existing in the fuel cycle, with special attention to breeding, burning and isogeneration policies. This work includes the economic analysis made with the TR_EVOL code of this reference scenario, where the objective is the calculation of the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) for every mentioned policy. Two different databases providing the unit costs for investment cost, O&M cost and fuel costs have been applied in this work. Specific analyses have been made regarding the costs contributing to the LCOE to understand the differences between the databases.

title: Thickness Assessment for Accident-Tolerant FeCrAl Fuel Cladding Based on Elastoplastic and Creep Buckling Analyses
abstract: FeCrAl alloy cladding is considered to be one of the most promising candidates for near-term application in the accident-tolerant fuel (ATF) framework. However, it has a higher neutron absorption cross section compared with conventional Zircaloy cladding, and its thickness tends to be reduced to maintain the neutron economy. Structural stability may be lost if the thickness cannot withstand the high external pressure during reactor operations.Therefore, the present study assesses the minimum allowable thickness of the ATF FeCrAl cladding based on mechanical integrity to prevent a cladding collapse under normal operating conditions. A finite-length C35M FeCrAl alloy cylindrical shell model with various initial ovalities was developed. The elastic, elastoplastic, and creep buckling features were further revealed by a finite element analysis, where the cladding collapse from the long-term effects of thermal creep and irradiation creep were of great concern.It was indicated that the creep lifetime of the cladding that satisfies the elastic or elastoplastic buckling requirements may not meet the operating requirement. For the case of a creep lifetime of 3 years and a pressure difference of 11 MPa, cladding with a minimum thickness of 0.4423 mm (with 0.5% ovality) would be required. A reference diagram of the minimum thickness necessary to prevent a creep buckling failure corresponding to variations in the creep lifetime, the initial ovality, and the pressure difference is provided.

Development and Verification of a Cross-Section Parameterization Method for a Rod-Controlled Gas-Cooled Micro-Reactor with Synchronous Control Rod Operation
abstract: As a novel reactor concept, the GCMR(Gas-Cooled Micro-Reactor) features compact size, inherent safety, and high efficiency. At present, Monte Carlo codes are primarily employed for core calculations of GCMR. However, the computational demand and long runtime of Monte Carlo codes make them unsuitable for fast simulation and online core monitoring. To address this issue, this paper proposes a cross section parameterization method based on the Monte Carlo code RMC. Specifically, the RMC code is first used to perform full-core calculations under representative operating conditions. Subsequently, the cross sections are iteratively corrected using SPH (Superhomogenization) factors, combined with Aitken acceleration techniques and boundary constants in a coupled manner, to construct a parameterized cross section library. The cross section under current operating conditions can then be obtained through interpolation with the cross section parameterization method according to the reactor state parameters, and full-core calculations are subsequently carried out using a diffusion code. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed cross section parameterization method shows good agreement with the one-step RMC calculations, while also demonstrating good computational efficiency. It provides a fundamental tool for rapid simulation and online monitoring of GCMR.

title: Estimation of internal and external heat loads by inverse conduction analysis of internally-cooled turbine vane
abstract: Quantifying the cooling performance of real hardware, internally-cooled gas turbine parts is challenging due to their characteristic dimensions and thermal properties and to the limited instrumentation access to their internal, cooled surfaces. Inverse heat conduction analysis methods are used in this context to estimate the heat loads generated by an internal cooling system from measurements of the resulting external surface temperature distribution of the cooled part. Existing works in the turbine cooling literature rely on bench-top testing facilities that do not reproduce a relevant external aero-thermal load, thus limiting the types of cooled components that may be tested with realistic internal flow behavior. The objective of this study is to extend traditional inverse conduction analysis and to demonstrate experimental and numerical methods to estimate the internal cooling performance of a real hardware-like nozzle-guide vane operating with engine-representative internal and external thermal loads. Thermal transient tests conducted with the test article installed in a linear cascade wind tunnel generate the external surface temperature responses necessary for the proposed iterative post-processing procedure to estimate both the internal and external heat loads. In particular, this work focuses on the description of the experimental test procedures developed and of the numerical post-processing approach. Internal and external heat load estimates are presented for a series of test conditions defined by combinations of different cooling system Reynolds numbers and the tunnel’s mainstream turbulence intensity. The results demonstrated it was possible to reproduce reference results with an acceptable accuracy within an evaluated experimental uncertainty of approximately 20%, suggesting the possibility of studying more complex and realistic test cases.

title: Experimental and modelling investigation of thermohydraulic performance of CO₂ finned-tube condensers
abstract: Carbon dioxide is a promising refrigerant for refrigeration and heat pump applications because of its environmental sustainability. However, unlike supercritical gas coolers, the thermohydraulic behaviour of subcritical CO₂ finned-tube condensers remains inadequately investigated and understood because of complex condensation and two-phase flow phenomena. This study presents a combined experimental and numerical investigation of a CO₂ finned-tube condenser operating under subcritical conditions. Experiments were conducted using a dedicated CO₂ test facility equipped with a two-row finned-tube heat exchanger and comprehensive instrumentation for measuring refrigerant- and air-side operating parameters. A distributed segment-by-segment effectiveness–NTU model was developed and validated to predict local and overall thermohydraulic performance. The model captures the coupled heat transfer, phase-change, and pressure-drop processes occurring in both the superheated and two-phase regions of the condenser. Validation against 30 operating conditions demonstrated deviations within ±10% for heat transfer rate, ±15% for refrigerant-side pressure drop, and ± 10% for air-side pressure drop. The effects of refrigerant mass flow rate, air velocity, and inlet air temperature on local and average heat transfer and pressure-drop characteristics were systematically examined. The results provide new insight into the evolution of condensation, vapour quality, and local heat transfer coefficients along the flow path, and offer a reliable tool for the design and optimisation of high-efficiency CO₂ refrigeration and heat pump systems.
