Experimental Investigation of Filling Ratio Effect in a 12-Turn High Temperature Oscillating Heat Pipe
abstract: Abstract A 12-turn high temperature oscillating heat pipe (HTOHP) charged with NaK-78 was tested experimentally to investigate the effect of filling ratio on thermal performance and orientation robustness. The HTOHP was fabricated from stainless steel 316 with a total length of 711.2 mm and tested in a closed chamber. Five filling ratios were tested (30%, 40%, 50%, 60%, and 70%) at heat inputs ranging from 500 W – 3250 W for inclination angles of 90°, 60°, 30°, 0° (horizontal), -30°, -60°, and -90°. For all cases, the effective thermal conductivity increased with heat input. The 40% filling ratio yielded the highest effective thermal conductivity (a maximum of 1836.8 W/m·K at 3250 W and 30°) of all tested filling ratios but began to fail at 0° when oscillations were no longer aided by gravity. The 70% filling ratio yielded the second highest effective thermal conductivity, outperforming 30%, 50%, and 60% in almost all cases and operated at all tested angles (including the -90° case of evaporator above the condenser).

title: Dimensionless Conduction Heat Rate Models for 1D Geometries and 3D TPMS Structures with Convection Boundary Conditions
abstract: Abstract New dimensionless conduction heat rate-based (DCHR-based) models for transient conduction in one-dimensional geometries (the plane wall, the solid cylinder, and the solid sphere) subject to convection boundary conditions are developed using a semi-analytical methodology. The new models permit quick prediction of instantaneous dimensionless surface temperatures and normalized cumulative energy inputs (both of which range from 0 to 1) that are in good agreement with values found using exact solutions over nine orders of magnitude of dimensionless time. Building on a recently reported similarity in heat conduction behavior exhibited by (i) three-dimensional triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) structures and (ii) the one-dimensional plane wall for constant temperature or constant heat flux conditions, the new DCHR-based plane wall models are then used to predict the thermal response of four distinct types of TPMS geometries heated by convection. Prediction of the instantaneous values of the surface temperatures and cumulative energy inputs for the TPMS geometries using the new models is demonstrated, and all predictions are compared to benchmark computational solutions of the transient, three-dimensional heat conduction equation for the conditions considered. Excellent agreement between the predictions of the DCHR-based models and computational predictions for the TPMS structures exists over approximately nine orders of magnitude of dimensionless time.

title: Effects of Contact Angle on Bubble Dynamics During Nucleate Boiling: A Coupled Level-Set and Volume of Fluid (CLSVOF)-Based Numerical Investigation
abstract: Abstract Understanding the influence of surface wettability and microlayer evaporation during bubble dynamics associated to nucleate boiling is an important aspect of phase change heat transfer and till date it is not widely explored. In the present study, boiling and associated bubble dynamics have been simulated in saturated pool boiling condition using water at the atmospheric condition. The study involves full numerical investigation of Navier-Stokes equations together with a mass transfer and a surface tension model. The growth and departure diameters of the vapor bubbles were predicted using a coupled level-set and volume of fluid approach. A microlayer evaporation model similar to that used by Pandey et al. (2018) was employed in this investigation. The study focuses on the changes in microlayer structure owing to various surface wettability (varied contact angles). The predicted departure diameters of the bubbles were compared with the available experimental and computational results. An increase in interfacial thermal resistance at the liquid–vapor boundary was observed as microlayer evaporation progressed.

title: Apparent Radiative Properties of Reconfigurable, Diffuse-Specular Origami-Inspired Cavities
abstract: Abstract Dynamic control of apparent radiative surface properties enhances the design and optimization of spacecraft thermal management systems. This work focuses on engineered surfaces that achieve dynamic variation in effective radiative properties through cavity effects. Specifically, the objective is to demonstrate how actuation of origami-inspired cavities with mixed diffuse–specular reflectance can be used to dynamically control apparent radiative properties. The collapsible nature of these cavities enables a transition between intrinsic and apparent radiative behavior through surface actuation. This study presents a Monte Carlo Ray Tracing (MCRT) investigation of the apparent radiative properties of several isothermal, opaque, and gray origami-inspired geometries, namely, a V-groove, Miura-Ori, and Barreto's Mars tessellations. Results demonstrate how geometry and specularity ratio influence the apparent absorptivity of complex surfaces under collimated and diffuse irradiation. For V -grooves exposed to collimated radiation, apparent absorptivity is generally higher at small actuation angles and for specular surfaces; for example, with intrinsic absorptivity α = 0.3 and γ = 40°, the apparent absorptivity increases by approximately 27% as the specularity ratio increases from 0 to 1. Fully folded Miura-Ori tessellations with specular surfaces approximate a black surface, similar to the V -groove as it collapses. In contrast, Barreto's Mars tessellations exhibit peak apparent absorptivity at intermediate actuation angles, with maxima occurring at γ = 40° (0.82), 35° (0.65), 30° (0.47), and 20° (0.22) for intrinsic absorptivities of 0.7, 0.5, 0.3, and 0.1, respectively.

title: Experimental Investigation of Film Cooling Effectiveness at Different Enthalpies
abstract: Abstract Experiments were carried out to assess the effectiveness of opposing jet film cooling at hypersonic flow conditions by utilising a simple flat-faced cylindrical injector. Two different enthalpy conditions, 2.8 MJ/kg and 4.9 MJ/kg, were generated using the shock tunnel and expansion tunnel facilities, with air as the test gas. The flat-faced cylinder had a 2 mm orifice at its centre, through which the nitrogen gas coolant was injected. Coaxial surface junction thermocouples were used to obtain the convective heat flux values. The analysis of the flowfield and shock structures was done using high-speed schlieren imaging. Coolant gas was injected at pressure ratios (PR) of 3.3 and 5 into the freestream. It was observed that the injection of coolant successfully caused reductions in the heat flux for all the cases, and an improvement in cooling effectiveness was observed as the pressure ratio was increased. While comparing low and high enthalpy conditions at the same pressure ratio (PR= 5), it came to light that cooling effectiveness was higher for the low enthalpy case, which is attributed to the higher coolant mass flow rate and higher diffusivity. Additionally, while comparing two different enthalpy cases having similar coolant mass flow rates, namely the PR=3.3 low-enthalpy case and the PR=5 high-enthalpy case, it was observed that the cooling effectiveness was contingent upon how well the coolant gas diffused across the flowfield.

title: Thermal-Bioconvection In A Rotating Phototactic Medium
abstract: Abstract Thermal-bioconvection in rotating phototactic suspensions plays a pivotal role in optimizing processes within biofuel systems, photobioreactors, and microbial ecosystems by enhancing fluid transport and biomass distribution. This study explores the complex interaction between thermal gradients and phototactic responses in a rotating suspension of microorganisms confined between a rigid lower boundary and a stress-free upper surface. The system undergoes uniform vertical-axis rotation, and stability characteristics are examined using MATLAB's bvp4c solver. The analysis examines how key dimensionless parameters, the Taylor number, the thermal Rayleigh number, the Lewis number, and the critical total light intensity, govern bioconvection onset. Results indicate that the critical bioconvection Rayleigh number rises with increasing rotational strength (Taylor number) but decreases with higher thermal driving (Rayleigh number), enhanced Lewis number, and greater phototactic sensitivity. Interestingly, the critical thermal Rayleigh number remains largely unaffected by the Lewis number and light intensity but is sensitive to variations in rotation. These insights underscore the importance of thermal and rotational coupling in shaping phototactic bioconvection, with direct implications for the design and control of efficient biotechnological fluid systems.

title: A Sparse-Data-Guided Inverse PINN for the Recovery of Thermal-Hydraulic Fields in Supercritical Water Reactor
abstract: Abstract Supercritical water reactors (SCWRs) are the generation-IV nuclear reactors having low carbon footprint and capable of providing outstanding thermal efficiency. Precise mapping of wall heat flux is vital for SCWR safety to mitigate localized hotspots and maintain the structural integrity of fuel cladding. But, due to rapid thermophysical property shifts in water's pseudo-super critical zone and limited data availability of the reactor core it becomes challenging to model thermal hydraulics in the pseudo-critical region of water. Again, inverse physics-informed neural networks are known for their capability to reconstruct unknown time dependent profiles when governing physics of any system is known to an extent. Available PINN studies have utilized the dense grid of temporal data, which may not be always available in reality. So, to address these gaps in this study we have established a very limited data guided multi-stage inverse physics-informed neural network (PINN) architecture integrated with SCWR thermal-hydraulic model THRUST that simultaneously recovers transient bulk fluid temperature and transient wall heat flux distributions under the assumption of constant mass flux and a prescribed range of linear pressure drop. A benchmark validated recovery through an analytical temperature field and simulated heat flux profile demonstrated reliable reconstruction. Extensive parametric and ablation studies establish the robustness of the architecture, aiding to the first time PINN integration on the thermal hydraulics of SCWR like system where data sparsity is a real constraint.

title: A Simple Lumped Model for the Prediction of Global Warming Due to Increasing Greenhouse Gas Concentrations
abstract: Abstract The objective of this study is to prove the hypothesis that the Earth's average equilibrium surface temperature increase as a function of increasing greenhouse gas (GHG) concentrations can be predicted with reasonable accuracy using a simple lumped energy balance model (EBM), provided the radiation transport component of the problem is modeled accurately. To accomplish this goal, spectral and total incoming and outgoing transmissivities of a multilayer atmosphere are first computed using line-by-line (LBL) calculations from the spectral absorption coefficients of carbon dioxide, water vapor, and methane, which are computed using the HITRAN database under various atmospheric conditions (varying temperature, pressure, and concentrations). The total absorptivity and emissivity of the Earth's surface are also computed from high-resolution spectral reflectance data. These quantities are then incorporated into a model based on global energy balance of the Earth to predict its equilibrium average surface temperature. The effects of clouds and heat losses due to phase change and conduction/convection are treated semi-empirically. The model has just one calibrated parameter and predicts a rise of 1.28 deg in the Earth's temperature when the carbon dioxide concentration is increased from 250 ppm to 400 ppm, which is consistent with observed changes. Addition of approximately 2 ppm methane to an atmosphere with 400 ppm carbon dioxide is found to have the same effect as the addition of 40 ppm of carbon dioxide (440 ppm total carbon dioxide): a rise of an additional 0.3 deg. The climate sensitivity is found to be ∼2 deg.

title: Fixed-Grid Sharp-Interface Numerical Solutions to the Three-Phase Spherical Stefan Problem
abstract: Abstract Many metal manufacturing processes involve phase change phenomena, which include melting, boiling, and vaporization. These phenomena often occur concurrently. A prototypical 1D model for understanding the phase change phenomena is the Stefan problem. There is a large body of literature discussing the analytical solution to the two-phase Stefan problem that describes only the melting or boiling of phase change materials (PCMs) with one moving interface. Density-change effects that induce additional fluid flow during phase change are generally neglected in the literature to simplify the math of the Stefan problem. In our recent work (Soleimani et al., 2026, “Analytical and Numerical Solutions to the Three-Phase Stefan Problem With Simultaneous Occurrences of Melting, Solidification, Boiling, and Condensation Phenomena,” ASME J. Heat Transfer-Trans. ASME, 148(1), p. 012401.), we provide analytical and numerical solutions to the three-phase Stefan problem with simultaneous occurrences of melting, solidification, boiling, and condensation in Cartesian coordinates. The problem was set in a semi-infinite domain with two moving interfaces—melt and boiling fronts. The solid, liquid, and vapor phases of the PCM have distinct thermophysical properties, including density, thermal conductivity, and heat capacity. All relevant jump conditions, including density and kinetic energy, were accounted for in the three-phase Stefan problem. Our current work builds on our previous work to solve a more challenging problem: the three-phase Stefan problem in spherical coordinates for finite sized particles. There are three moving interfaces in this system: the melt front, the boiling front, and the outer boundary, which is in contact with the atmosphere. Although an analytical solution could not be found for this problem, we solved the governing equations using a fixed-grid sharp-interface method with second-order spatio-temporal accuracy. Using a small-time analytical solution, we predict a reasonably accurate estimate of temperature (in the three phases) and interface positions and velocities at the start of the simulation. To derive small-time analytical solutions, low- and high-density contrasts between phases are considered separately. Our numerical method is validated by reproducing the two-phase nanoparticle melting results of Font et al. (2015, “A Mathematical Model for Nanoparticle Melting With Density Change,” Microfluid. Nanofluid., 18(2), pp. 233–243). Finally, we solve the three-phase Stefan problems numerically to demonstrate the importance of kinetic energy terms during the phase change of smaller (nano) particles. In contrast, these effects diminish for large particles (microns and larger).

title: Piezo-Actuated Enhanced Nucleate Boiling: From Saturated to Controlled Flash Regimes in Two-Phase Direct-to-Chip Cooling for Artificial Intelligence Superchips and Data Centers
abstract: Abstract Two-phase direct-to-chip cooling is emerging as an important thermal management pathway for the rapidly increasing thermal design powers of modern AI superchips while maintaining data center energy efficiency. This paper presents a combined passive–active approach that transitions high-performance saturated heterogeneous nucleate boiling to a stabilized and controlled flash-nucleate boiling regime using low-power piezoelectric actuation that produces feather-like in-plane and out-of-plane microvibrations of the heated surface. Experiments on microstructured copper cold plates (CPs) with dielectric fluids, at 100–140 kPa pressures, establish baseline enhanced nucleate boiling (ENB-1) performance in partial flow-boiling configurations typical of direct-to-chip flow loops. These results quantify cold-plate behavior and indicate that physics-guided modifications of the experimentally tested microstructures and flow-loop design, as modeled and proposed for further experimental testing, can substantially increase heat-transfer coefficients and critical heat flux (CHF). Activation of megahertz piezo-actuators with low-frequency modulation near antiresonance generates small microvibrations that modify nucleating bubble dynamics and their characteristic frequencies. This triggers a rapid transition to a controlled, stabilized high-pressure (400–500 kPa) heterogeneous flash-nucleate boiling regime (ENB-2), sustained at the boiling surface by “on–off” microlayer heating and acoustic streaming mechanisms. This transition from ENB-1 to ENB-2 accompanies a short-duration (tens of milliseconds) increase in interfacial mass transfer across bubble microlayers, producing transient heat extraction of 200–400 J from underneath the heated surface, that is, from the chip to the ENB-2 condenser with a sustained high pressure at the vapor exit of the cold plate. Three-dimensional transient conduction simulations predict chip-level temperature reductions of about 15–20 °C for low-thermal-inertia test vehicles and future chip implementations. Baseline experiments show nucleate boiling heat transfer with critical heat flux near 50–60 W/cm2 and a lower heat-transfer coefficient (HTC) of 1–2 W/cm2 °C. The tested and deployed architecture is amenable to further optimization to higher CHF (135–175 W/cm2 or more) and associated HTC (up to 150 W/cm2 °C) for ENB-1 and 10–20 °C cooler chips through ENB-2. Observed ENB-2 condenser performance suggests a shift from the ENB-1 condenser to a direct-contact tank/pool condenser for ENB-2, which would allow sustained waste-heat recovery from the vapor at, say, 70 °C and 400 kPa. That is, a stabilized flash-boiling regime supports lower junction temperatures, improved chip reliability, and more energy-efficient next-generation AI data centers.

European supercritical water-cooled small modular reactor: Design and analysis
abstract: This paper presents the design concept and in-depth analysis of a European Super-Critical-Water-cooled Small Modular Reactor (SCW-SMR), developed within the framework of the Joint European-Canadian-Chinese (ECC-SMART) project, aimed at advancing next-generation nuclear reactor technologies. The reactor features an innovative horizontal fuel assembly configuration with seven heat-up stages and intermediate mixing zones, specifically designed to enable passive residual heat removal through natural circulation. The horizontal core configuration generates unique natural circulation patterns in the vessel that improve heat removal efficiency during accident conditions. Key innovations include the elimination of high-pressure injection requirements through the use of subcooled water inventory, the reliance on the large volume of feedwater at 280 °C as a thermal buffer, and the successful demonstration of passive decay heat removal for extended periods that exceed 72 h. Based on extensive material testing within the ECC-SMART, the design specifies 310S stainless steel and Alloy 800H as alternative candidates for fuel cladding. Comprehensive safety analyses demonstrate the reactor’s capability to manage design basis accidents, including long-term station blackout (LTSBO) and large-break loss-of-coolant accidents (LBLOCA) using primarily passive safety systems. Detailed thermal-hydraulic analyses confirm acceptable peak cladding temperatures below 625 °C during normal operation and below 780 °C during design-based accidents. Neutronic analyses and coupled neutronic-thermal-hydraulic simulations confirmed strongly negative reactivity coefficients and demonstrated feasibility of a two-year burnup cycle without fuel shuffling. The European SCW-SMR design is a 290 MW t h reactor operating at 25 MPa with core outlet temperatures of 500 °C, achieving thermal efficiency approaching 44%. The design represents a significant advancement in Generation IV reactor technology, combining the inherent simplicity of supercritical water cooling with enhanced passive safety features suitable for small modular reactors deployment.

Multiphysics Analysis of a 325 MHz-Quadrupole Resonator for Surface Resistance Characterization of Superconducting Material
abstract: The quadrupole resonator (QPR) is a dedicated instrument for characterizing the radio-frequency surface resistance of superconducting materials. In this work, a low-frequency QPR with a fundamental frequency of 325 MHz is designed and systematically investigated through multi-physics simulations, including electromagnetic, mechanical, and thermal analyses. Compared with existing QPRs, the lower frequency enables improved separation of BCS and residual resistance contributions, although introducing increased sensitivity to geometric dimensions and mechanical perturbations. Electromagnetic simulations show that the electric-field distribution on the rods exhibits a strong frequency dependence, whereas the magnetic field on the sample remains relatively stable across harmonic modes. A detailed tolerance study indicates that rod misalignment significantly affects field distribution, yielding a conservative alignment requirement of -0.2° to 0°. Mechanical simulations demonstrate that pressure fluctuations and microphonics dominate frequency shift, while Lorentz force detuning has a relatively minor impact. Thermal analyses confirm the validity of the RF–DC compensation technique with negligible systematic error and show that substrates with high thermal conductivity significantly enhance thermal stability at high fields. This work provides guidance for the fabrication tolerance and stable measurement of the low-frequency, multi-harmonic QPR systems.

title: Numerical modeling of nitrogen transport and loss during laser powder bed fusion of high nitrogen steels
abstract: High Nitrogen Steels represent a highly promising material class for Laser Powder Bed Fusion, but their processing is challenged by significant nitrogen loss due to a drop in solubility upon melting. To systematically investigate the underlying degassing kinetics and nitrogen transport mechanisms, this study establishes a high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics model utilizing the Volume of Fluid method. The continuous species conservation framework accounts for convection-dominant transport, integrating a temperature-dependent nitrogen solubility limit and an interfacial mass transfer sink term at the free melt pool surface. The numerical model is successfully calibrated and validated against single-track experiments on Fe-15Cr-0.3C-N steel substrates across varying surface energy densities, demonstrating good agreement with both experimental melt pool geometries and a spatial nitrogen concentration profile measured via Wavelength Dispersive X-ray Spectrometry. The results reveal that the final nitrogen distribution across the melt pool depth is fundamentally governed by intense keyhole degassing coupled with complex convective transport. Marangoni convection drives nitrogen depleted melt backwards, inducing steep surface concentration gradients, while recirculation vortices transport the degassed melt deeper into the substrate. Using a novel Nitrogen Retention Index, parametric analysis demonstrates that higher surface energy densities prolong active surface degassing, thereby intensifying nitrogen loss.

SOFC powered cruise ships using future fuels: A comparison of cruising range
abstract: The global maritime industry needs to reduce CO 2 and pollutant emissions in order to comply with stringent emissions regulations and for climate change mitigation. Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) are under consideration to be used as power plants for future ships. They offer advantages such as high efficiency, low emissions, fuel flexibility, and high-temperature heat output. However, their low power density brings concerns about their suitability for high-powered and space-constrained mobile applications such as cruise ships. This study addresses this concern by evaluating the cruising range that SOFC-powered cruise ships could attain when fuelled by a variety of future green fuels. Thermodynamic process models are developed for evaluating system performance. The size of each system component is calculated for estimating total space requirements. These SOFC systems are then optimised to maximise the cruising range of ships powered by them, while adhering to the volume constraints expected on cruise ships. Results show that SOFC cruise ships fuelled by green diesel or methane achieve a range of 4800–8600 nautical miles. Therefore, these ships could be used for ocean crossings. Most typical cruise itineraries are shorter, and can be fulfilled by almost all the fuels under consideration. Hydrogen-fuelled ships offer the shortest range — less than 1500 nautical miles. Irrespective of the choice of fuel, SOFCs attain high electrical efficiencies (44–65%) throughout their lifetime, and also satisfy a cruise ship’s heat demands. Therefore, this study suggests that SOFC-powered cruise ships are technologically feasible, motivating further economics- and logistics-based studies.

Exergoeconomic and thermodynamic analysis of low-GWP CO₂ mixtures for heat pump applications
abstract: The environmental impact of heat pumps is strongly influenced by the choice of working fluid. State-of-the-art refrigerants are mainly hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), which exhibit high Global Warming Potential (GWP), or hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs), which raise concerns related to PFAS formation. The transition toward low-GWP alternatives often entails a reduction in cycle performance; however, it also opens opportunities for innovative system configurations and improved thermodynamic matching. One of the main source of inefficiency in heat pumps arises from irreversibilities in the evaporator and gas cooler, particularly when operating between finite heat-capacity streams. In this context, mixtures based on carbon dioxide (CO₂) represent a promising route to enhance cycle performance while reducing environmental impact. This study presents a comprehensive thermodynamic and exergoeconomic analysis of a transcritical heat pump cycle employing binary mixtures of CO₂ and selected organic compounds. The system includes an internal heat exchanger, and each mixture is optimized with respect to composition and key performance indicators. Results are compared to those of a baseline pure CO₂ cycle. Two case studies—a ground-source heat pump for district heating and a high-temperature heat pump for industrial waste-heat recovery—are investigated to identify optimal working conditions and assess economic viability. The analysis shows that CO₂ mixtures with dimethyl ether (DME) increase the Coefficient of Performance (COP) by up to 38%, reduce gas-cooler pressure by 30–151 bar in the baseline system, and improve second-law efficiency by 3–5 percentage points, leading to a reduction in the levelized cost of heat depending on electricity prices.

Heat Transfer Model For Micro Scale Flow Boiling Based On Interpretable Machine Learning
abstract: Abstract High heat transfer is achieved in micro scale flow boiling by coupling latent heat of vaporization and vibrant vapor bubbles in microchannels. The difference between micro scale and conventional flow boiling is the relative significance of surface-tension in the four forces, which are included in: Froude number (FrLO), Boiling number (Bo), Bond number (Bd), and dimensionless gas velocity (JG) as the core influential factors, revealing their synergistic interactions, identified by SHAP analysis of developing an interpretable machine learning model by covering complex micro scale flow boiling regimes, wide operating conditions range, and significant scale effects inherent. The analysis reveals that FrLO, Bo, Bd, and JG are the core features influencing the micro scale flow boiling heat transfer, with their effects exhibiting distinct segmented or threshold behaviors. This makes our model be universal for various working fluids, saturation temperature, tube diameters, vapor qualities, mass fluxes and heat fluxes based on dimensionless numbers to achieve high-precision prediction of the heat transfer coefficient in evaporating microchannels. Based on the physical thresholds and interaction mechanisms determined by the SHAP interaction analysis (FrLO ≈ 50, JG ≈ 12, Bd ≈ 1, Bo ≈ 00005), a new correlation was developed by embedding the co-ordination coupling terms (FrLO×Bd and JG × Bo) and the vapor quality penalty factor into the correlation structure. This work is not only helpful to understand the basic mechanism of microscale flow boiling, but also provides a new theoretical method for improving the prediction of heat transfer in microcircuits.

Experimental Comparison of R600a Domestic Refrigerator with Fin and Metal Foam Evaporator Under Tropical Conditions
abstract: Conventional fin-and-tube evaporators in domestic refrigeration systems exhibit reduced performance under elevated ambient conditions, particularly in tropical climates. This study experimentally evaluates a 190 L domestic refrigerator modified with an externally wrapped copper metal foam coated evaporator operating with isobutane refrigerant, which has a low global warming potential. A dual-evaporator configuration enabled side-by-side comparison with a fin-tube evaporator under identical ambient temperatures of 30 °C–40 °C and cabinet temperatures of 0 °C–15 °C. Key performance indicators included the coefficient of performance, evaporator cooling capacity, compressor power input, and volumetric refrigeration capacity. Integration of open-cell copper foam with 90% and 30 pores per inch improved phase-change heat transfer and refrigerant distribution, resulting in a 25%–31% increase in coefficient of performance, a 14%–18% rise in cooling capacity, a 10%–19% enhancement in volumetric refrigeration capacity, and up to 12% reduction in compressor power compared with the conventional system. These improvements are attributed to intensified nucleate boiling, enhanced thermal conductivity, and uniform superheat development. The enhancement strategy allows drop-in retrofitting without changes to system layout, refrigerant charge, or control logic, offering a scalable approach for improving efficiency in tropical climates.

title: Cooling Performance and Heat Flux Evolution of Sparse Sessile Droplets: An Experimental Study
abstract: Spray cooling is widely used in various fields to enhance heat transfer. However, there is scant research on sparse spray cooling under low-pressure and low-flow conditions. In this paper, the dynamic morphological evolution and heat transfer characteristics of sessile droplets generated by spray were experimentally investigated. The effects of the number of sprays, wall temperature, and wall wettability on cooling performance were explored. The results indicate that the morphology of the sessile droplets was jointly determined by the number of sprays and the initial wall temperature, transforming from uniform small droplets to a merged liquid film, which significantly affected the evaporation time and heat transfer efficiency. The wall temperature drop amplitude showed a non-monotonic variation trend of “first increasing and then decreasing” with the number of sprays. The optimal number of sprays increased as the initial wall temperature rose, specifically from 30 to 50 as the wall temperature is raised from 50 °C to 80 °C, and the overall cooling effect of hydrophilic surfaces was superior to that of hydrophobic surfaces. The heat flux distribution of sparse spray cooling indicated that, at the initial cooling stage, the latent heat of vaporization dominated, accounting for 53% to 82% of the total heat flux, and this proportion increased with the rise of the initial wall temperature and was jointly regulated by the number of sprays and wall wettability. As the droplets evaporated, the dominant factor of heat flux gradually reverted to natural cooling dominated by convection and radiation. The basic heat transfer performance of sparse spray cooling is clarified, and a theoretical basis as well as data support are provided for the design of high-efficiency spray cooling technology.

Ex-Core Neutron-Flux Reconstruction Using Machine-Learned Green’s Kernels and Flux-Gradient Measurements
abstract: Accurate reconstruction of the neutron-flux distribution in a reactor core is essential for power-shape monitoring, diagnostics, control, and irradiation experiments, but dense in-core instrumentation is often impractical in advanced reactors (high temperature, corrosive coolants, and irradiation constraints) and microreactors (limited penetrations and access). This work presents GRACE (Green’s-kernel Reconstruction from ACcessible Ex-core measurements), a physics-directed framework for reconstructing three-dimensional neutron-flux fields from boundary measurements by embedding a Green’s-function representation of one-group diffusion into a neural parameterization of the kernel. By recasting flux estimation as an inverse boundary-value problem, GRACE identifies an effective Green’s kernel that can be reused as a boundary-to-interior propagator across operating configurations, reducing reliance on scenario-specific surrogates trained on large simulation libraries. Numerical validation using an OpenMC model of the Purdue University Reactor (PUR-1) demonstrates accurate reconstruction, with mean fractional errors below 5%, for previously unseen control-rod configurations using only simulated boundary data. To provide the boundary-gradient input required by the reconstruction, we introduce and demonstrate a quadrupole sensor for measuring the neutron-flux gradient at the core boundary. An activation-based prototype using gold wires was deployed at PUR-1, yielding reproducible gradient signatures and agreement with OpenMC predictions at the few-percent level. These results demonstrate that flux-gradient information can be obtained experimentally, establishing a path toward core-monitoring strategies based entirely on ex-core measurements.

title: Effect of Uncertainties in the MSRE Model Salt Properties Using SPECTRA/SUE Analysis
abstract: The reliable prediction of heat transfer in molten salt reactors (MSRs) critically depends on the accurate characterization of the molten salt thermophysical properties. However, significant uncertainties remain in key thermophysical properties, such as thermal conductivity, dynamic viscosity, density, and specific heat capacity, largely due to limitations in historical measurement techniques and the limited availability of high-quality experimental data. These uncertainties can directly influence the assessment of convective heat transfer behavior in MSR systems.In this work, sensitivity analyses were performed using the existing Molten Salt Reactor Experiment model implemented in the SPECTRA code, with a specific focus on heat transfer during normal operation. The analyses were carried out using SUE, an uncertainty quantification and sensitivity analysis tool developed at NRG PALLAS to investigate the influence of uncertainties in thermal conductivity, viscosity, specific heat capacity, and density on the heat transfer coefficient (HTC). Both deterministic sensitivity analyses and stochastic sampling approaches were employed, and a global sensitivity assessment based on the Plischke method was applied to quantify and rank the relative importance of these thermophysical parameters.The results demonstrated that thermal conductivity has the strongest positive impact on the HTC, identifying it as the dominant parameter governing heat transfer predictions. Viscosity showed a smaller but negative effect, while specific heat capacity exhibited a comparatively weak positive influence. The effect of density was found to be less significant than that of thermal conductivity.The sensitivity indices obtained using the Plischke method confirmed these findings, with viscosity and specific heat capacity exhibiting similar secondary effects. Very similar results obtained from deterministic and random sampling approaches indicate the robustness of the sensitivity analysis and highlight the importance of accurately characterizing molten salt thermophysical properties for reliable heat transfer modeling in MSRs.

Flow control and heat transfer enhancement by vapor-guiding structures in two-phase immersion cooling utilizing lotus-type porous copper
abstract: Silicon carbide (SiC)-based inverters play an important role in simultaneously achieving CO 2 emission reduction and energy efficiency. However, in boiling immersion cooling systems that do not require pumps, improvement of critical heat flux (CHF) is essential for cooling SiC chips. In the present research, the authors aim to enhance the CHF by introducing a vapor-guiding structure onto a heat transfer surface utilizing lotus-type porous copper. First, liquid supply paths are investigated utilizing inclined structures. The results demonstrate that liquid supply from the upper direction of the lotus copper is dominant. Based on the findings, a U-shaped structure that promotes liquid replenishment is proposed. The results show that, when the groove depth is 1 mm, no noticeable effect of the U-shaped structure is observed due to the large flow resistance in the grooves. On the other hand, for a groove depth of 3 mm, the CHF is improved by more than 20% compared with the case without the U-shaped structure. Therefore, the results indicate that, in addition to controlling the amount of vapor discharged from the lotus copper, regulating the vapor discharge path is effective in enhancing the CHF.

Influence of Gravity Orientation on Downward Condensation of Refrigerants in Metal Foam-Enhanced Tubes: An Experimental Investigation
abstract: Enhancing condensation in refrigeration and air-conditioning systems can be achieved with tube inserts. This experimental study explores how combining metal foam-filled tubes and inclined tube orientation utilizes gravity effects to improve heat transfer performance. The effects of metal foam pore densities, tube inclination angle, mass flux, and vapor quality on condensation heat transfer coefficient and pressure drop of R134a flow were studied here. A total number of 240 experiments were performed over a mass flux of 54−90 kg/(m2·s), vapor quality of 0.2−0.8, using metal foams with pores per inch (PPI) of 10 and 15 and porosity of 0.85. Compared to plain tubes, the metal foam-filled tubes with PPI of 10 and 15 showed an increase in heat transfer by up to 3.21 and 2.97 times, respectively, accompanied by a pressure drop rise. The change of inclination angle from condensation downward flow (−90°) to horizontal flow (0°) nearly doubles the heat transfer rate at constant conditions, while the pressure drop remains almost unaffected. The maximum performance evaluation criterion value of 1.879, obtained for the tube with PPI of 10 at −60° inclination, vapor quality of 0.2, and mass flux of 90 kg/(m2·s), representing the optimum experimental conditions of this study.

Role of Ni on Cu-rich cluster formation in neutron irradiated reactor pressure vessel steels
abstract: The role of Ni on formation of Cu-rich clusters (CRCs) in neutron irradiated reactor pressure vessel steels is studied. The Ni concentration dependence of the size, the number density, and the chemical composition of the CRCs, as well as the residual Cu concentrations in matrix, are estimated by using atom probe tomography. Very low Ni samples exhibit a much lower CRC number density than higher Ni samples, while containing a significantly larger number of Cu atoms in the CRCs, which decrease drastically with increasing Ni content. These results are interpreted in terms of the reduction of the critical nucleation energy of the CRCs in the presence of Ni. In addition, the presence of Ni causes the Cu cores in the CRCs to become more diffused by mixing other solute elements. It is also found that the residual Cu concentrations in the very low Ni samples decrease even at low irradiation fluence compared with those in the higher Ni samples, indicating that the kinetics of the CRC formation under neutron irradiation are much faster in the very low Ni samples than those in the higher Ni samples. This phenomenon is partly attributed to the differences in the behavior of the irradiation-induced interstitial atoms in addition to well-known vacancy trapping by solute; the presence of Ni suppresses the radiation-enhanced diffusion of Cu due to the suppression of the interstitial migration by forming interstitial-solutes complexes including Ni. title: An experimental study on the time dependence of diffusive mass transfer of single oxygen bubbles
abstract: In the vast majority of gas–liquid engineering applications, the liquid phase contains a range of dissolved gaseous species. These dissolved process gases transfer from the liquid phase to the gaseous phase countercurrent to the typically desired mass transfer of gas to liquid. In process design, the resulting change in the composition of the gaseous phase is usually neglected, although a temporal change in the composition of the gaseous phase can directly influence the mass transfer performance over time. The current fundamental study quantifies the mass transfer performance of oxygen bubbles to liquid phases saturated with another gas. For this purpose, the oxygen mass transfer from a bubble to degassed, helium-, nitrogen-, argon- and carbon dioxide-saturated water is studied. Light Sheet Fluorescence Microscopy is used as imaging system for Planar Laser-induced Fluorescence measurements of dissolved oxygen concentration fields, delivering local instantaneous Sherwood numbers, diffusion coefficients and mass transfer coefficients. For the first time, the study showcases that the mass transfer performance from a gaseous dispersed to a liquid continuous phase is independent of time if mass transfer occurs in one direction only. If mass transfer occurs in both directions, the mass transfer performance of the dispersed phase is significantly lower and its time dependence higher to liquids containing gaseous species with high solubilities, such as carbon dioxide in water. Furthermore, the results suggest that applying intrinsic values, such as diffusion or mass transfer coefficients, obtained for binary systems in multicomponent systems can lead to high uncertainty.

Numerical Modelling of Bubble Growth and Dynamics in Forced Flow over a Wavy Wall
abstract: Abstract This study deals with single bubble growth during nucleate flow boiling on an uneven wall. A model problem, bearing the most important features of a real wavy-wall case, is defined and solved. The equations are based on macro region modelling of the bubble and describe its growth from the initial state to detachment from the surface and consequent motion. The model includes a simultaneous solution of conservation equations for the liquid and gaseous phases. The complete three-dimensional formulation is discretized using an original in-house numerical code, based on level-set and multi-grid methods, realized in MATLAB. The model is validated vs. two cases existing in the literature, namely, bubble growth, detachment and consequent motion in pool and flow boiling on a flat horizontal wall. Then, different cases of bubble growth are studied for horizontal and vertical uneven walls. It is demonstrated that under certain conditions, the bubble would grow but its separation from the surface is obstructed by the waviness and thus delayed. It is also shown how a growing bubble affects the flow field inside a cavity, shifting or even locally and temporally destroying the vortex structure. This effect would be important in a real situation, where a growing and detaching bubble is usually closely followed by another bubble growing at the same spot. The findings of the present study will contribute to development of comprehensive models that would combine detailed flow and heat transfer modeling with physically-sound bubble dynamics description for real surfaces.

Mitigation of steam-oxidation in uranium nitride fuel pellets by carbon addition
abstract: Uranium nitride (UN) is an accident-tolerant fuel candidate for light-water reactors because of its high uranium density and thermal conductivity. During fabrication, oxygen- and carbon-related impurities can be introduced, yet their influence on the steam oxidation of UN has not been well quantified. To address this gap, we fabricated UN pellets with controlled additions of UO2 and carbon, and investigated their behavior under flowing steam at 350°C. Pristine UN pellets showed partial surface oxidation after 30 min, followed by complete disintegration after 90 min. UO2-added pellets were less stable and disintegrated within 45 min. In contrast, carbon addition markedly improved the steam oxidation tolerance, as evidenced by intact pellet surfaces with reduced spallation. UN pellets containing 0.25–1.40 wt% carbon retained their shapes and exhibited weight gains below 0.2% even after 240 min. Overall, our experimental results underscore the need to carefully control fabrication-related impurities, as minimizing oxygen contamination and moderately incorporating carbon are effective measures for improving the steam oxidation resistance of UN pellets.

title: Secondary flow and peripheral heat flux distribution in square channels with macroscopic random roughness
abstract: We perform numerical simulations of conjugate heat transfer in square ducts for two representative rough surfaces (grit-blasted and graphite) and two fluid–solid conductivity ratios, using both DNS and RANS with the Spalart–Allmaras model. The effect of the QCR extension is also assessed, with a smooth-wall case serving as a baseline. DNS captures the altered heat-transfer distribution and secondary flows caused by roughness, whereas RANS tends to circularize velocity and temperature fields, yielding parabolic Nusselt profiles with limited sensitivity to geometric details. The QCR correction improves RANS predictions for grit-blasted roughness, where secondary flows resemble the smooth case, but degrades accuracy for the graphite surface, where eddy orientation is reversed. Despite local discrepancies, RANS agrees well with DNS in global metrics, with errors typically below 5%. For the first time, the heat-flux distribution along the duct perimeter is examined in detail, revealing that it depends not only on the roughness intensity but also on its morphological characteristics. These findings support the use of RANS for average heat-transfer prediction in rough-wall conjugate heat transfer, while underscoring the need for high-fidelity simulations to resolve the spatial complexity introduced by roughness.

abstract: This study presents a physics-guided neural network model for predicting the spectral emissivity of sandblasted titanium surfaces. The proposed approach integrates Agababov’s model with a multi-parametric description of surface roughness and accounts for chemical contamination induced by corundum (Al 2 O 3 ) particle embedding. Fifteen Ti-6Al-4V samples were prepared using five abrasive grain sizes and three projection pressures, producing surfaces with arithmetic mean roughness ranging from 0.53 to 3.72 μ m. Emissivity measurements were performed in the spectral range of 2–23 μ m with a spectrometer. The proposed neural network architecture consists of two parallel branches. The first branch estimates the roughness factor using eight surface descriptors. The second branch predicts the evolution function of the material based on the parameters of the sandblasting process. A Fourier Amplitude Sensitivity Testing (FAST) analysis was employed to identify the most influential roughness parameters, revealing that the arithmetic mean peak curvature (Spc) and the developed interfacial area ratio (Sdr) exhibit the highest sensitivity indices. The model achieves an average prediction error below 2.5 ± 1.37 % on all tested surfaces, outperforming existing analytical approaches that rely on a limited number of roughness parameters and do not account for chemical contamination effects. Analysis reveals that corundum contamination contributes 35–50% of the increase in total emissivity depending on the sandblasting conditions. This finding emphasizes the necessity of accounting for chemical modifications in radiative property models for functionalized surfaces.

Trade-off between repository footprint and radiotoxicity in geological disposal of vitrified high-level waste from spent MOX fuels: quantitative assessment of simplified minor actinide separation
abstract: Radioactive waste management remains a critical challenge for the sustainability of nuclear energy systems, particularly for closed fuel cycles utilizing mixed oxide (MOX) fuel. MOX fuel contains significantly higher concentrations of minor actinides (MAs) and heat-generating nuclides compared to uranium dioxide (UO 2 ) fuel, necessitating distinct disposal strategies. This study evaluates the effect of a proposed “simplified MA separation” process (recovery ratios of 70% and 90%) on the environmental load of geological disposal for vitrified high-level waste from spent MOX fuel (MOX-HLW). The term environmental load is defined as the physical/spatial footprint. We quantitatively assessed the repository footprint and radiological impact based on nuclide migration and potential human intrusion scenarios. The results demonstrate that, without separation, MOX-HLW of no-countermeasure baseline case requires a repository footprint approximately 6.7 times that of UO 2 -HLW due to the high heat generation from Am-241. Simplified MA separation with 90% efficiency effectively reduces the footprint to levels comparable to those of UO 2 -HLW by enabling higher waste loading. However, a fundamental trade-off was identified: increasing waste loading to minimize footprint maintains a constant Am-241 inventory per canister due to thermal constraints, resulting in no reduction in the potential exposure dose from Am-241 radiotoxicity in inadvertent human intrusion scenarios. Furthermore, the exposure dose from nuclide migration is dominated by long-lived fission products (specifically Cs-135), which are unaffected by MA separation. These findings reveal that the effects of upstream nuclear fuel cycle conditions, such as MA separation during reprocessing and the waste loading of vitrified waste, are deeply embedded in the repository thermal design and the evaluation of future human-induced events for MOX-HLW disposal. Therefore, it is necessary to derive a comprehensive optimal solution from various combinations of conditions by focusing on these trade-off relationships.

title: Impact of Trap Centers on the Scintillation Performance of TlSr2Br5:Eu2+ Single Crystal
abstract: In this research we present the scintillation characteristics of Eu 2+ -doped TlSr 2 Br 5 single crystals for radiation detection applications. These scintillators were grown from the melt using the Bridgman method. A comprehensive set of characterization techniques was employed to evaluate the performance of this scintillator, including X-ray excited luminescence, photoluminescence, thermoluminescence, scintillation light yield, energy resolution, and decay time measurements. A comparison between Eu 2+ -doped and undoped TlSr 2 Br 5 crystals revealed no significant improvement in light yield, energy resolution, and decay characteristics upon doping. Thermoluminescence analysis confirmed the presence of intermediate and deep trap centers in pure and Eu 2+ -doped samples. These trap centers likely act as carrier trapping sites, delaying radiative recombination and thereby limiting scintillation efficiency. This study also highlights the critical role of trap centers in governing the scintillation performance of this material. Improvement in the scintillation performance of this material could be achieved through appropriate defect engineering strategies.

abstract: Passive anode recirculation using ejectors is an energy-efficient, lightweight, and cost-effective alternative to electrically driven blowers for hydrogen recirculation in proton exchange membrane fuel cell systems. This study develops and validates a computational fluid dynamics methodology for predicting the performance and internal flow behavior of needle ejectors. Two-dimensional Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (2D-RANS) simulations using a Reynolds stress model with adjustable GEKO parameters are compared with high-resolution large eddy simulations (LES) and experimental entrainment ratio measurements. LES reveals a considerably shorter primary jet and stronger mixing than conventional RANS turbulence models predict. Based on these findings, two calibrated GEKO parameter sets are identified. The performance-validated set reproduces the experimental entrainment ratio across five load points with an average relative deviation below 3%, but overpredicts the jet length. In contrast, the flow-field-validated set closely reproduces the LES-resolved velocity fields and mixing behavior, while the entrainment ratio deviates by 13.5% on average. These results highlight the trade-off between global ejector performance calibration and physically resolved internal flow prediction. While the performance-validated set is limited to similar boundary conditions and geometries, the flow-field-validated set appears more generally applicable because it is calibrated against the enhanced mixing observed in LES. If the LES-predicted flow-field behavior is confirmed experimentally, the proposed flow-field-validated RANS parameterization provides a directly applicable and computationally efficient simulation methodology that advances ejector geometry optimization beyond conventional models and enables shorter mixing chambers and reduced nozzle exit positions, thereby improving packaging, cost, and system integration in future PEM fuel cell applications.

abstract: The study of neutron diffusion in nuclear reactors is pivotal for ensuring safe and efficient reactor operation. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of multi-energy group neutron diffusion, focusing on the derivation of spatial functions for cubic and spherical reactor geometries and the development of volume-integrated multigroup point kinetics equations. Analytical solutions for the time-integrated multigroup point kinetics equations are derived using Hermite piecewise polynomial methods for one-energy group, two-energy groups, and four-energy groups, incorporating temperature feedback effects. Numerical results are provided for step and ramp reactivity insertions in cubic and spherical reactors, analyzing delayed supercritical, supercritical, and subcritical cases for the spherical reactor. The study further evaluates the impact of temperature feedback on reactor dynamics. Results demonstrate high accuracy in the proposed analytical solutions, with significant implications for reactor design and safety analysis. This work provides a robust framework for modeling neutron behavior in multi-energy group systems, offering valuable insights for both theoretical and applied nuclear engineering.

Evaluation of Neutron-Induced Radiation Generated by a Vehicle-Mounted System for Hazardous Material Detection
abstract: Compact neutron generators enable prompt gamma neutron activation analysis as an effective technique for subsurface material identification in applications such as unexploded ordnance and land mine detection. Their integration into mobile platforms introduces complex mixed neutron-photon radiation fields that require quantitative evaluation. In this study, neutron and secondary gamma radiation transport from a compact deuterium-tritium neutron generator integrated into the optionally manned ground vehicle TAERO, a platform adapted for off-road demining operations, is investigated using Monte Carlo simulations.Spatial distributions of neutron flux and gamma dose rate are analyzed at locations corresponding to the vehicle operator and onboard electronic systems within a material-representative vehicle geometry. Neutron-induced displacement damage in silicon is additionally evaluated as a metric of radiation exposure for electronic components. The analysis focuses on the influence of distance, structural scattering, and local shielding on radiation field characteristics and on the derivation of distance-dependent dose parameterizations relevant to operational deployment.The presented approach establishes a framework for characterizing the radiation exposure associated with compact neutron-based sensing systems deployed on mobile demining platforms. These outcomes are employed to establish operational limits and safety-relevant constraints for the engineering design and integration of mobile neutron-based systems.

title: Reliability Analysis and 30 Years of Operational Performance of the GHARR-1 Control Rod System
abstract: This study evaluates the 30-year operational reliability of the Ghana Research Reactor-1 (GHARR-1) control rod drive mechanism (CRDM) from its criticality on December 17, 1994, to August 7, 2025. To address a 4.93-year left-truncation period (1994–1999) when records were undocumented, a conditional reliability framework was utilized to analyze 31 subsequent failure events. Failures were categorized by physical nature (mechanical versus electrical) and maintenance logic (repairable versus non-repairable). The results indicate that the system has transitioned from its stable useful-life phase into a definitive wear-out phase. The most frequent failure mode was the inability of the control rod to move upward (n = 12), exhibiting the highest failure rate (λ = 0.4668 yr−1) and a mean time between failures of 2.14 years. While electrical failures were more prevalent (n = 22), primarily involving instrumentation drift and circuit malfunctions, mechanical failures (n = 9) such as structural wire snaps and sudden rod drops emerged predominantly during the later operational stages (at 25–30 years). The clustering of safety-critical failures in the final five years demonstrates that after 30 years, the CRDM is nearing its design-life threshold. The study concludes that standard annual maintenance is insufficient for aging miniature neutron source reactor facilities and recommends a transition toward predictive, condition-based maintenance strategies. These empirical findings provide essential benchmarks for aging management and life extension protocols for similar research reactors globally.

title: Balance of Plant Modeling and Real-Time Hardware-in-the-Loop Integration with the Microreactor Automated Control System
abstract: The advent of novel microreactor technology has driven a focused effort to explore safety and efficiency improvements that can be achieved through the use of automated system control. Development of control strategies, especially for initial demonstration, requires an adequate surrogate environment to safely research failure modes and control integration with realistic hardware delay. However, efficiency gains from control strategies are improved when the scope of controller action is expanded to include system-level dynamics such as downstream heat extraction and mass flow. For this reason, a balance-of-plant (BOP) model of a representative microreactor system has been developed using the TRANsient Simulation Framework of Reconfigurable Models library in Modelica. This model captures a reactor and primary NaK coolant loop that represent corresponding system components of the Microreactor Applications Research Validation and EvaLuation (MARVEL) design as well as a secondary coolant loop and heat extraction representative of the Microreactor Agile Non-Nuclear Experimental Test Bed (MAGNET). This model configuration allows for hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) integration with microreactor automated control system (MACS) hardware in real time through a Python-based gRPC client. Real-time simulation of model performance with emulated hardware and communication delay suggests that under independent proportional-integral-derivative control of BOP model drum dynamics and downstream heat extraction, stable power load following is achievable. A slight delay in load following, filtering of high-frequency dynamics, and localized temperature fluctation suggest room for improvement through the development of higher-level control strategies. The simulated coupling of the MAGNET facility lays the groundwork for future digital twin analysis with a coupled MACS-MAGNET HIL demonstration.

Regulatory readiness for SMRs in Greece: An institutional gap analysis of a latent EU newcomer
abstract: Greece has begun to examine small modular reactors (SMRs) without holding any of the institutions of a declared nuclear program, which raises the question of whether it is a latent European Union (EU) newcomer rather than a conventional one. The 19 infrastructure issues of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Milestones framework are applied as a qualitative gap-analysis matrix, read through Euratom obligations, WENRA expectations, and comparator evidence from Poland, Estonia, and the United Arab Emirates, with issue-specific decision rules and named evidence anchors reported for every rating. Greece meets 4 issues, partially meets 8, and does not meet 7, so it is neither institutionally blank nor program-ready. EU-derived radiation protection, safeguards, and environmental permitting coexist with the absence of program ownership, a commercial nuclear framework act, financing architecture, and backend policy. Apparent readiness is therefore conditional rather than substantive, and the latent EU newcomer is proposed as an analytical category that separates inherited compliance from program-specific governance. The 12 to 15 year roadmap derived from the diagnosis is an institutional sequencing estimate, not a deployment forecast. Findings reflect Greek readiness as of mid-2026, including observer participation in the Nuclear Alliance meeting of 26 June 2026.

title: Cold energy recovery and reuse in artificial ground freezing for large-scale projects: Experiments and numerical modeling
abstract: Artificial ground freezing (AGF) is widely used for temporary support in subsurface construction. Current practice allows the frozen ground to thaw naturally once structural support is no longer required, leading to uncontrolled and inefficient dissipation of stored cold energy. Large-scale, multi-phase construction projects, where frozen-ground requirements shift across spatial locations over time, offer an opportunity to conserve energy by reusing residual cold energy across the site. This study proposes a cold-energy recovery and reuse framework for sequential AGF, in which cold energy from a decommissioned frozen zone is extracted and repurposed to pre-cool or freeze adjacent ground. The approach uses a heat transfer fluid loop to recover cold energy from frozen ground and transfer it to unfrozen ground. In this study, a laboratory-scale experimental setup is established, and a transient numerical model is developed, validated, and exploited to simulate cold-energy recovery and reuse under various operating and ground conditions. The results show that between 11– 15 MWh of energy can be recovered from frozen ground under representative field conditions, which can significantly reduce the energy utilized to cool adjacent unfrozen ground by up to 80%. Furthermore, the study reveals an imbalance between the energy recovered and utilized, arising from the predominance of sensible energy recovery in frozen ground and the combined sensible and latent energy storage in unfrozen ground.

NaBr and NaI–silica gel composites as novel sorbents for adsorption desalination and thermochemical energy storage driven by ultra-low-grade heat
abstract: Composite sorbent materials based on sodium bromide (NaBr) and sodium iodide (NaI) embedded in mesoporous silica gel are proposed as novel working pairs for adsorption heat transformation applications targeting ultra-low-grade thermal sources. Unlike widely investigated salt hydrates such as CaCl₂ and LiCl, alkali halides remain largely underexplored despite their favorable thermodynamic properties for low-temperature operation. Three salt loadings (20, 25 and 30 wt%) were synthesized and characterized, with the 30 wt% composites showing the best performance in terms of water uptake and cycling stability over six consecutive hydration–dehydration cycles below 80 °C. Equilibrium data, fitted through the Dubinin–Astakhov model, were used to assess thermodynamic performance under application-relevant boundary conditions. For adsorption desalination, the 30NaBrSG composite exhibited stable water vapor exchange Δw of 0.38–0.40 kg/kg. Crucially, while LiCl-based composites outperform 30NaBrSG at desorption temperatures above 60 °C, their equilibrium curves predict a significant reduction in water vapor exchange below 50 °C — a range where 30NaBrSG retains stable performance, making it uniquely attractive for ultra-low-grade waste heat valorization. For thermochemical energy storage, the 30NaISG composite achieved energy storage densities of 318–428 kJ/kg at desorption temperatures of 50–60 °C, competitive with chloride-based materials at low charging temperatures while offering reduced corrosion risk. These results establish NaBr/SG and NaI/SG as a new class of composite sorbents for renewable and waste heat-driven applications in a temperature range currently underserved by existing materials.

RC thermal model for evaluating heat transfer mechanisms in a seasonal snow storage unit
abstract: Snow is a renewable source of thermal energy which can be used for cooling purposes. In winter cities, seasonal snow storage is an underutilised yet promising technology for cold thermal energy storage. It offers potential to utilise local resources for urban building cooling and support hybrid district cooling systems, thereby enhancing energy security and carbon neutrality in cold-climate regions. Existing snow physics models are computationally intensive and designed primarily for avalanche forecasting or hydrological applications. To bridge the gap, this study aims to investigate methods for snowmelt modelling in the context of snow storage applications. A simplified three-layer resistor-capacitor thermal model is developed to capture the dominant heat transfer mechanisms in an insulated snow storage, without compromising computational efficiency. These include processes such as conduction through snow and woodchip insulation, surface convection, solar radiation and absorption, rain-induced flux, evaporative cooling and ground heat input with a multi-layer implicit finite difference insulation model. The model is simulated for a hypothetical snow storage facility in Estonian climate conditions. The resistor-capacitor framework successfully captured critical feedback loops between precipitation events and accelerated thermal conductivity changes in the insulation layer. Validated against reference simulation data for a sawdust-insulated snow storage, the model reproduced end-of-season retained volumes to within 0.8% (10 cm insulation) and 1.4% (20 cm insulation) of the Skogsberg-Nordell benchmark. This work provides a foundation for further development of purpose-built snow storage models and highlights the potential of snow as a sustainable thermal energy storage medium.

Thermoelectrically cooled Helmet with graphene-fabric composite liner for thermal management
abstract: Helmets are key parts of personal protective equipment (PPE) for workers and first responders in extreme environments. However, the metabolic heat generated by the head can accumulate within the helmet space, thus increasing the risk of heat stress in humans. This study presents a cooling helmet prototype that combines active thermoelectric cooling with a graphene-fabric composite liner. The prototype integrates a commercial thermoelectric cooler (TEC) with a graphene-fabric composite liner that functions as a heat spreader inside the helmet. Owing to graphene's high in-plane thermal conductivity, the liner spreads localized cooling from the TEC over a larger area, while the fabric substrate improves conformability and wearability. An incandescent bulb was used as a controlled and repeatable internal heat source, and the thermal responses were characterized using thermocouples and infrared thermography. In the transient heat-spreading test, under simultaneous heating and cooling, the liner temperature decreased by ~2.7 °C within 15 min and was approximately 5.2 °C lower than the heating-only condition. Infrared images showed that the graphene-fabric composite liner expanded the cooling-affected area to more than 12 times that of the TEC alone. Long-duration and climate-chamber tests further confirmed localized cooling near the TEC source and enhanced lateral cooling spread throughout the thermally conductive interlayers. Although the selected commercial TEC cooling capacity, along with the interfacial thermal resistance, slightly limited the overall performance, the results demonstrated the feasibility of using a TEC-assisted graphene-fabric heat-spreading liner for helmet thermal management and identified key directions for future optimization.

Theoretical Evaluation of Production Routes For 89 Zr: Cross Sections, Integral Yields, and Impurity Analysis
abstract: Zirconium-89 (89Zr) is an important radionuclide for immuno-PET imaging due to its relatively long physical half-life, which makes it suitable for tracking monoclonal antibodies and enhancing tumor detection. The present study provides a theoretical analysis of production routes for 89Zr. Excitation functions were calculated using the nuclear reaction codes EMPIRE and TALYS, employing equilibrium (Hauser-Feshbach) and preequilibrium (exciton) reaction models. The calculated cross sections were compared with available experimental data retrieved from the EXFOR database. Model performance was evaluated using three statistical deviation factors to assess the agreement between the theoretical predictions and the experimental measurements. In addition, cross sections of dominant impurity-producing reactions were analyzed to identify the optimal incident energy range that maximizes radionuclidic purity. Stopping powers were calculated using the SRIM code, and thick target yields were subsequently determined. Among the investigated production routes, the 89Y(p,n)89Zr reaction was found to be the most efficient and practical method for producing high-purity 89Zr, with an optimal proton energy range of 6.5 to 16 MeV.

title: Applicability of Regulatory Guide 1.99 Rev. 2 and ASTM E900-15 Embrittlement Trend Curves to High-Yield-Strength RPV Steels for Small Modular Reactors
abstract: This study evaluates the applicability of Regulatory Guide 1.99 Rev. 2 (RG 1.99) and ASTM E900-15—candidate models for future regulatory adoption—to SA508 Gr.3 Class 2 high-strength steel, a reactor pressure vessel material under considered for innovative small modular reactors. As a regulatory-basis pre-assessment, materials from a combined Korean and U.S. surveillance database were classified as Class 1- or Class 2-equivalent based on the unirradiated yield strength and ultimate tensile strength, and the residuals of each model were statistically analyzed by product form. Under RG 1.99 Position 1.1, the forging residuals of Class 2 were significantly lower than those of Class 1. This result reflects a conservative overprediction of the transition temperature shift and is therefore acceptable from a regulatory safety standpoint. Under RG 1.99 Position 2.1, the unit-specific chemistry factor recalculation eliminated all significant class differences. ASTM E900-15 yielded similar conclusions while resolving the high-fluence underprediction bias of RG 1.99. No combination of model and product form exhibited a nonconservative bias for Class 2 within the analyzed surveillance database. These conclusions are limited to retrospectively classified Class 2-equivalent materials. Therefore, direct validation using actual SA508 Gr.3 Class 2 materials remains necessary.

title: Numerical investigation of the effective heat transfer coefficient for red clay hollow bricks
abstract: This study presents a numerical investigation of the effective heat transfer coefficient in red clay hollow bricks, accounting for the combined effects of heat diffusion in the solid clay and natural convection and thermal radiation within the air-filled cavities. Heat conduction through the solid material is modelled analytically, while the convective transport in the cavities is solved using the Fast Boundary-Domain Integral Method. To enhance computational efficiency, the H 2 -approximation is employed to reduce the cost associated with the boundary-domain integral formulation. A parametric analysis is carried out for bricks with varying numbers of cavities and under different temperature boundary conditions, enabling a systematic evaluation of their influence on the overall thermal performance. The results provide new insights into the interplay between cavity geometry, boundary conditions, and effective heat transfer mechanisms, offering guidance for the design and optimization of energy-efficient building materials.

Data-Driven Discovery of Dimensionless Numbers and Governing Laws: A Scaling Technique for Nuclear Test Facility Design
abstract: New designs of water-cooled reactors that include thermal-hydraulic systems undergo safety analysis during the licensing process. For economic reasons and safety concerns, the systems are first tested at reduced-scale test facilities. A proper scaling ensures that dominant thermal-hydraulic safety-related phenomena are captured, even though unavoidable scale distortions occur. Some existing scaling methods, based on prior knowledge of the physical phenomena at stake, can quantify such distortions. They are limited, however, when the phenomena are nonlinear and coupled, or even not formalized as an equation. Dimensionless numbers play a central role in the scaling techniques, as their scale invariant properties help preserve the similarities between the reactor and test facilities. Building on this principle, this paper proposes a data-driven alternative to traditional scaling techniques. From a dataset of physical variables describing the phenomenon of interest, the method identifies a governing law that captures the dominant safety-related phenomenon. This governing law is expressed in terms of dimensionless numbers, which are physically meaningful combinations of dimensional variables and are automatically inferred by the algorithm. Based on a clear mathematical formulation, the proposed data-driven method combines advanced regression analysis with the constrained optimization of a cross validation–based objective function. Two variants are presented: one assuming that the output of the nondimensional governing law is known, and an extension in which this output is estimated. Both variants identify the dominant input dimensionless number as well as the explicit form of the governing law. As a proof of concept, the method was tested on a simulated dataset representative of single-phase natural circulation in a passive heat removal system.

Neutronic analysis of Yttrium Hydride temperature feedback coefficient in HALEU UMo fuelled microreactors
abstract: The emerging interest in terrestrial and space microreactors has highlighted the need for innovative core design solutions. Selecting an adequate moderator is challenging for solid-core microreactors operating at high temperatures, where few weight-efficient options are available. Yttrium hydride (YH) is an appealing candidate due to its high hydrogen content and superior high-temperature retention compared to other hydrides. However, YH exhibits a positive temperature feedback coefficient (TFC), posing a significant safety risk that could offset its advantages. This work studies the YH TFC across various configurations, from simple unit-cells (fuel pins, moderator pins, and layers) to a realistic space heat-pipe reactor (PoliMi-TASI design) modified with moderator layers. The TFC is broken down into contributions defined by the 4-factor and 6-factor formulas. Neutron transport is simulated employing a Monte Carlo approach via OpenMC. The thermal utilisation factor provides the predominant contribution to the TFC, leading to positive values for most analysed configurations. Furthermore, analysis of the moderated PoliMi-TASI design reveals the MTC depends not only on the moderator-to-fuel ratio but also on layer thickness: for a fixed ratio, thinner layers yield a smaller MTC. This analysis clarifies the physics behind the YH TFC, guiding future design improvements for the PoliMi-TASI reactor.

Oxygen substitution-induced structural, mechanical, and electronic evolution in UC1-xOx: A first-principles study for TRISO UCO fuel applications
abstract: Uranium oxycarbide (UCO) TRISO fuel kernels undergo irradiation-driven redistribution of carbon and oxygen, leading to the formation of oxygen-substituted carbide domains (U C 1 - x O x ). The intrinsic properties of these domains influence dimensional stability and fission-product behaviour. In this work, density functional theory calculations within the GGA + U framework were combined with special quasi-random structures (SQS) to investigate structurally disordered U C 1 - x O x with oxygen concentrations of 0–16 at.% on the anion sublattice. Occupation matrix control was applied to ensure consistent convergence of the uranium 5f states, and a 1 K-type antiferromagnetic configuration was used to examine magnetic behaviour. Oxygen substitution preserves the rock salt structure up to 16 at.% O and produces a non-monotonic lattice response, with an initial lattice contraction at low oxygen content followed by lattice expansion at higher concentrations. The formation enthalpy becomes increasingly negative with oxygen addition, indicating enhanced thermodynamic stability of the carbide lattice. Simultaneously, uranium magnetic moments increase, and the density of states at the Fermi level decreases, reflecting stronger 5f localization and enhanced U-O bonding interactions. Elastic calculations show that oxygen incorporation increases C 44 and shear-related moduli, while C 11 remains nearly unchanged, accompanied by a reduction in Poisson’s ratio. Overall, these results establish clear composition structure property relationships for U C 1 - x O x in the low-oxygen composition range relevant to irradiation conditions in TRISO UCO fuels.
