Modeling Decay Heat with a Simplified Depletion Chain in OpenMC
abstract: OpenMC can be used to computationally model depletion and produce estimates of decay heat. As an input to depletion simulations, OpenMC requires a depletion chain that details the nuclide transmutation pathways. The simplified CASL depletion chain was designed to track relatively few nuclides while still accurately modeling the effective neutron multiplication factor and nuclide number densities. However, the CASL chain dramatically underestimates decay heat due to the many nuclides it does not contain. In this work, we modify the CASL depletion chain to improve its accuracy while maintaining its computational efficiency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of adding pseudo-nuclides to the CASL chain, with each pseudo-nuclide capturing the behavior of a large group of nuclides. We further introduce “delay nuclides,” which dramatically improve the accuracy of decay heat estimates.

Low-Order Bessel-Type PID Dynamics in Lithium-Based Tritium Breeding and Heat Removal Systems
abstract: Lithium plays a dual role in deuterium-tritium (D-T) fusion systems by enabling tritium breeding in blankets and providing an efficient heat removal medium in liquid-metal components. However, most existing investigations treat neutronic behavior, jet thermohydraulics, and feedback control as largely decoupled layers, and there is currently no compact analytical framework that simultaneously links lithium-based tritium breeding, jet thermal response, and controller dynamics. In this work, we integrate nuclear cross-section data for D-T and lithium reactions with a reduced thermohydraulic model of a liquid lithium jet and an operator theoretic formulation of feedback control. The resulting blanket/jet configuration should be interpreted as a conceptual, reduced-order demonstration of how two Li-based subsystems can be coupled in a unified analytical framework rather than as a fully realistic reactor design in which an International Fusion Materials Irradiation Facility–type neutron source is directly attached to a self-sufficient power blanket. We derive a low-order model describing jet thermal expansion under deuteron beam loading and demonstrate that a continuous-time proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller, expressed in operator form, can be locally embedded within a family of Bessel-type differential operators acting on the tritium inventory tracking error. The results suggest that lithium-based breeding and heat removal systems admit low-order, PID controllable dynamics that can be interpreted in terms of localized Bessel modes, providing a compact analytical framework for guiding future controller design and blanket/jet optimization.

title: ASNR Work on the Nuclear Criticality Safety of TRISO Fuel
abstract: The French nuclear energy landscape is currently experiencing a renewal, including innovative reactor designs. Among innovative reactor concepts, some use TRi-structural ISOtropic (TRISO) particle fuel. The implementation of such new fuel presents a challenge for nuclear criticality safety (NCS) assessment during operations in nuclear power plants, in manufacturing and reprocessing facilities, as well as during transportation. To support future NCS assessments, the newly established French nuclear safety authority (ASNR), resulting from the merging of the former authority and its technical support organization (IRSN), needs to compute its own criticality safety standard values for TRISO fuel. These values, as well as sensitivities to various physical parameters relative to TRISO fuel, will be necessary to perform NCS assessments and to define the NCS parameters to be ensured during fuel fabrication. This paper presents a summary of the main studies performed at the ASNR regarding the NCS assessment of TRISO fuel throughout 2025.

title: Supervisory Control of Nuclear Power Plants Using Finite State Automata
Core Deformation Reactivity Analysis Using a Neutronics–Thermal-Hydraulics–Structural Mechanics Coupled Method for FFTF LOFWOS TEST #13
abstract: Accurate evaluation of reactivity feedback caused by core deformation—including core bowing and radial expansion—during power increases in sodium-cooled fast reactors requires comprehensive modeling of the interactions among neutronics, thermal-hydraulics, and structural mechanics in the core. Conventional evaluation methods for core design studies often lack accuracy due to oversimplified modeling. To address this, Japan Atomic Energy Agency has developed a high-fidelity evaluation method that couples multiple analysis codes to simulate these complex phenomena. In this study, the evaluation method was applied to analysis of the Fast Flux Test Facility (FFTF) loss of flow without scram (LOFWOS) TEST #13 using the experimentally measured core flow rate and inlet temperature as boundary conditions. The coupled analysis successfully reproduced the non-monotonic temporal variation of net reactivity observed experimentally. Sensitivity analyses of core design parameters related to core structural mechanics revealed that the S-shaped bowing of fuel assemblies, driven by specific contact conditions, is the primary mechanism of negative feedback. Notably, initial assembly pad gaps and pad compressive stiffness significantly influence the feedback magnitude and timing, highlighting the critical impact of core structural design. These results demonstrate that the developed coupled analysis method is a valuable tool for the design and licensing of fast reactors, supporting both safety and economic competitiveness.

title: Development and Deployment of a Machine Learning–Based Predictor of Moisture Carryover in Boiling Water Reactors
Monte Carlo investigation of spectral modifications induced by a W/Al selective filter in 6 MV flattening filter-free photon beams
abstract: This study investigated the impact of a selective tungsten/aluminum energy filter [SF (W/Al) ] on the spectral characteristics of 6 MV Flattening Filter-Free (FFF) photon beams. The analysis included the energy spectrum and fluence, pinpointing the photon and electron energy ranges that contribute most to energy deposition on the water phantom surface. Monte Carlo (MC) simulations were performed using GATE for a 10 × 10 cm 2 field size at a source-to-surface distance (SSD) of 100 cm. The simulation model was validated against Varian phase-space file (PSFs) data using the gamma index criterion of 2%/2 mm. Excellent agreement was obtained, with gamma pass rates reaching 99% for percentage depth-dose (PDD) curves and 98% for lateral dose profiles. The spectral analysis demonstrated that FFF beams substantially increased the contribution of low-energy particles to surface dose deposition compared with flattened (FF) beams. Relative changes of 139.68 ± 2.18% for photons and 60.35 ± 2.71% for electrons, relative to the FF beam, were observed within the energy ranges of 0.49–0.525 MeV and 0.28–0.315 MeV, respectively. After introducing the SF (W/Al) , the corresponding relative changes decreased to 114.76 ± 1.82% for photons and 38.24 ± 1.76% for electrons within the same energy ranges, corresponding to relative reductions of 17.84% and 36.64%, respectively. These findings demonstrate that using a dedicated filter to control low-energy fluence selectively is an effective strategy to reduce surface dose and improve the clinical safety of FFF photon beams while preserving their therapeutic properties.

title: Fuel Cycle Features of RFBB Fast Reactor with Silicide Fuel and Lead Coolant
abstract: The development of innovative fast nuclear reactor systems offers a reliable and sustainable solution to the world's growing energy demand. In particular, breed-and-burn systems that use uranium as an efficient fuel could help significantly reduce nuclear waste and eliminate the need for expensive fuel reprocessing plants. The purpose of the present paper is to design a core for a rotational fuel-shuffling breed-and-burn reactor with silicide fuel and lead coolant (RFBB-SL). Compared to other breed-and-burn reactor designs, RFBB offers a more practical pathway by combining high fuel burnup with manageable material constraints and operational flexibility. We reveal the core’s fuel cycle features by analysing reactor burnup parameters through neutronic calculations. First, core simulations fully loaded with natural uranium fuel were conducted to assess the feasibility of achieving a critical equilibrium state. The configuration and fuel enrichment for the start-up core were determined based on this equilibrium state condition. A start-up core fuelled by uranium silicide with enrichments ranging from natural to 12% could operate with different shuffling intervals for 750 MW th and 250 MW th power reactors. The worth of the six peripheral control rod assemblies was between -5% and -2.8% for both cores. Heat removal analyses showed that a small, low-power start-up core for an RFBB-SL design is viable and that the maximum temperatures of the fuel, cladding, and coolant in the hottest channel can remain below their safety limits for a 250 MW th power reactor. Hence, the reactor could achieve a subcritical state even in a one-rod stuck scenario. Based on the obtained results, a practical RFBB-SL core combining slightly enriched uranium in silicide fuel and lead coolant under appropriate operating conditions can achieve an equilibrium state and sustain breed-and-burn mode for a long period.

title: Refined Multiphysics Coupling Analysis in Optimized Isotope Production
abstract: ABSTRACT Aiming to balance efficient Californium-252 (Cf-252) production with reactor safety, this study investigates the Ultra-high Flux Lead Bismuth Reactor (UFLBR) and develops six progressive core schemes: no target, targets only, targets with moderator, layered target-moderator arrangement, spectrum-optimized layered arrangement, and spectrum-optimized arrangement based on neutron unidirectional flow. A neutronics-thermal-hydraulics-structural mechanics coupling framework is used to evaluate Cf-252 yield, heavy-nuclide conversion, temperature distribution, stress, and deformation. Results indicate that targets alone produce negligible Cf-252 in the fast spectrum, whereas moderation and layered spectrum regulation greatly enhance production. The spectrum-optimized layered scheme achieves the highest conversion rate of 1.67%, but also induces severe local power and thermal-mechanical risks. By introducing neutron unidirectional flow, thermal neutron backflow is effectively suppressed while favorable target-region spectra are retained. This scheme yields 11.7 g Cf-252 per fuel cycle with a 1.22% conversion rate, about 3.94 times that of the HFIR C78 campaign. Meanwhile, maximum fuel, cladding, coolant, and target temperatures remain below safety limits, and deformation stays within engineering margins. The proposed iterative optimization strategy provides a general reference for isotope-production scheme design and feasibility assessment.

title: Experimental Investigation of Persistence Spectra, Spatial Correlations, and Vortex Structures in a Randomly Packed Pebble Bed Using Time-Resolved PIV
Comparative SRIM Investigation of Lutetium-Based Alloys and Lead for Alpha-Particle Shielding Applications
abstract: Due to increasing concerns regarding the toxicity, high density, and environmental limitations of lead-based shielding materials, heavy rare-earth elements such as lutetium (Lu) are gaining attention as potential alternatives for radiation protection applications. In this study, the interaction of 10 MeV alpha particles with pure lutetium and two engineered lutetium-based alloys (Lu–B and Lu–W) was investigated using SRIM simulation. Key shielding parameters, including electronic and nuclear stopping powers, projected range, longitudinal straggle, and lattice displacement damage, were evaluated and compared with those of pure lead (Pb). The Lu–W alloy exhibited a projected range of 36.1 μm, slightly lower than that of Pb (36.5 μm), indicating superior stopping efficiency against 10 MeV alpha particles. In contrast, the Lu–B alloy achieved approximately 21.5% weight reduction while maintaining acceptable shielding performance. Radiation damage analysis further revealed that Lu–W produced the highest vacancy concentration due to enhanced collision cascades, whereas Lu–B showed comparatively reduced defect formation, suggesting improved radiation tolerance. Despite its lower atomic number compared with lead, lutetium demonstrated excellent attenuation behavior and structural stability, highlighting its potential as a lightweight and environmentally safer shielding material. These findings suggest that lutetium-based composites are promising candidates for advanced aerospace systems and next-generation nuclear shielding technologies.

title: Training and inter-laboratory comparison of TL/OSL techniques within the Korea retrospective dosimetry network
abstract: ABSTRACT In this study, education and hands-on training on thermoluminescence (TL) and optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) techniques were provided to Korea retrospective dosimetry network members who were not familiar with the techniques, followed by a blind inter-laboratory comparison (ILC) to evaluate the effectiveness of the training and the participants’ practical performance. Smart bands (MiBand4) were used as blind test samples, and surface-mounted resistors and display glass extracted from the devices were applied to dose reconstruction. Each participating institution performed beta source calibration, dose reconstruction, and uncertainty evaluation using its own TL/OSL reader. For most reported results, the uncertainty intervals included the reference dose. In the En-value analysis based on averaged results, all cases satisfied the acceptance criterion except for the resistor result from one laboratory. Several outliers were identified, and additional analysis of the raw data suggested that low signal intensity, possible bias in beta dose-rate calibration, reader condition, and sample-to-sample variation contributed to these deviations. The results showed that the trained participants were able to follow the overall workflow and perform dose reconstruction using their own measurement data.

title: Frequency-dependent in-cabinet seismic demand for NPP cabinets using shell-based efficient FE model
Verification of the FLUKA code for RPV neutron dosimetry and radiation damage based on the NUREG/CR-6115 PWR benchmark problem
abstract: Accurate neutron dosimetry is fundamental for the safety assessment of pressurized water reactor (PWR) pressure vessels (RPVs). To meet U.S. NRC Regulatory Guide 1.190 verification mandates, this study systematically evaluates the FLUKA Monte Carlo code using the deep-penetration NUREG/CR-6115 benchmark. Three customized user routines were developed for high-precision spatial-energy sampling across 157,500 core nodes, secondary fission suppression, and 1/8 symmetry specular reflection. Combined with regional importance biasing, highly efficient variance reduction was achieved. Calculated RPV fast neutron fluxes align within ±5% of MCNP reference solutions, while calculated-to-expected (C/E) ratios for activation reaction rates converge within 0.97–1.03 relative to DORT references. These results strictly satisfy RG 1.190 criteria, confirming FLUKA's high reliability for RPV neutron dosimetry. To demonstrate engineering applicability, an integrated RPV degradation assessment was conducted. A single simulation run explicitly quantified 3D fast neutron flux, macroscopic DPA maps, depth-dependent primary knock-on atom (PKA) energy spectra, and a 40-year temporal isotopic activation evolution. Ultimately, this study validates FLUKA for complex shielding analyses and showcases its robust potential for multi-scale radiation damage evaluations.

title: Experimental study on disturbance wave characteristics of the bottom annular liquid film in a horizontal narrow rectangular channel
abstract: The disturbance wave characteristics of annular flow in narrow rectangular channels are crucial for the accurate prediction of dry-out type critical heat flux in nuclear reactor fuel assembly systems. To investigate the wave evolution mechanisms and associated characteristics of annular liquid films in a horizontal narrow rectangular channel, the adiabatic air-water flow experiments were carried out using a test section with dimensions of 30mm×1mm×1000mm. An electrical-based liquid film sensor matrix for narrow rectangular geometries was developed to enable high-frequency acquisition of liquid film thickness time-series data on the bottom wide wall. The mean amplitude and frequency of the disturbance waves on bottom wide wall of the horizontal narrow rectangular channel were quantitatively extracted by a threshold identification method. Experimental findings reveal that the mean disturbance wave amplitude exhibits a pronounced upward trend as the superficial liquid velocity rises. Meanwhile, the disturbance wave frequency demonstrates a positive correlation with superficial liquid velocity and increases moderately with superficial gas velocity, without exhibiting a strong linear dependence on gas velocity in the present narrow rectangular channel geometry. Based on these observations, predictive correlations for both amplitude and frequency of disturbance waves within horizontal narrow rectangular ducts were formulated and subsequently validated against both the present experimental dataset and independently published data from existing literature. The validation outcomes confirm that prediction deviations for both models remain bounded within ±25%, demonstrating satisfactory accuracy and practical applicability in engineering contexts. The present study advances the mechanistic understanding of interfacial fluctuation dynamics and disturbance wave development in annular flows confined within rectangular geometries, while simultaneously furnishing a theoretical foundation for assessing dry-out risks and guiding the safety design of compact nuclear reactor fuel assemblies.

Cam-driven mechanisms approaching the ideal cycle and internal extended surfaces on MTD beta-type Stirling engines without external heat exchangers
abstract: This study assesses MTD (Moderate Temperature Differential) beta-type Stirling engines without external heat exchangers, where heat exchange occurs through the internal chamber surfaces. Its originality lies in the combined analysis of two design strategies not previously assessed together for this engine type: Fourier-based cam-follower mechanism approaching the ideal Stirling cycle, and internal surface enhancement using radial fins and longitudinal cylindrical pins with complementary piston and displacer geometries. Engine performance was evaluated with a second-order non-isothermal model based on mass and energy conservation, using air at atmospheric charge pressure as the working fluid, for a temperature differential of 280 K, rotational speeds from 50 to 1000 rpm, and convective heat transfer coefficients (h) from 100 to 500 Wm −2 K −1 . Performance is reported as specific work ratios relative to the sinusoidal engine with conventional chambers. Cam-driven engines with conventional chambers are preferable at low speeds and h > 200 Wm −2 K −1 , with a maximum specific work ratio of 1.25 at 50 rpm and h = 500 Wm −2 K −1 , whereas at high speeds sinusoidal engines with enhanced internal area perform best, with the pinned geometry yielding 3.11 at 1000 rpm and h = 100 Wm −2 K −1 . At intermediate speeds, the preference depends on h, with surface enhancement becoming increasingly beneficial as speed increases. Accounting for regenerator pressure drop through an uncoupled analysis preserves these trends but narrows the region where cam-driven kinematics remains advantageous. The results identify, for the MTD beta-type engines considered, when near-ideal cam-driven kinematics or internal surface enhancement provides the greater relative specific-work benefit.

Modeling of microbubble-induced fouling mitigation and self-cleaning on heat transfer surfaces
abstract: Fouling is a significant problem in milk processing and routine cleaning is essential. Microbubbles (MBs) have attracted increasing attention for various cleaning applications and experimentally proved effective in mitigating milk fouling during thermal processing. However, no models have been proposed for characterizing the interactions between MBs and fouling deposits. In this study, computational fluid dynamics models derived from a milk fouling kinetic model and a sphere bubble dynamic model were developed. The models were fitted and validated by skim milk fouling experiments conducted using a spinning disc apparatus at different disc rotational speeds with MBs generated by circulating milk through a venturi-type injector. Three experimental scenarios were modeled: no milk circulation, milk circulation with and without MB infusion. The predicted fouling thermal resistances align well with the experimental values, with strong agreement observed at high disc rotational speeds under which the induced swirl flow becomes dominant over the circulating flow. The dominance of swirl flow promotes MB accumulation near the disc, thereby enhancing their impact on fouling removal. The developed models confirm that MB collapse is the main mechanism causing fouling removal and can serve as a reliable tool to estimate the efficiency of MB-induced self-cleaning in industrial thermal processes.

title: Numerical study on defect formation mechanisms in V-groove welding induced by torch offset-driven molten pool instability
abstract: Weld seam offset is an inevitable consequence of automated welding systems, yet its effect on internal defect formation through molten pool thermal and fluid dynamics remains poorly understood. This study presents a three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) investigation of the heat transfer and flow field evolution in V-groove gas metal arc welding (GMAW) under torch offset conditions of 0 mm, 1 mm and 2 mm, where the 0 mm condition serves as a reference case revealing the burn-through behavior resulting from excessive heat concentration at the root. A high-fidelity numerical model was established and validated against experimental non-destructive evaluation (NDE) results including radiographic testing (RT) and ultrasonic testing (UT) for the 1 mm and 2 mm offset conditions, with CFD-derived defect geometries shown to correspond directly with characteristic NDE signal patterns. The results demonstrate that although both offset conditions induce initial thermal asymmetry, the resulting molten pool dynamics differ fundamentally. Under the 1 mm offset, a transient clockwise circulation develops following biased droplet impingement but subsequently stabilizes into a quasi-symmetric thermal and flow field, restoring uniform solidification behavior. In contrast, the 2 mm offset sustains a persistent unidirectional circulation throughout the welding process, consistently directing convective heat transport toward the near-side bevel and maintaining the far-side wall near the solidus temperature. This thermally driven asymmetry governs side-wall lack of fusion, while a void entrapment mechanism driven by the asymmetric pool dynamics accounts for the trapped porosity and root defects observed experimentally. The findings provide a physically grounded thermal framework for understanding how offset magnitude translates into distinct defect morphologies in automated V-groove welding.

Flow boiling heat transfer of propane (R290) inside tubes. A review of experimental databases and correlations
abstract: Heat pumps will be central in the path towards decarbonizing the heating sector, highlighting the importance of low-GWP refrigerants to meet climate-neutrality targets by 2050, with propane (R290) representing one of the most promising long-term alternatives. The boiling heat transfer coefficient (HTC) is a key parameter in the design of heat exchangers for these devices. This review provides a comprehensive and comparative analysis of experimental studies and correlations for boiling HTC inside smooth and microfin tubes with propane. A total of 2889 experimental datapoints from 32 studies were analysed, covering inner diameters from 0.96 to 9.43 mm, mass velocities from 50 to 600 kg/m 2 -s, saturation temperatures from -35 to 44 °C and heat fluxes from 2.48 to 227 kW/m 2 . The effects of the main parameters governing the boiling HTC are systematically analysed. A tube-diameter/flow-pattern classification is employed to assess the performance of 29 boiling HTC correlations for smooth and microfin tubes. Additionally, 68 dryout datapoints are compared with 7 correlations. The results demonstrate that no single correlation of boiling HTC provides consistent accuracy across the range of operating conditions considered. Instead, correlation performance is shown to depend strongly on tube diameter and flow pattern. The best-performing correlations are identified by analysing their performance across different operating domains using standard accuracy metrics. Furthermore, a lack of experimental data on the influence of oil during boiling, particularly inside microfin tubes, as well as on the effect of reducing the inner diameter in conventional tubes was identified, highlighting the need for further research in these areas.

title: Design and Annual Performance Assessment of A Line-Focus Fresnel Lens Solar Collector Under Local Solar Conditions
abstract: Abstract A large share of global energy demand is the heat demand. In Türkiye, a significant portion of this demand originates from low and medium-temperature industrial applications. For reducing CO2 emissions, it is important to use solar thermal systems to meet the industrial heat demand as much as possible. However, the high installation costs of traditional concentrated solar thermal systems limit their adoption in industrial applications. To address this challenge, this study develops a cylindrical Fresnel lens solar collector, which offers a cost-effective, low-carbon alternative for industrial heat applications below 250°C. For this purpose, a coupled optical?thermal modeling framework which combines wavelength-dependent ray tracing with receiver heat-loss analysis and annual simulations based on typical meteorological year data is employed. The developed system is then evaluated for different provinces in Türkiye. Under normal incidence, the collector achieves an optical efficiency of 49.57% and a geometric concentration ratio of 14.43. Annual performance results indicate that an 8 m collector array with a 330 L storage tank can reach operating temperatures of up to 180°C under representative summer conditions.

A framework for probabilistic risk assessment of nuclear power plants coupled with data centers using causal analysis
abstract: The rapid growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is driving an unprecedented increase in electricity demand from Data Centers (DCs). Nuclear Power Plants (NPPs) are increasingly being considered as reliable low-carbon energy sources capable of supplying the required baseload power. However, the coupling introduces new operational interdependencies that may affect the overall plant safety and reliability, which are not captured by traditional Probabilistic Risk Assessment (PRA) frameworks. This work proposes a Bayesian Network (BN)-based framework for the risk assessment of NPPs coupled with DCs. The BN structure explicitly captures the causal relationships from component failures and cyber-attacks to initiating events and their progression to core damage, consistent with standard PRA logic. The BN parameters are estimated through both literature-informed engineering judgment and data-driven learning from data generated with a system simulator integrated within a Monte Carlo Simulation, while epistemic uncertainty is propagated with probabilistic parameter modeling. The framework enables the estimation of the Core Damage Frequency (CDF) increase due to coupling, identification of the most impactful failures and cyber-attacks, and extraction of the most probable causal paths that lead to core damage. Application to multiple coupling configurations involving Pressurized Water Reactors (PWRs) and Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) demonstrates the capability of the approach to provide both quantitative risk estimates and interpretable insights, supporting risk-informed design and operation of integrated NPP-DC systems.

title: Acquisition-specific motion deblurring in X-ray radiography using a dual-acquisition residual-domain framework
abstract: Motion blur in X-ray radiography can obscure fine anatomical structures and lead to repeat imaging. This study presents a dual-acquisition residual-domain framework that combines a normal-dose motion-blurred image with an auxiliary low-dose fast-acquisition image for acquisition-specific blur-kernel estimation and restoration. The estimated kernel and residual-domain input are used for residual-domain Richardson–Lucy (RL) restoration, followed by gain-controlled restoration and detail recovery. The method was evaluated through simulation studies using line-pair and ex vivo human dental phantoms and controlled C-arm experiments using an anthropomorphic chest phantom. Across 20 repeated ROI-based evaluations, dental phantom SSIM increased from 0.87 ± 0.02 to 0.94 ± 0.02 and PSNR from 33.81 ± 0.22 to 35.70 ± 0.26 dB, with higher SSIM and PSNR than Wiener, non-blind RL, and total variation–regularized RL deconvolution. In C-arm experiments, BRISQUE decreased from 19.40 to 9.51 in the upper-spine case and from 31.03 to 19.98 in the lower-spine case, while SNR remained near normal-dose levels. CNR remained comparable to the normal-dose level in the upper-spine case and increased in the lower-spine case. The framework improved visibility under small-amplitude, approximately linear motion blur, although sequential acquisition introduces registration and additional-exposure considerations.

Neutronic and depletion analysis of a 5 MWth heat pipe cooled reactor with TRISO fuel and fluoride salt using MCS
abstract: This study investigates the neutronic performance, depletion behavior, and safety characteristics of a 5 MWth Sejong TRISO-fueled molten salt filled heat pipe cooled reactor. It employs tristructural-isotropic (TRISO) uranium-oxycarbide fuel, LiF-BeF 2 (FLiBe) molten salt coolant, and a beryllium-oxide (BeO) reflector. The Monte Carlo code MCS is used for three-dimensional burnup analysis over a 5 year cycle. The core adopts a pebble bed with 21,600 TRISO-embedded pebbles and 665 sodium heat pipes, achieving passive heat removal and a thermal spectrum that enhances neutron economy and control drum effectiveness. Depletion under all-control-drums-out shows smooth reactivity decrease from k-eff starting at 1.06075 at beginning-of-cycle and reaching 1.01138 at end-of-cycle. This is accompanied by limited spectral hardening and flattened radial power distributions, indicating benign fuel utilization and power peaking. Parametric studies clarify the roles of FLiBe, BeO, and carbon in shaping the spectrum, demonstrating pronounced BeO and carbon moderation and F-19 resonance absorption effects on the intermediate energy flux. Safety analyses of drum rotation, drum seizure, and shutdown rod insertion failure confirm sufficient control margin and fault tolerance. The combination of passive heat pipes, integrity fuel and coolant, and redundant shutdown systems supports a safety-driven microreactor concept.

title: Vacuum leak detection and localization based on remote handling and laser spectroscopy coupling
abstract: For the leakage detection and localization in the vacuum chambers of future fusion reactors, this paper proposes a design method based on the coupling of remote operation and laser spectroscopy. By using a pulsed laser to ablate solid targets, the design excites leaked gases in the environment and generates a spectrum. Spectrometers and detectors are used to collect information on atomic spectral lines in the area, enabling leak detection. A remote-operated robot is then used to transport the spectrometer to different areas of the vacuum chamber for continuous sampling. The precise location of the leak can be determined based on the distribution trends of the leak gas concentration gradient. To fully validate the feasibility of leak location, this paper analysis the diffusion behaviour of the leaking gas under different gas types and background pressures using finite element software. The results show that the mass fraction distribution of the leaking gas within the vacuum chamber exhibits a monotonically decreasing spatial gradient along the primary direction of diffusion. This gradient exhibits a distinguishable decay pattern under various leakage gas conditions (air and water vapor) and at different background pressures, demonstrating the feasibility of using concentration gradients to locate leaks.

title: Diffusion of Tritium in Li4SiO4 Crystal: A first-principles study
abstract: Li 4 SiO 4 is a promising solid-state tritium breeder material due to its high lithium density and low tritium retention. Under irradiation, lithium vacancies are the predominant defects formed, influencing tritium release behavior. This study systematically investigates tritium adsorption and diffusion in different lithium vacancy configurations within Li 4 SiO 4 using first-principles calculations. The investigation covers three stages: first, adsorption and migration characteristics within vacancies; second, adsorption sites and migration behaviors after escape; finally, diffusion coefficients for both processes. The results show maximum adsorption energies of -1.597 eV (within vacancies) and -1.638 eV (after escape). The minimum migration energy barriers within the three vacancy configurations are 0.231 eV, 0.129 eV, and 0.091 eV, with corresponding optimal escape barriers of 0.236 eV, 0.373 eV, and 0.766 eV. The optimal migration pathways were identified as T Ⅳ →T Ⅲ →O37, P Ⅴ →P Ⅲ →P Ⅱ →O19, and O Ⅴ →O Ⅳ →O30. At 900 K, diffusion coefficients are 1.63×10 -7 m 2 /s (within vacancies) and 2.96×10 -8 m 2 /s (escape), with the former being approximately one order of magnitude higher, indicating greater mobility within the vacancies. The results provide an atomistic understanding of the individual stages of tritium migration and can indirectly inform subsequent breeder material design and fabrication.

title: Main control board fire risk assessment considering loss of control
abstract: Main control board (MCB) fires in the main control room (MCR) can significantly affect nuclear power plant fire risk because panel damage may degrade plant monitoring, control functions, and operator response. Although NUREG-2178 explicitly includes loss of control (LOC) in the MCB fire event tree, practical fire probabilistic safety assessment (PSA) applications have often treated LOC through simplifying assumptions because explicit evaluation criteria are lacking. This study proposes a practical definition and evaluation procedure for LOC and applies it to a reference nuclear power plant fire PSA model. LOC is defined as a condition in which required operator actions cannot be performed because instrumentation information or control functions needed to execute operating procedures become unavailable due to fire-induced panel damage. The procedure evaluates LOC using the diagnostic feasibility and action feasibility of required operator actions while considering both primary and secondary cues. From quantified minimal cut sets, 145 representative panel damage-human failure event (HFE) combinations were evaluated, and only two were classified as LOC. Risk quantification shows that assuming LOC for all scenarios with no loss of habitability (LOH) yields conservative MCB fire risk estimates, whereas incorporating secondary cues and explicit LOC evaluation produces more technically balanced results.

Enhanced momentum dissipation in bubble column reactors: design and experimental analysis of swirl flow optimization
abstract: This study aims to develop a new momentum-dissipation system for Bubble Column Reactors (BCRs). The operation of BCR primarily depends on various two-phase flow factors, including geometric configurations (e.g., gas injection), operational conditions (e.g., temperature, pressure, and liquid and gas flow rates), and gas–liquid mass transfer. However, the bubble injection geometry plays a crucial role and influences other parameters, such as the gas void fraction and interfacial area. In this study, a bubbly flow rig was built, primarily featuring a bubble-injection mechanism that induces swirl in gas–liquid bubbly flows. Different open-channel configurations were designed to dissipate momentum, which is essential for reducing the liquid’s rotary motion while promoting bubble swirl within the static liquid. This allows for the measurement of liquid-phase velocity field and a qualitative assessment of bubble–liquid slip behavior. Accordingly, a PIV technique was successfully applied to single and two-phase systems in a laboratory setting. Water and air served as the working fluids. The experiments aimed to assess the impact of four fins with different geometries, including simple holes and open channels, on velocity vectors across the horizontal plane and, consequently, on liquid momentum. Additionally, the velocity fields with swirl gas injection were compared to those without air injection to evaluate the behavior of interacting fluids. Results show that 90° and 180° open channels produce significantly greater momentum dissipation than the straight channels and simple hole fins. Among the four geometries, the 90° open channel achieves the highest dissipation, outperforming the 180° configuration. Two-plane PIV is used to experimentally map the hydrodynamics of a swirl-injection bubble column reactor equipped with a collar with fins, providing new insight and design guidance for swirl-driven multiphase reactors.

Lilith: An Enduring Plutonium Critical Assembly
abstract: The Jezebel plutonium critical assembly, operated from 1954 to 1977, has been a benchmark for validating nuclear data, particularly for fast 239Pu fission, over the past 70 years. However, since its disassembly decades ago, there have been issues with Jezebel’s legacy, including incomplete documentation, limited opportunities for long-term system parameter observations, and a lack of means to test new advancements using the same assembly.Given these challenges, there is a pressing need for a new, enduring benchmark plutonium critical assembly capable of providing ongoing validation and data collection. Such an assembly would assist in nuclear data validation, reactor kinetics, dosimetry, and many other areas of nuclear research while helping maintain U.S. leadership in plutonium research.The concept of Lilith, a new enduring plutonium assembly currently under development, is introduced as a potential solution to address these needs. The design of Lilith focuses on a simple geometry, low uncertainties, and a planned lifetime of 100 years. Lilith will use a cylindrical design, which will allow for easier manufacturing and greater flexibility in adjusting its components over time.The enduring nature of the system will enable ongoing validation of nuclear data, analytical methods, dosimetry, reactor kinetics, and material properties across decades. This would also provide the opportunity for new measurements of reactor kinetics parameters using neutron noise methods, and long-term criticality studies, while tracking changes in the plutonium system over time. This work highlights the importance of such a system for future advancements in nuclear technology and the need to ensure the continued availability of such research capabilities.

title: Variance Budgeting for Probability Tables in the Unresolved Resonance Region
abstract: Resonance self-shielding in the unresolved resonance region (URR) is driven by the variance of the cross-section distribution, which probability tables are designed to represent. This paper identifies two mechanisms by which standard nuclear data processing distorts this variance. First, the multiplicative normalization used to enforce mean consistency between the probability table and the evaluated cross section inadvertently rescales the variance. Second, when the evaluated cross section carries resonant structure within a probability table energy bin, the transport code sees both this within-bin structure and the full probability table fluctuation content, double counting the variance. A variance-preserving affine transformation is derived that enforces the evaluated mean while preserving the variance and is extended to a per-reaction variance-budgeting methodology applicable when the evaluated cross section carries within-bin structure. The method is implemented in NJOY/PURR and validated through a controlled 235U transmission study. Integral benchmarks using the HEU-MET-INTER-011 suite show that standard processing overpredicts the URR self-shielding reactivity worth by approximately 150% relative to the variance-preserved result, demonstrating that the effect is quantitatively significant for the ENDF/B-VIII.1 235U evaluation.

abstract: In fusion reactors, large angle neutron scattering reactions significantly affect neutronics calculations, especially for the reactor blanket. Previous studies highlighted discrepancies in evaluated nuclear data, emphasizing the necessity for benchmarking large angle scattering cross sections. While the authors’ group previously developed a benchmark experimental system using the foil activation method, gaseous elements like fluorine could not be validated. This study introduces a new method that uses solid compounds containing the gaseous element to indirectly evaluate its large angle scattering cross section. Applying this method, benchmark experiments for fluorine were performed using graphite and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) as the targets, and the fluorine contribution was extracted. The results were then compared with MCNP5 simulations using different nuclear data libraries and an excellent agreement was observed for ENDF/B-VIII.0 and JEFF-3.3. Future work will aim to reduce experimental uncertainties.

Site selection procedure in Germany: Considerations on a depth limit for a high-level radioactive waste repository in claystone
abstract: The depth of a repository for high-level radioactive waste is an important aspect with respect to both long-term and operational safety. In contrast to the minimum depth, no relevant constraints are given in the German legal regulations for a maximum value. To define such a limit, various safety-related aspects of claystone host rock are considered. This evaluation takes place within an early stage of the German site selection process. The available data are evaluated, and the respective assessments are discussed, ranging from aspects of construction and operation of the repository to its post-closure period. Furthermore, tunneling experience in relevant claystones is evaluated. It is concluded that a favorable depth is neither the maximum depth of existing underground excavations nor the maximum achievable with available techniques. Instead, it is the depth for which experience indicates that under the current assumptions, the extended operation of a nuclear waste repository can be well conducted without jeopardizing operational and long-term safety. The major argument for limiting the repository depth is robustness, which means that the repository as a whole can be operated safely, requires no extraordinary measures like resources, techniques, or time, and can be built with well-established techniques. It can be summarized that those requirements are unlikely to be met for a repository in claystone at depths greater than 1000 m.

Solving the Nonperturbative Neutron Noise Equation by Monte Carlo Methods
abstract: Power reactor noise, which describes the fluctuations of the neutron flux around its mean value, is a valuable tool in nuclear reactor monitoring. In recent years, several numerical tools have been developed to solve the Fourier-transformed Boltzmann equation that underpins neutron noise theory in the frequency domains. Among the proposed computational strategies, Monte Carlo methods are motivated by the need to perform high-fidelity simulations of the neutron noise field.The numerical treatment of the noise equations usually relies on the “orthodox” linearization, a first-order approach that consists of neglecting the product of the perturbed quantities. This approximation is known to fail for the higher-order harmonics of the noise fields induced by mechanical vibrations, a case of interest in real-world applications.In view of these considerations, in this work we propose a strategy to directly solve the noise equation in the frequency domain using a nonperturbative approach, i.e. without resorting to linearization. This strategy is naturally suited to Monte Carlo methods, but also extends to deterministic approaches. We present the general theory and the full implementation; furthermore, a proof of concept is carried out on a few relevant benchmark configurations, along with parametric studies and performance analysis.In the investigated applications, the nonperturbative Monte Carlo algorithm is shown to be both more accurate and efficient than its linear theory counterpart. Besides, an intermediary “upward frequency” approximation is introduced as a beneficial tradeoff between the accuracy of nonperturbative noise computations and the reliability of linear theory noise computations. Overall, the proposed strategies show great potential for the simulation of the noise resulting from mechanical vibrations.

title: Financing Nuclear Decommissioning in Ghana: An Evaluation of Public-Private Partnership Models
abstract: This review looks at how Ghana can use public-private partnership (PPP) models to obtain long-term funding for the decommissioning of its current research reactor and upcoming nuclear installations. Ghana’s current legal framework would benefit from strengthened institutional capacity, clearer financial assurance procedures, and the establishment of dedicated decommissioning funds.This review uses a comparative legal institutional analysis alongside international best practices from other countries and lessons learned from Ghanaian industries. The paper outlines a phased set of policy recommendations by identifying the technical, financial, regulatory, and sociopolitical risks associated with nuclear decommissioning. These recommendations include the creation of a national coordinating institution, long-term capacity building initiatives, and legal reforms to integrate decommissioning finance within nuclear safety regulations.The results demonstrate that well thought out PPP mechanisms can improve safety performance, lower uncertainty, and bring Ghana’s nuclear program into line with global best practices. These mechanisms are bolstered by transparent fund governance, robust regulatory oversight, and innovation-driven contracting.

How factual knowledge reshapes the determinants of public acceptance of high-level radioactive waste disposal facilities: An integrated risk perception and TPB (Theory of Planned Behavior) framework
abstract: Public acceptance of high-level radioactive waste disposal facilities (HLRWDFs) remains a critical barrier to nuclear waste governance worldwide. Although the knowledge-deficit model predicts that greater public knowledge raises acceptance, empirical evidence in the HLRWDF context is limited and contradictory. This study examines how objective knowledge moderates the determinants of HLRWDF acceptance through an integrated framework combining the Risk Perception Paradigm and the Theory of Planned Behavior. Survey data from 1,898 nationally representative South Korean adults were analyzed using hierarchical multiple regression and moderation analysis, with respondents stratified into below- and above-average groups using a seven-item factual knowledge scale. Across the full sample, trust and attitude were the strongest positive predictors, whereas objective knowledge exerted a significant negative direct effect, directly challenging the knowledge-deficit model. The low-knowledge group was driven primarily by trust and perceived risk, while the high-knowledge group was additionally shaped by personal norms, national benefits, and positive emotions, with social norms exerting a suppressive effect. Moderation analysis confirmed that knowledge significantly moderates the effects of both social and personal norms. These findings indicate that public engagement strategies for HLRWDF siting should be differentiated by knowledge level, and provide theoretical evidence against the linearity assumption of the knowledge-deficit model.

Monte Carlo Simulation of Medical Isotopes Production by Irradiation of nat U and 232 Th Targets with P, α, 9 Be and 12 C
abstract: Advances in nuclear technology and modern medicine have driven the development of a variety of radiopharmaceuticals, labeled with medical isotopes, that play an important role in the treatment and diagnosis of various diseases. With the decommissioning of high-flux nuclear reactors, high-energy proton-induced spallation reactions on thorium are now becoming an alternative and the most commonly used method for large-scale production of isotopes such as 225Ac and 227Th.However, investigations into isotopes produced by irradiating thorium and uranium targets with other types of particles remains relatively limited. Additionally, the thickness of the conventional 232Th targets used for isotope production is significantly less than the proton range, resulting in the underutilization of a large portion of the proton beam.This study aims to identify the most effective incident projectile and materials for the production of 225Ac, 223Ra, 225Ra, 227Th, and 99Mo via the bombardment of the thick target with accelerated protons, α-particles, 9Be, and 12C to increase the supply of 225Ac or other medical isotopes.This work considers a water-cooled spallation target that consists of a mixture of heavy water and thorium metal particles (232Th + D2O) or uranium metal particles (natU + D2O). This design not only addresses the heat dissipation issue of the target material, but also simultaneously enhances the isotope yield. The Monte Carlo transport code PHITS (particle and heavy ion transport code system) was employed to calculate and compare the effects of the different beam energies, types of incident projectiles, and target materials on the isotope yields, secondary particle flux distributions, and energy deposition.The predictions indicate that, compared to the widely investigated proton bombardment schemes on thorium targets in existing studies, irradiation with 9Be achieves the highest isotope yields, as it facilitates the production of more high-flux neutrons or other secondary particles to drive isotope breeding, but it also leads to increased energy deposition. Moreover, under identical incident particle conditions, thorium targets generally exhibit a higher isotopic yield than uranium targets, while also demonstrating lower energy deposition, making them more efficient for isotope production.In conclusion, when adopting a water-cooled spallation target, 9Be bombardment of a thorium target is more likely to achieve higher efficiency in isotope production within a relatively short irradiation time.

title: Generation of Small Droplets for Molten Salt Reactor Fluoride Fuel Salt Sampling
abstract: The analysis of molten salt samples benefits significantly from using small, uniform samples. One such analysis technique that requires these samples is the diamond-based microfluidic alpha spectrometer (DiMAS), which relies on depositing very small quantities of molten fluoride salts on its surface to enable high-resolution alpha spectrometry. To facilitate this, a pneumatic droplet generator for molten fluoride salt has been developed. The system employs a fast-acting solenoid to pulse argon gas through a heated vessel, allowing it to dispense droplets through a diamond orifice. A parameter study was performed to identify the optimal settings for producing small, consistent droplets. The results indicate that the system can reliably produce salt droplets around 1 mm in diameter. Further analysis of the findings was undertaken to explore design changes and operating conditions that could further improve performance for future implementation with DiMAS and other analysis techniques.

title: Atmospheric Dispersion of Radioactive Materials Modeled by Stochastic Differential Equations
Influences of coexisting seawater components on Am and Eu adsorption amounts by Fe 3 O 4
abstract: The stagnant water at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station (1F NPS) is thought to be under neutral pH conditions and containing alpha (α) nuclides and seawater components. Therefore, it is necessary to examine the influences of seawater components that may interfere with adsorption of α nuclides as competing ions under neutral pH conditions. In this study, the influences of coexisting cation components, sodium (Na), calcium (Ca) and magnesium (Mg) on the adsorption amounts of americium (Am) and europium (Eu) by magnetite (Fe3O4) was examined in batch tests. It was found that the influences of these components on Eu adsorption amounts by Fe3O4 decreased in the order of Ca > Mg ≈ Na, indicating that Ca is main competing component. After 7 days immersion under a liquid-solid ratio of 100 mL g–1, Eu adsorption amounts by Fe3O4 decreased only 10% when initial concentration of Eu was 1.0 × 10–3 Eq L–1 and concentration of Ca was increased 1000 times from 2.5 × 10–5 Eq L–1 to 2.5 × 10–2 Eq L–1. A similar test conducted using low concentrations of Am indicated that the Am adsorption amounts by Fe3O4 decreased only 7% when initial concentration of Am was 1.8 × 105 Bq L–1 and concentration of Ca was increased 100 times from 2.5 × 10–5 Eq L–1 to 2.5 × 10–3 Eq L–1. Therefore, we concluded that Am could be removed without having to significantly increase the amount of Fe3O4 even when there are coexisting seawater components.

Fast Thermal-Hydraulic-Neutronic Model to Simulate Transient Behavior of an Aqueous Homogeneous Reactor
abstract: Mo 99 is a widely used radioisotope in nuclear medicine, particularly for producing Tc 99m . The Aqueous Homogeneous Reactor (AHR) is a promising method for producing Mo 99 . This paper presents a coupled neutron point kinetics and thermal-hydraulics model for ARGUS, a kind of AHR, which utilizes uranyl sulfate liquid fuel in the reactor core. This research aims to develop an accurate and computationally efficient model to predict the transient behavior of ARGUS. The effects of transient reactivity insertion on the overall reactor performance have been studied. Analysis of the reactor's performance demonstrates the effectiveness of its safety features, which are attributed to negative feedback mechanisms such as temperature feedback and void feedback. When power output rises, there's a rapid increase in void formation, which generates strong negative feedback. In 1$ step reactivity insertion, the power initially increases to 366.5 kW but after 10 seconds returns to 78 kW due to void feedback. This model can contribute to developing an optimized control system for AHRs.

title: Design and development of a 65 kA/50 μH multi-layer spiral air-core pulse inductor for the CRAFT Quench Protection System
abstract: Superconducting magnets in Magnetic Confinement Fusion (MCF) devices are subject to severe quench risks during high-current operation, demanding a highly reliable Quench Protection System (QPS) to ensure device safety. As a critical passive component in the artificial zero-crossing QPS, the high-current pulse inductor must maintain stable performance under extreme conditions, including high peak current, large rise rate (d i /d t ), and strong electromagnetic impact. To satisfy the 65 kA/50 μH requirements of the Comprehensive Research Facility for Fusion Technology (CRAFT) and eliminate the magnetic saturation in conventional iron-core inductors under high-current pulses, this paper proposes the design and development of a multi-layer spiral air-core pulse inductor. Firstly, structural parameters are designed using analytical calculations and electrical parameters are validated correspondingly. Furthermore, its electromagnetic, mechanical, and thermal performances are verified via Finite Element Method (FEM) under 65 kA pulse excitation. A prototype is manufactured and tested by LR parameter measurement and LC resonant pulse discharge tests. The results demonstrate that the pulse inductor achieves 50.74 μH inductance and 5.9 mΩ resistance at 500 Hz, with negligible temperature rise and minor structural deformation under 65 kA pulses. Stable operation and high reliability are verified through more than 100 pulse tests. This work provides an engineered and practical solution for high-current pulse inductors applied to QPS of fusion superconducting magnets.

title: Compton scattering-based localization and activity reconstruction of radioactive sources in low- and intermediate-level waste drums
abstract: Traditional Segmented Gamma Scanning (SGS) and Tomographic Gamma Scanning (TGS) reconstruct activities in low- and intermediate-level radioactive waste drums by assuming radionuclide distributions, which often differ from actual source distributions and lead to inaccurate detection efficiencies and large activity reconstruction errors in practical nondestructive measurement applications. This paper proposes a Compton scattering-based method for direct radioactive-source localization and activity reconstruction in a waste drum with unknown source number and positions. Valid events consisting of one Compton scattering interaction and one photoelectric absorption interaction in the first two layers of a CZT detector were used for source localization, followed by efficiency calculation and activity reconstruction. For single sources emitting 0.662 and 1.333 MeV gamma rays, the localization error was less than 1 cm. For multiple sources, distinguishability depended on source spacing. When the spacing was 6 cm or larger, individual sources were resolved, with localization errors generally below 1 cm. When the spacing was less than 6 cm, multiple sources were reconstructed as one broadened peak; the resulting localization deviations ranged from 1 to 2.3 cm, with a maximum of 2.26 cm. For distinguishable sources, the reconstructed activity error was within ±5%, whereas unresolved multi-source cases showed a maximum error of -15.96%.

Thermoelastic effects on material temperature in hydrogen/oxygen premixed flame–material interaction: A numerical study
abstract: Accurate prediction of the material temperature field during hydrogen flame heating is essential for assessing thermal loading and material integrity. In the present work, a thermo-mechanically coupled numerical model is employed to investigate transient flame–material interaction between a laminar hydrogen/oxygen premixed strained flame and a solid material. Particular attention is paid to the influence of the thermoelastic (Gough–Joule) effect on the material temperature evolution. The results show that the Gough–Joule effect acts as an additional heat source and accelerates the heating process. By using flame with high strain rate, neglecting the Gough–Joule effect results in noticeable error in the predicted time required for the material to reach the yield-strength condition. The relative importance of the Gough–Joule effect is found to increase monotonically with flame strain rate. These findings indicate that thermoelastic coupling can substantially influence transient flame–material interaction under rapid hydrogen-flame heating and should be considered when accurate prediction of the material temperature field is required.

title: Flow-Directed Oil Cooling of an Outer-Rotor PMSM for Electrohydraulic Applications
abstract: The continuous torque of compact outer-rotor permanent-magnet synchronous machines (PMSMs) driving hydraulic pumps for hydraulic actuation is often limited by winding temperature. This paper proposes an improved flow-directed oil-cooling arrangement that supplies 24 axial stator channels and eight end-winding jets from a common pump. A nonlinear hydraulic-network model is used to select cooling-path dimensions and estimate flow distribution, while effective heat-transfer coefficients derived from analytical correlations and physically motivated assumptions are applied in a computationally efficient three-dimensional thermal finite-element model. The concept is implemented and validated in an outer-rotor PMSM prototype originally rated at 7 kW and 22.3 Nm. At 7 kW, 3000 rpm, and an oil flow rate of 1 L/min, the mean measured winding temperature decreased from approximately 155 °C with the original oil-circulation arrangement to 92 °C, while the model predicted 97 °C at the corresponding sensor-equivalent location. The improved cooling arrangement enabled continuous motor operation at 150% of the original rated torque at 3.7 L/min, with a mean measured winding temperature of approximately 91 °C and a corresponding model prediction of 96.5 °C. The validated model predicts that the winding temperature at the sensor-equivalent location reaches 155 °C at approximately 52 Nm, or 230% of the original rated torque. The combined experimental and sensitivity results support a broader design principle: moderate cooling distributed over several thermally critical surfaces can be more effective than maximizing the local HTC over a limited area.

Optimization of Chemical Etching Conditions and Evaluation of Detection Performance for the DX-22 Solid-State Nuclear Track Detector
abstract: This study optimized the chemical etching conditions of the newly developed UV-polymerized poly(allyl diglycol carbonate) detector DX-22 and evaluated its detection performance. An orthogonal design followed by single-factor experiments was used to investigate the effects of NaOH concentration, etching temperature, and etching time on track morphology, track density, and background counts. The optimal conditions were 6.5 mol/L NaOH, 65 °C, and 8 h. Under these conditions, etched alpha-particle tracks showed clear contours, relatively uniform morphology, predominantly elliptical shapes, low background, and a track density of 201.8 tracks/mm 2 . CR-39 was used as a reference detector for indoor radon measurements. DX-22 and CR-39 showed consistent spatial track-density trends, with relative area errors of 6.46%-12.93% between fitted response curves. The field comparison was not intended as an absolute radon calibration, and standardized radon-chamber calibration and uncertainty evaluation remain necessary for quantitative dosimetric application. Overall, DX-22 demonstrated promising potential for radon monitoring and radiation protection.

Parametric liquid-cooling design for Li-ion batteries based on flow regime analysis
abstract: This study presents a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model to predict transient temperature distributions in a prismatic lithium‑ion polymer (LiPo) battery cooled by forced water circulation through four distinct cooling circuits during constant‑current discharge. A novel methodology emphasizes the influence of dimensionless parameters on thermal and electrical responses, addressing a gap in existing literature and improving understanding of battery cooling strategies. The cooling circuit is modeled as a recirculating system, reflecting practical implementations rather than the common open‑loop assumption, and capturing the additional instability and complexity inherent to recirculation. Transient electrochemical–thermal behavior is simulated using Newman’s pseudo‑2D approach, treating porous electrodes as a collection of equal‑sized, isotropic, homogeneous spherical particles. The model couples electrochemical dynamics with conjugate heat transfer in the cell and cooling circuit. Validation was performed in a controlled chamber using experimental measurements and infrared thermography during discharge; simulated temperature, state of charge, and voltage curves were compared against experimental data. Results show strong agreement between simulations and experiments, demonstrating the model’s reliability for predicting LiPo battery behavior and their cooling circuits. Key battery parameters — effective capacity, specific energy density, specific heat capacity, electrical conductivity, and specific thermal capacity — were carefully estimated and validated to provide reliable reference values for modeling batteries of the same type. By systematically analyzing the role of relevant parameters —temperature, Reynolds number, flow velocity, heat flux, and pressure— on battery–cooling interactions, the model analyses their relative effects and provides actionable guidance for optimizing thermal management strategies in battery applications. This research provides practical value for battery designers and engineers developing systems that integrate batteries, facilitating improved efficiency, performance and safety.

MAEO: Scalable Multiobjective Animorphic Ensemble Optimization for large-scale optimization applications
abstract: Multiobjective optimization remains challenging for many scientific and engineering problems due to the need to balance convergence, diversity, and computational efficiency across high-dimensional objective landscapes. This work presents the Multiobjective Animorphic Ensemble Optimization (MAEO) framework, a parallelizable ensemble strategy that unifies state-of-the-art evolutionary algorithms within an island-based architecture, overcoming the limitations of relying on a single optimizer, as implied by the No Free Lunch theorem. MAEO uses a parameter-free hypervolume indicator for island performance assessment and a strict Pareto-rank-based individual scoring formulation that incorporates crowding distance and nadir-point proximity to ensure consistent selection pressure within each front. The framework is initiated using four algorithms (NSGA-III, CTAEA, AGEMOEA2, SPEA2) and evaluated through extensive benchmarking on 12 DTLZ/ZDT functions under 36 dimensionality settings using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with both hypervolume and inverse generational distance metrics. Results show that MAEO achieves balanced convergence–diversity performance, outperforming or matching some of the leading multiobjective optimization algorithms across different benchmark problems. To demonstrate practical applicability, MAEO is applied to the equilibrium-cycle optimization of a small modular nuclear reactor. Eight discrete design variables (seven assembly enrichments and burnable absorber configuration) and three objectives (levelized fuel cost, peak soluble boron concentration, fuel cycle length) are optimized under two safety constraints. The algorithm carried out 80,000 evaluations using computer simulations. MAEO identifies core designs that lower both the levelized fuel cost and the peak boron concentration, while preserving fuel cycle length and meeting all safety constraints. These findings highlight MAEO’s effectiveness for high-dimensional and large-scale engineering optimization.

Code to code comparison of a dba sequence in a generic iPWR between MELCOR and ASTEC codes
abstract: Nowadays, several integral Pressurised Water Reactor (iPWR) designs are close to the licencing stage since they are based on the well-established technology of large Light Water Reactors (LWRs), incorporating evolutionary design features aimed at enhancing the inherent safety of the plant through integral configurations and adoption of passive safety systems. However, a sound demonstration of iPWRs’ capability to address Severe Accident (SA) should be carried out for a comprehensive safety review process. In this context, the international scientific community is increasingly focusing on assessing SA integral codes in simulating typical iPWRs’ phenomenology during postulated accidental scenarios. The Horizon Euratom project “Safety Analysis of SMR with Passive Mitigation strategies – Severe Accident” (SASPAM – SA), coordinated by ENEA, investigates the applicability, the transfer of the large LWR knowledge and know-how to iPWRs, in view of SA and Emergency Planning Zone (EPZ) licensing analyses needs. In this regard, the present work carried out within the SASPAM-SA project presents a comparative analysis between the SA codes MELCOR and ASTEC. The goal of the study is to evaluate the capability of the codes in simulating the dominant thermal–hydraulic phenomena during a postulated Design Basis Accident (DBA) scenario in a generic 300 MWe iPWR, considering the full availability of the reactor passive safety systems. The code-to-code benchmark highlights the main consistencies and possible discrepancies between the codes.

First-Principles Evaluation of Thermal Neutron Scattering and Cross Sections in Beryllium Oxide
abstract: This work addresses the long-standing uncertainty in the thermal neutron scattering description of beryllium oxide (BeO), a key moderator and reflector material in advanced reactors. Conventional evaluations rely on semi-empirical phonon models that misrepresent the phonon gap and high-energy optical modes, which can bias the calculated cross sections and transmission. Here, density functional–theory phonon spectra with two exchange-correlation functionals are used to generate self-consistent thermal scattering laws, neutron cross sections, and transmission through realistic BeO slabs.The resulting elastic and inelastic cross sections remain compatible with standard evaluations and measurements, yet reveal sizable model-dependent differences at low temperature and in the vicinity of the phonon gap, where inelastic cross sections can differ by more than a factor of 2. At reactor-relevant temperatures, the ab initio–based data reproduce the measured total cross section and the reference evaluation within a few tens of percent, and predict the thermal energy transmission through 15-cm BeO slabs between roughly 60% and 70%.These results show that ab initio lattice dynamics provide a robust route to update the BeO scattering data when experimental phonon information is limited, and they establish a direct quantitative link between microscopic phonon properties and macroscopic moderation and shielding performance in nuclear systems.

title: TRISO-ATOPS: A Mechanistic Source Term Model for Gas-Cooled Reactors
abstract: Source term modeling for TRistructural ISOtropic (TRISO) fuel has been performed for previous reactor designs, but few are available in the open literature. Thus, there is a need to develop a simple, versatile, and mechanistic model of fission product release and transport in gas reactor cores that can be applied to a variety of reactors through user inputs and reactor-specific radionuclide inventories. To meet this need, the TRISO Analysis Tool for Predictive Source terms was developed. This model calculates the release of the key safety-important fission products by diffusion through the kernel, silicon carbide, and graphite based on fuel and graphite temperatures in the reactor under normal operation. These releases from the fuel enter the coolant where some can plate out on cooler surfaces. A cleanup model is included for designs with a coolant purification system for removing fission gases. This initial distribution of fission products in the reactor serves as an initial condition for potential releases under postulated accident conditions. From this initial condition, the model calculates the fission product release for any transient temperature profile, and the fission product releases can then be used to assess radiological dose to the workers and the public using conventional radiological dose tools. Data on the diffusion of fission products is based on historic German TRISO experiments and the more current Department of Energy advanced gas reactor TRISO fuel development program. The example cases in this work demonstrate the flexibility of the model.

Theoretical interpretation of current-to-flux ratio in low-energy neutron transport
abstract: A physical value, current-to-flux ratio (CF ratio), is known in neutron transport theory. In boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT), it is recognized to be a very crucial design index. However, even now, the theoretical interpretation of the CF ratio is not yet clear. As detailed in the present paper, if considering the current (angular) distribution, in a low-energy slowing-down field of neutron in such as BNCT, in the exit region of the moderator assembly (beam shaping assembly (BSA)), it was found that the current distribution of neutrons shows a cosine distribution. In the present study, a new mathematical model was proposed and by numerical experiments the availability was thoroughly discussed. As a result, observation of the cosine distribution in the exit region of the moderator assembly was found to be caused by a rapid and linear change of the flux intensity at around the exit surface. In addition, the CF ratio was theoretically proved to be less than 2/3, meaning that in BNCT the regulation, CF ratio > 0.7, cannot be realized if employing a flat surface at the exit of the BSA.In conclusion, in the low‑energy neutron transport of such as BNCT, if the CF ratio is fixed, the current distribution in the exit region of an assembly like a BSA is fixed, and it becomes a cosine distribution. This result is quite crucial and valuable especially in the neutronics design of BNCT as well as in other neutron transport applications in nuclear engineering.
