title: Assessment of gas capture via tunnel ventilation following an underground chemical explosion
abstract: In October 2023 an underground chemical explosive test, Physics Experiment 1-A, was executed in a tunnel at the Nevada National Security Site. This test was part of a series of multi-physics experiments focused on enhancing nuclear explosion monitoring techniques. Part of the experiment included monitoring ga movement. As part of the facility operations, there were two events during the first five days of the experiment where the ventilation system was operated to purge gases from the facility. These events afforded an opportunity to evaluate the mass of gases emitted to the atmosphere during these ventilation events and compare to the total mass produced during the experiment. This provides a basis for estimating the fraction of gas produced in an underground test that might be expected to be released through natural and engineered pathways. Using several approaches, an estimate of between 1 and 9% of the total gas produced by the experiment was captured and discharged to the atmosphere during these events. The percentage of gas captured was nominally equal to the percentage of the plume volume that was bisected by the facility tunnels and represents a similar fraction to that assumed as potential releases for underground nuclear tests.

title: Thermal Creep Behavior of Precipitation-strengthened Wrought FeCrAl Cladding Tube at Different Temperatures
abstract: FeCrAl alloys are recognized as an excellent candidate material for accident-tolerant fuel cladding tubes. However, thermal creep behaviors of FeCrAl alloy cladding tubes and the associated microstructural evolution have not been comprehensively investigated. This work addressed this gap by evaluating the axial thermal creep behavior of precipitation-strengthened wrought FeCrAl alloy cladding tubes at the temperatures of 360°C and 475°C, respectively. Creep test results indicated that there was a threshold stress for the FeCrAl alloy cladding tubes, because the thermal creep strain rate increased rapidly when the thermal creep stress was larger than a specific stress level. Consequently, a power-law thermal creep constitutive model with a threshold stress was established according to the thermal creep test results. Creep failure was primarily caused by shear stress. In addition, microstructural analysis indicated that the grain size of the FeCrAl alloy cladding tubes initially increased and subsequently decreased with increasing applied stress. Both the dislocation density and the proportion of low-angle grain boundaries demonstrated a decreasing trend with increasing stress levels.

title: CFD Simulation of Hydrodynamics in a Pulsed Sieve Plate Column Using ANSYS Fluent: An Integrated Multiphase Modeling Approach
abstract: This study presents a Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) investigation of a Pulsed Sieve Plate Column (PSPC) using ANSYS Fluent, combining a Eulerian-Eulerian two-fluid model with an empirically modified drag correlation, a Population Balance Model (PBM), and a Random-Forest-based surrogate model coupled with a Genetic Algorithm (GA) for pulsation parameter optimization. The modified drag correlation accounts for droplet swarm and Strouhal-number effects under pulsation and is presented as a calibrated closure rather than a first-principles result. Simulations were compared against experimental data from a laboratory-scale column (internal diameter 50 mm, height 1.5 m) operating with a kerosene-water system. The CFD-PBM framework reproduced dispersed-phase holdup within 5% of experimental values for the tested Dc = 50 mm kerosene-water system and the Sauter mean droplet diameter (d32) within 6-9% of the measured values, outperforming the standard Schiller-Naumann drag model, which exhibited holdup deviations of 12-21%. A dimensionless Pulsation Efficiency Number (PEN) is introduced, and a generalized form (PEN*) incorporating plate spacing and column diameter is derived using Buckingham π analysis to eliminate the geometric inconsistency of the original composite metric. The GA-Random-Forest optimization framework predicts operating conditions capable of improving the overall mass transfer coefficient by 23.5% (95% prediction interval: 18.1-28.9%) relative to the baseline operating conditions.

title: Practical Validation of Zeolite-Modified Cementation for Real Intermediate-level Liquid Waste under Waste Acceptance Criteria (WAC)
abstract: Intermediate-level radioactive liquid waste (ILLW) generated at the Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute (KAERI) requires robust solidification for safe long-term disposal. Although bituminization has been widely applied, its limitations in mechanical stability and long-term durability necessitate alternative approaches, while conventional cement waste forms remain constrained by high porosity and limited capacity for immobilizing mobile radionuclides such as cesium. This study evaluates the performance of zeolite-modified cement waste forms using real ILLW obtained from the KAERI Radioactive Waste Treatment Facility (RWTF). Zeolite was incorporated at 3, 5, and 10 wt.% and the specimens were assessed in accordance with domestic Waste Acceptance Criteria, including compressive strength, thermal stability, and radionuclide leaching behavior. All specimens satisfied regulatory requirements, maintaining compressive strengths above 3.44 MPa after thermal and immersion aging. Zeolite addition significantly reduced Cs-134 and Cs-137 release and increased leachability indices beyond the regulatory threshold. The 10 wt.% specimen exhibited the lowest effective diffusivity, while 5 wt.% provided comparable performance with improved material efficiency. These results demonstrate that zeolite-modified cementation is an effective and practically applicable approach for enhancing cesium immobilization in real ILLW, supporting its use in long-term radioactive waste disposal.

title: Field- and Filter-dependent tissue-maximum ratios for 6 MV photon
abstract: Accurate characterization of the tissue–maximum ratio (TMR) is important for beam modelling and dosimetric verification, particularly for flattening-filter-free (FFF) beams and non-reference fields. This study characterized TMR for 6 MV flattened (FF) and FFF photon beams from an Elekta Versa HD across square fields from to . Central-axis water-phantom measurements using PTW microDiamond and Semiflex detectors were compared with GATE/Geant4 Monte Carlo simulations. For the reference field, simulated percentage depth-dose values agreed with measurements within 1 percentage point between 10 and 30 cm depth. TMR increased systematically with field size beyond the buildup region. At 10 cm depth, measured TMR increased from 0.6887 to 0.8215 for FF and from 0.6829 to 0.8130 for FFF. At 20 cm, the corresponding ranges were 0.4432-0.6016 and 0.4366-0.5830. Monte Carlo-measurement differences remained within 0.011 TMR units. The ratio also increased with field size, confirming that it is not field-size invariant outside reference geometry.

title: Combined Effects of Joule Heating and Nonlinear Thermal Radiation on Stagnation-Point Flow of a Second-Order Nanofluid over an Exponentially Stretching Surface
abstract: This article examines the stagnation-point flow and thermal transmission of a second-order nanofluid over an exponentially stretching surface, incorporating Joule heating and a magnetically induced field. The mathematical model includes nonlinear thermal radiation, activation energy, zero mass flux, and thermal slip boundary conditions to capture realistic transport phenomena. Using similarity transformations, the governing PDEs are reduced into coupled system of nonlinear ODEs, which is subsequently solved numerically using the MATLAB BVP4C solver. The findings demonstrate that the induced magnetic field is enhanced by raising the magnetic field parameter and magnetic Prandtl number. Higher estimations of the second-order fluid parameter lead to increases in both the skin friction and the heat transfer rate, highlighting the role of fluid elasticity in thermal transport. Further, the fluid temperature rises with increasing thermophoresis, Brownian motion, and thermal radiation parameters, whereas the concentration field declines with higher Lewis number and concentration slip parameter. The proposed model is applicable to magnetohydrodynamic cooling systems, liquid-metal nuclear reactor cooling, electromagnetic casting, polymer extrusion, and thin-film coating processes, providing valuable insights for improving heat transfer and thermal management in advanced engineering systems.

title: Application-specific performance assessment of desiccant wheel design and operational parameters for industrial drying and HVAC dehumidification
abstract: Moisture removal with desiccant wheels is widely recognized for being effective and energy-efficient across various applications. Their effective dehumidification and energy efficiency performance is influenced by a combination of design and operational parameters. However, most existing studies investigated different parameter sets and employed diverse performance indicators and definitions, making it difficult to determine whether parameter assessments obtained for one application remain applicable to another. This study investigates how application-specific expectations for performance indicators affect the assessment of desiccant wheel design and operational parameters. Industrial drying and heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) dehumidification applications are considered as two illustrative applications with different requirements for process outlet air conditions, and the analysis is conducted under hot/humid and cool/humid process inlet air conditions, corresponding to 30 °C/85% relative humidity (RH) and 20 °C/85% RH, respectively. The results show that regeneration inlet air temperature produced the largest overall performance variations, followed by wheel rotation speed and regeneration air velocity, although their effects differed among dehumidification performance, dehumidification coefficient of performance (DCOP), and sensible energy ratio (SER). Regarding design parameters, in drying application, the process/regeneration area ratio ( φ ) exhibited the highest normalized Morris sensitivity for most of the evaluated indicators. Under the HVAC–hot/humid baseline, coating amount exhibited the highest normalized Morris sensitivity for most indicators, whereas the process-to-regeneration area ratio was more influential for most dehumidification-related indicators under the HVAC–cool/humid baseline. The results show that performance objectives determine the desired directions and relative priorities of the KPIs, which may lead to different preferred parameter settings within the investigated conditions and parameter ranges. The results offer valuable insights into the design and operation of desiccant wheels, aiming to enhance their application in fields such as HVAC systems and industrial drying processes.

Multi-physics study on the thermal response of a coupled inductive power transfer pad
abstract: Inductive power transfer is an important technological alternative for charging infrastructure, crucial for accelerating the future adoption of electric vehicles. The magnetic components of an inductive charging pad generate inevitable thermal losses, which, if not properly managed, can exceed the pad’s safe operating temperature. Accurate simulation of thermal responses is therefore essential for evaluating the pad’s suitability for real-world applications. However, despite the requirement for coupling in real-world power transfer applications, many existing studies have only considered the thermal response of a single pad; The effects of coupling on the thermal response of an IPT system are unknown. This paper presents an experimental and multi-physics numerical study that aims to address this gap by investigating the influence of coupling on the thermal response of an IPT system. The numerical framework comprises three coupled modules: electro-magnetic, fluid dynamics, and solid heat conduction. Results indicate that a closely coupled IPT system experiences a more severe thermal response, with temperatures up to 100% higher than a single pad at the same operating current. This is due to increased thermal losses from magnetic coupling, and a reduced capacity for heat dissipation due to the surrounding geometric and thermo-fluid boundary conditions. In all cases, convection and radiation heat transfer mechanisms are significant and must be considered. Under constant pad separation, increasing the power transferred increases the discrepancy between a single pad system and an equivalent coupled IPT system. Under constant power transfer, increasing the pad separation decreases the discrepancy between a single and equivalent coupled IPT system. The key conclusion of this study is that the effects of coupling on the thermal response of an IPT system are significant, and must be considered to properly design and analyse an IPT system for long-term use in key aspects of charging infrastructure.

Empirical Modeling and Flow-Regime Analysis of Condensation Heat Transfer in Micro/Minichannels
abstract: Over 2,000 condensation heat-transfer data points from 29 sources in micro/minichannels were compiled for empirical modeling and flow analysis. The new condensation heat transfer correlation fits 87% of the data within ±50%. The correlation was also successfully tested using available flow-regime-specific data, indicating the equations’ universal applicability across all flow regimes. A sensitivity analysis revealed that buoyancy and gravitational forces were dominant during condensation in micro/mini channels. A flow analysis based on widely reported flow maps showed that condensing flows in micro/minichannels were predominantly in the transition and annular (wavy and smooth) regimes. Confinement or surface-tension effects were detected even in tubes with diameters over 1.5 mm. Apart from these few exceptions, in general, macrotube effects were dominant in most minichannels with diameters greater than 200 μm.
